column121: Multiple aircraft inbound to SAF airport. Radar controller managing sequence by vectoring aircraft into the valley north of SAF. Audio quality of the frequency was serviceable until Aircraft X. When the aircraft was approximately 15NW of the airport; the pilot was given descent to 13000 feet. The read back was barely intelligible. After the preceding aircraft was reported to have arrived; radar controller issued the approach clearance. Once again; barely intelligible. The spot where the receiver quality issues present; is around SAF airport and the valley to the north of it. With high terrain and volume of traffic in the area; the frequency is an urgent safety issue.

column121: Aircraft X was in the pattern doing full stop taxi backs on rwy XX. They exited at Taxiway 1 and I issued them instructions to taxi via Taxiway 2 to rwy XX and to cross rwy XY and rwy XZ. Numerous aircraft were in the pattern on XX both touch and goes and full stop. Aircraft Y was on a right downwind for rwy XZ; just entering the downwind; the only aircraft  assigned rwy XZ. I anticipated there was ample time for Aircraft X to cross rwy XZ prior to Aircraft Y turning base. The pattern was complex with a mix of performance in the aircraft  needing constant control; and extending upwinds/downwinds on rwy XX to make it work. I got tunnel vision on rwy XX ops. My ground controller (new CPC) spoke up and said 'he should have probably had held short' and I scanned my rwy XX ops thinking they meant that; when they clarified they meant rwy XZ; I saw Aircraft X clearing the rwy XZ hold short bars with Aircraft Y short final; I am not sure if they were passed the displaced threshold. I did not observe when Aircraft X entered the runway reference my aircraft  on final. They were also unable to say when the threshold was crossed. Neither pilot said anything.That taxi route usually takes just a moment and I anticipated they would clear of the intersection well before my arrival as the arrival was only entering the downwind when I issued the instructions. Aircraft X must have taken closer to several minutes to cover the distance. We were short staffed this day and I was working Controller in Charge (CIC) as well as local.My tunnel vision led to me not verifying Aircraft X's position during my rwy XZ operation. I was shocked at the slow speed of the taxi. I will recommend to my fellow controllers that we issue paper stops during these increased volume sessions when we have control of both runways. I also spoke with my ground controller and mentored them to be assertive if they suspect their local controller has missed something; even if they aren't CIC qualified. Perhaps in future configurations like today we should have the CIC only combined with ground.

column121: While we were less than 1000 feet off the ground ATC cleared Aircraft Y for take off from runway 15R. The ATIS did not say anything about using 15R only landing 04R and departing 9 with winds 320 at 05 knots. We were not told when we checked in about traffic holding 9n multiple intersecting runways nor were we expecting 15R to be in use with a tailwind.  After Aircraft Y was  cleared for takeoff both me and my FO questioned each other where the airplane was where the intersection of the two runways were; and how this would work with our location to the runway. I queried ATC about them clearing some one to take off with us that close and ATC said yes they were cleared. Having never seen this operation in over a decade of operating in Boston and mixed with a voice I have never heard working the tower in Boston before I told the FO I don't like this and he agreed. With it being night and our location to the threshold of 15 R we could not see the departing traffic and I told the FO let's go around. He agreed it was bad and we initiated a go around. ATC seemed surprised we were going around but mixed with the surprise of a departure from a runway we were not expecting in an unknown operation with ATC's less than stellar recent performance throughout the country recently we were not going to hang around and see if it would work. We went around then landed shortly there after with no issues.

column121: Near mid air collision.While on the DRYYE TWO arrival into DAL between SCOPS and SWAY at 5000; I noticed and airfield off the right side of the airplane as I sat right seat. PF had autopilot on; ALT was level and being maintained while navigating laterally with LNAV on the STAR. I glanced over at the MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) to see what the Identifier of the airport was. It was not listed. When I looked back outside; a glider appeared 2-3 o'clock about 100 feet off the right wing; same altitude! I notified ATC immediately. No evasive action taken as the event happened so fast and the glider was behind the airplane by the time I'd be able to grab the stick. On the ground I was able to find out the airport was TA11; TSA Midlothian TX a private strip that has a glider program. Airfield is less than 1 mile from mode c veil and one mile south of the arrival center line. PF never saw the glider.Cause:  No TCAS indications no TA/RA; glider must not have had ADSB. No ATC radar alert or traffic advisory.Response:  Notified ATC; immediately assigned a heading that turned us about 10 deg left.Suggestions:  Only VFR chart reveals caution area for intense glider activity.

column121: Flight from ZZZ. Upon reaching cruise altitude; we were contacted by ZZZ [ARTCC] of a possible blown tire.  A report from the departing aircraft behind us stated they saw tire debris on the RWY during their takeoff.  We had no indications from the flight deck of a tire issue as we did not hear or feel anything abnormal.  Coordinated with dispatch via SATCOM to include Maintenance Control and the Chief Pilot for best course of action.  Station ops and Maintenance Control were to gather additional information as to the origin on the tire debris and get back to us.  No conclusive data was determined except that it was a Air Carrier X main landing gear re-tread tire. The FO and I had an extensive discussion of multiple outcomes and possibilities.  Reviewed Flight Manual procedures for tire damage; gear extension malfunctions; expedited landing; and evacuation procedures. We descended to a lower altitude to reduce landing weight and continued to ZZZ1.  Briefed with the flight attendants was conducted. Requested priority handling with ZZZ1 [ARTCC].  A soft  landing was made followed by a fire and rescue inspection at the end of the runway that revealed damage to the left Main landing gear outboard tire. The outer tread had separated from the tire leaving marks under the wing and flaps.  With an all clear from Airport Rescue and Firefighting and the tire still inflated.; we taxied to the gate without further incident.
column123: Upon reaching cruise altitude; ZZZ [ARTCC] notified us that ZZZ [Tower] had an aircraft departing runway XX out of ZZZ behind us; that saw what appeared to be tire material falling from the aircraft. We had no indications of any problems inside the airplane. Takeoff was smooth and normal and gave us no indication that there was a problem. We used the next three hours to work with dispatch; Chief Pilot and Maintenance Control to run checklist and determine the best option for a priority handled landing in ZZZ1 as a precaution.  Upon landing  an inspection from the fire crew they did find the left main gear outboard tire shredded.  The tread separated but tire remained inflated.

column121: On climb out at about 8000 feet; we received a EICAS message that we had Bleed 1 Over Pressure. We followed the QRH procedure and the message was cleared. Once we got to about 15;000 feet; the message of Bleed 1 Over Pressure reappeared and we once again followed the QRH procedure. This time the message did not extinguish so we were forced to follow the rest of the procedure. Once we realized that we were going to have to do a single engine approach and landing; we requested priority handling and told ATC we wanted to return to ZZZ. We followed our checklists. We advised dispatch through ACARS of our situation; we notified the FAs and passengers; and we set up the aircraft for the ILS XXL and ran the QRH checklist for single engine approach and landing. We requested the emergency vehicles to be on standby by the runway just to be safe. We landed safely and had no issues returning to the gate and deplaned the passengers safely and normally through the jet bridge.Suggestions: All crew members should be removed from duty for 24 hours following a situation like this. I think it's critical to CRM and crew well being.

column121: Pre-departure (Doors closed; Jet bridge retracted).After cabin doors were closed and the jet bridge was retracted; ground personnel notified the flight deck of a 'propane-like' odor detected near the aircraft. The source of the odor could not be immediately identified by the ground crew.I immediately briefed the flight attendants on the situation and instructed them to disarm all doors in anticipation of a possible emergency deplaning.Contacted Maintenance Control to report the odor and seek technical guidance. Logged the discrepancy in the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook as: 'Ground crew reported propane smell; source undetermined.'Maintenance personnel arrived for an initial assessment and reported that no odor was detectable at that time. However; to comply with fume protocols; Maintenance determined the aircraft needed to be taken out of service for a more thorough investigation.Based on the lack of any detectable odor or smoke in the cabin; I determined that an emergency deplaning/evacuation was not required. I maintained frequent communication with the passengers; explaining that the delay to push was a proactive safety measure to allow Maintenance to investigate an external report. We coordinated with Operations to reconnect the jet bridge; deplaned via normal procedures; and completed a ship change. The flight subsequently departed without further incident.Cause: An unidentified odor reported by ground personnel created a potential safety hazard. The fact that the source was not determined warranted further investigation. The threat of having a fume event in the cabin remained until the source was positively identified.Maintenance requirements necessitated removing the aircraft from service to ensure airworthiness; despite the odor being transient.Early notification to the cabin crew and passengers prevented alarm; primed the crew and passengers to be able to detect any abnormal smell in the cabin; and ensured the crew was prepared for a rapid deplanement if the situation escalated.Staying at the gate and performing a ship change was the most appropriate course of action when the source of a reported combustible smell could not be verified.

column121: While climbing through 10;000ft we noticed a bad smell which became stronger and began to bother us. Given our path ahead we talked about a return to ZZZ as it was only becoming more bothersome. We stopped our climb at 25;000ft and decided to don our oxygen masks and notify ATC of our intentions along with requesting priority handling. We ran all appropriate checklists and set up for the longest runway due to an overweight landing of around 153;000lbs. We planned on meeting ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) to inspect our brakes on the runway upon landing. The landing was uneventful and when we came to a complete stop I opened my window and we removed our masks and continued communications via headset / hand mic. This helped to greatly dissipate the odor. With the aid of the fire chief we calculated that we were not in the caution range with our brakes and vacated the runway. We took a few minutes to coordinate some things with the cabin and return to a gate. We requested ARFF to follow us due to a long taxi and check our brakes upon shutdown. They simply said that we were 'ok'. Paramedics met us at the gate as our Flight Attendant was feeling ill. Both Captain and I were not feeling great as well and could taste this strong odor in our throats and elected not to continue with a new aircraft.Cause: The aircraft underwent a check for severe turbulence upon landing and we were told the stick shaker was activated on the previous leg. Possibly this had something to do with the odor.
column123: After departure while climbing through 10;000 we noticed a smell on the flight deck that was becoming stronger and more unpleasant; the FO and myself started to experience discomfort in our throats. I made the decision at that point to return to ZZZ. We donned oxygen masks and established crew communication; I then checked with the flight attendants if there was any odor in the cabin; they told me that there was no odor in the cabin. We requested priority handling leveled off our climb at FL250 and told ZZZ [ARTCC] ATC that we were going to return to ZZZ. We also told him we would need a short delay so that we could accomplish all of the non normal checklists.We received vectors back to ZZZ for runway XX; we asked for and were granted a single frequency approach frequency and called for ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) to meet us once we stopped on the runway.The heavy weight landing (153;000lbs) was uneventful; when we stopped; we briefed the fire chief to check our brake temperatures. The fire chief reported normal temps.We calculated the brake energy; determined that we were not in the caution range and made arrangements to taxi to the gate. ARFF followed us to the gate. Once at the gate the fire chief rechecked our temperatures and reported normal.We had paramedics standing by to check on our number one flight attendant who felt nauseous and light headed.After landing and once the door was opened she began to feel better and agreed to stay on the airplane until the passengers deplaned.After the passengers disembarked; we discussed the smoke issue with maintenance; and I debriefed the flight attendants.I completed two AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logbook) entries.Cause: None apparent

column121: On Departure from ZZZ and climbing through approximately 14;000 feet; the crew received a Left Engine Oil Pressure High Crew Alerting System (CAS) message (which was intermittent twice more) and there was a positive exchange of controls to the captain as we went through the process to troubleshoot with the QRH2.  Shortly after; this was followed by a Left Bleed Leak.  Crew reduced thrust on the left engine and performed the immediate action item per the QRH2 of addressing the bleeds. We advised ATC of our desire to run a few checklists and need to level off at a lower altitude. Following our checklist (and having known previously that the aircraft had just come out of maintenance for a Left Engine Remove & Replace); crew opted to return to ZZZ and advised Dispatch; ATC; and the passengers of the return. No emergency was declared. ATC recleared crew to ZZZ via vectors and crew continued in for the ILSXXR with no further issues excluding the possibility of an overweight landing. Landing was made smoothly and Thrust Reversers were applied. Once on the ground; crew advised Dispatch; Chief Pilot; as well as Maintenance. The passengers were offloaded as well and kept informed of the situation. Suggestions: We can always use events like these; to improve in many facets; whether it be operationally; procedural; etc..even with events that are caused by a malfunction in the aircraft equipment or system.
column123: Crew elected to return to departure airport due to LEFT ENGINE OIL PRESSURE HIGH EICAS message; this was confirmed with the engine gauges.  The same crew had flown the plane on a maintenance flight check the day prior with no issues. The plane was then subsequently flown to ZZZ on a positioning flight; also without issue.  The OIL PRESSURE light would extinguish then come back three separate times. We also received a LEFT BLEED LEAK. the decision to return was made swiftly; a message sent to Ops. Eventually; both messages would not return; but I did not want to work the engine too hard to possibly re-aggravate the issues. Minimal throttle adjustments were made. The aircraft flew normally during vectors and descending back to ZZZ. We may have landed overweight by (later calculations) 228 pounds.  I did not want to remain in the air with a questionable engine; so elected to land. We did a visual approach to runway XXR; backed up by the ILS. Approach and landing were normal; as was taxi in and shut down. Operations was called then Chief Pilot and maintenance.Cause: Extra fuel had been put on the aircraft before departure due to an ATC reroute.Suggestions: I was confident our weight was not excessive; and did not want to overwork a temperamental engine.  In hindsight; a few S-turns or delay vectors for a short time may have been prudent.

column121: I was flying touch and goes at ZZZ Airport; in Class D airspace. As I was taking off on runway XXR to do the touch and gos on XXL; 2 other planes already in the pattern has just reported significant wind shear on the approach to XXL; in the order of 10-15 knots. The tower when reported 'calm winds' along with the wind shear pilot report. As I came in on final for my first touch and go; I strongly felt the wind shear at about 500 AGL; about 100 yards from the runway. I initiated a Go Around on the first approach and let the tower know the wind shear was still there.On the 2cd and 3rd approaches; I was able to complete the touch and go without a lot of difficulty-the wind shear was still there but I felt it moving farther south away from the approach end of XXL.On the final approach; again I felt the wind shear about 400 yards south of XXL; but is seemed to calm down by the time I was over the runway threshold. The landing was very smooth without any significant crosswind. As was was rolling out preparing to do another touch and go; I reached to raise the flaps; I was going maybe 40-45 knots on the runway at that moment. Very suddenly the aircraft veered hard to the right. I felt if I tried to brake or try too much left rudder the aircraft would tip over; as the plane was moving quite hard and fast. I elected to accept the fact I was going to go into the grass off the right side of the runway. I did not hit any landing lights as I entered the grass. Once in the grass the plane slowed considerably; and I gave it left rudder and a little power and was able to exit the grass and get back on the runway without damaging the plane or any runway lights. The area of the grass I was in was flat and almost level with the runway; so the propeller did not hit the ground during this event.I then contacted the tower; told them I had entered the grass and was back on the runway; and was done doing any more touch and goes. I taxied down the runway to an taxiway and then the tower asked if I needed to stop and check the aircraft for damage. I told them no and was going back to my parking area. They gave my taxi instructions.Once back at the tie down; I inspected the aircraft and it looked undamaged.As to why this happened; I am just not sure. column121: Prior to the incident; the PIC (Instructor) conducted all appropriate checks on the aircraft; including run-up procedures; to ensure it was in an airworthy condition. After the pre-flight checks were completed; the student (acting PIC) conducted a takeoff briefing with the PIC. This briefing included all required items; including what would be done in the event of an aborted takeoff. After concluding the briefing; takeoff clearance was requested by the student. Takeoff clearance was shortly received; and the aircraft lined up for departure. The student then increased the throttles to verify correct engine performance and that all gauges indicated normal. The student then applied takeoff power and began to accelerate the aircraft down the runway. Both the PIC and the student expected to see the airspeed indicator begin to increase after releasing the brakes. However; the airspeed did not increase. The PIC immediately called 'REJECT' to abort the takeoff; notified the tower; executed a positive exchange of flight controls; and slowed the aircraft back to safe taxi speeds. The aircraft was then taxied clear of the runway and back to parking. Once the aircraft was fully shut down; the PIC exited the aircraft and performed a visual inspection. There was no damage to the aircraft and no hot brake condition. The pilot then continued the visual inspection of the aircraft and was able to identify that the pitot cover had been left on the pitot tube. While the student and PIC did conduct a preflight inspection; both missed the pitot tube cover. While the student is in training and is expected to know how to check for these items; the PIC ultimately is the one responsible for the safe operation of the aircraft and determining airworthiness. The corrective action is for both the student (but more importantly) the PIC to ensure that they are conducting a thorough inspection of the aircraft prior to accepting it for flight using approved checklists. The PIC elected to terminate flight operations for the day to allow the student and PIC the chance to debrief; reflect; and try again on another day.

column121: Climbing through about 34;500 MSL; we felt a sudden jolt and then pretty severe airframe vibration. We initially thought it may have been a flight control issue. Engine instruments were normal until we scanned down to the Vibration (VIB) gauge and noted it was pegged at 5.0. There was definitely a startle factor to the whole thing but upon noting the VIB; we both said we needed to reduce thrust on the left side. I started pulling the power back slowly but the VIB stayed high until I got all the way to idle. Then it settled around 1.8. We noted an odor but it fairly quickly dissipated. I asked the captain to ask for a lower altitude and he found the engine out page in the FMS to get our driftdown speed and altitude. Once we had it I set that in the Mode Control Panel and set max continuous thrust on the right engine. I think at this point I had the autopilot off because it had gone into Control Wheel Steering (CWS) at some point so I just took over until I could get it set back up. We decided to go back to ZZZZ1 so we coordinated that with ATC. We elected to go there because the captain and I both fly in there a lot so we are very familiar; and because we have Air Carrier X ops there. The right engine had all normal indications. We briefly discussed ZZZZ which was almost directly under us; but felt more comfortable going back to ZZZ1. That would also give us more time to run checklists and get set up without rushing through things. Around this time I took over the radios and the captain got into the QRH for engine vibration. I believe he sent a quick message to dispatch that we were turning back to ZZZZ1 and had also answered a call from the FAs. I got us all set up for our approach and landing in ZZZZ1; and after running the VIB checklist we decided to request priority handling so we would have Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) standing by. We discussed brake temps and our planned overweight landing and that we were unsure what was going on with the engine or how much damage it had. At this time we also decided to put on our oxygen masks for the remainder of the flight. I think this was after speaking with the FAs and asking if there was any odor in the back and they said there was a little bit. The initial odor we smelled up front lasted for less than a minute and then we were kind of distracted by the immediate issue of the vibrations and possible damage. Then the smell dissipated. But since the FAs said there was an odor and to play it safe; we donned our masks and established communications; and the captain ran the one engine approach and landing QRH. We never shut down the left motor as the vibration stayed below 2.0 at idle. He asked if I was comfortable landing it and I said I was as long as he would back me up with any info from the Head-up Display (HUD) as far as trends. We discussed the high ref speed due to flaps 15 at just above max landing weight. We completed that checklist and flew the RNP XX. Landed without incident just a few knots above ref; rolled down to the end of the runway and had ARFF check our engine and brake temps before taxiing back to a hard stand. After shutdown; mechanics came up to the flight deck and said there was severe fan blade damage. It appeared that a piece of the spinner hub broke off and was ingested by the engine. It damaged about 5 fan blades and took a quarter sized chunk out of the trailing edge of at least one of them. To prevent in future: Maybe mechanics should be checking for metal fatigue in these older 737-800s. I know we also have engines that run at a high VIB level but below 4.0 and we're requested to let maintenance know about that but just continue operations. Sometimes it's audibly noticeable like your old prop sync is out of whack and I've even had flight attendants call saying it sounds abnormally loud in back. I guess in hindsight we sort of treated this like 'engine severe damage' initially and ran the memory items for that rather than getting the QRH out for high vibration first. Maybe this was the right call and we saved the engine from shredding itself by leaving it at high RPM for too long. I don't think we ever attempted to increase the power on it again after going to idle. The sudden jolt we felt seemed to indicate that something had broken internally and I know we briefly discussed that out loud. We probably should have donned our oxygen masks right away and in the future I would do that as soon as an odor is noted. If it had not almost immediately dissipated I'm sure we would have donned them sooner and I realize that we should have because a fume could've still been lingering in the air. Other things we could have done better - probably should've started the APU in flight and had it ready to use in case the left motor fully seized at some point.

column121: Flight event was for night currency at SRQ.  I needed three takeoffs and landings by myself; before I could legally complete a later flight event with a crewmember to reestablish Night Vision Goggles (NVG) currency. Knowing runway 4/22 is difficult to see/use at night; when I called ATC (all positions combined on tower) for clearance; I requested runway 32 for closed traffic with full stop/taxi backs.  I was immediately asked by the controller if I could use the short runway instead.  Since I didn't hear anybody else using 4/22; I reluctantly accepted.  They also confirmed the type of aircraft I was.  Clearance was given with a reduced pattern altitude at or below 1;100'.  Taxi and runups were uneventful; however; traffic at the airport started to increase with a small surge of arriving practice approaches/night currency aircraft and airliners on runway 32.Upon being cleared for takeoff I was told to enter left closed traffic.  I thought this was odd because I would be operating towards incoming approach aircraft.  Takeoff and initial upwind leg was uneventful.  Right as I was leveling off on upwind; before turning crosswind; the controller called and I heard the instructions of 'make sure downwind is over approach end 32 please.'  I read back 'downwind over approach end 32'.  Workload was high with level off; configuration changes; check lists; turns; etc all happening quickly at the same time.  It is also worth noting this location and flight direction is difficult at night due to facing the blackness of the intercoastal/bay and gulf.  I was relying heavily on the GPS 530 and Horizontal Situation Indicator (HSI) to make sure upwind and crosswind leg headings were correct and instruments to make sure I was level.  Upon turning crosswind; approximately 2.3 miles away from runway 32 centerline; I couldn't see the runway edge lights.  I knew the general location but couldn't identify the beginning of the runway.  The lights for the runways are pretty directional and there are numerous buildings as well as trees on the west/southwest; so visibility from that position was pretty hard from that sideways angle.  Additionally; runway 32 has a long displaced threshold and the sequenced flashing lights (rabbit) is blocked by trees just southwest of their location.  Until you get south or high enough; especially when they are on low intensity; they can be difficult to see.  I finally got sight of the rabbit off my left and started my turn downwind.  After rolling out on downwind; I could see that I was slightly south of the southernmost rabbit light.  A few seconds later; I started putting in flaps when ATC called; 'Aircraft X yeah………turn heading 090 NOW'.  This was about 2 miles from crossing the centerline of runway 32.  I thought this was odd as they were turning me head on into approaching traffic.  I quickly executed an aggressive sharp turn to the right.  The introduction of flaps; sharp turn; and not being trimmed for this new configuration/input contributed to an inadvertent balloon above assigned altitude that I corrected as fast as I could.  After reading back 090; they then angrily responds back 'I have advised you to have the uh…your downwind over the approach end -numbers- for runway 32; traffic at your 1 o'clock; two miles; is Aircraft Y descending out of 1;400'.'  I can't remember if I responded. I believe I read back simply 'looking' as I was trying to identify the correct traffic and get the airplane trimmed for level so I could safely be eyes outside.  They called back to immediately descend at or below 500 immediately now.  They then pointed me out to Aircraft Y at 1;200' and told them to maintain at or above 1;600.  I had pulled power back to idle and dropped the nose aggressively to level off at 500'.  They called they were going missed (on training instrument approach) and had traffic in sight below them.  I also called back that I had traffic in sight as well.  I do not believe the Garmin 530 had issued a TA at any point; but I was diving and eyes outside; so I can't recall if I saw or heard it.At this point it was becoming clear from their previous transmission that they and I were working on different instruction expectations/situation awareness.  I had heard approach end 32 and they had claimed to have said approach end numbers 32.  My readback also did not include it; which was not noticed or challenged.)  The controller then responded back upset 'Aircraft X; you can expect a full stop after this one'.  Trying not to be confrontational and make a bad situation worse after having gone through a roller coaster ride; I simply responded 'Sorry about that'.I was then given instructions to enter the left downwind runway 22.  At this moment I was not stabilized in the pattern (45 degrees diverging away); low at 500'; and runway 4/22 is still hard to see at night unless you are pointing at it.  On my readback; I advised them that I might need to extend out to see the runway.  Their response was 'Yep; that's okay; uh were you confused on the instructions to keep your downwind over the approach end numbers runway 32?' At this point I am behind trying to fly the plane; reenter the pattern and not start any kind of disagreement over the radio. I responded back; 'I heard approach end; but I didn't hear numbers.'  Their response was 'yeah; that wasn't approach end though.'  Again; with the high workload and not wanting to argue; I simply responded back 'Roger'.I was then cleared to land on runway 22.  On final they notified me that there was traffic on 1-mile final runway 32.  I slowed down as much as I could and asked them on short final if spacing was good.  They called for me to do a go around and to extend upwind.  They told me to make right closed traffic this time and advised of traffic that was transiting the intercoastal at 500' that I would be pointing at.  Right as I crossed behind the traffic they gave me a turn for crosswind.  To keep them happy; I proactively kept the pattern tighter than I'd like (~1.1 nm) and made an uneventful approach/landing.  Upon slowing they cleared me to exit and taxi to the ramp.  During taxi in; they didn't mention anything further about what had happened on the flight.  I didn't attempt any further flight events and called it a night.Reviewing and digesting the data on the ground; I feel I was pretty much set up for failure.  In the air and in the moment; based on the conditions previously mentioned; I was not able to identify this.  Had they had given me a distance instead on their initial instruction; I might have been able to promptly decline; negotiate; or adjust my turns accordingly (assuming reasonable request).  Looking at centerline distances from runway 4/22; their last-minute request of flying downwind over the numbers of runway 32 would have put me on a 0.46 nm downwind cross track.  I am familiar with steep turns in this aircraft so to make that work; I would have to bank on both upwind/downwind and downwind/final turns nonstop at about 50-55 degrees.  This is obviously impractical and unsafe in the pattern for a turboprop multiengine Aircraft X.  Even if they had given the approach end of runway 32; as I had heard/perceived; this was still unreasonable as it was at 0.89 nm cross track from the farthest southernmost sequencing (rabbit) light.  Looking at my actual upwind/crosswind turn; using normal 30-degree bank; I rolled wings approximately abeam of this 0.89 nm distance point.  I still needed the extra distance to regain sight of the runway and turn downwind.  The reality is even if I had kept the turn going from upwind straight to downwind; I couldn't have complied with that request.  Assuming on my turn to downwind that night that I made no correction attempts after going wings level and just paralleled runway 4/22; I would have been on a 1.6 nm downwind.Additionally; it is worth noting:Due to company pressures; I flew again the next night to finish my night currency takeoff and landing requirements.  The same controller was working all frequencies again.  Before I called for clearance; an aircraft called for pattern work for runway 22.  I then called and requested pattern work for runway 32; which was granted.  I noted the controller told the other pilot to make sure their downwind leg was 1 nm.  While I am happy they used distance this time and not a ground fix in the dark; it really stuck out to me how unrealistic their expectations were of my aircraft/performance the prior night in comparison.Night currency flight was uneventful.  Subsequent NVG currency flight was also completed without any issues.  After both flights; I reviewed the downwind data for both pilots; and our downwind legs averaged 1.3 nm - 1.8 nm cross track distance using standard turns and procedures.Moving forward on future pattern night currency flights; I will be on higher defense to prevent events like this from happening again.  Additionally; due to poor lighting and visibility I will probably never accept night pattern work on runway 22 again for safety and liability concerns.  I will only accept runway 14/32 or go to a different airport.

column121: We pushed off the gate and started both engines. We completed the after start checklist and requested our taxi clearance. Upon increasing power on both engines the captain and I heard a loud whirring noise but assumed it was just the engines spooling or coming from the Nose Wheel steering but we both commented that it was louder than normal if it were the engines. Shortly after the noise; the flight attendants called and informed us that white smoke and a burning odor is filling the mid cabin. I informed the captain and we immediately stopped the aircraft. I informed ramp we were stopping and to standby then pulled out the Smoke/Fumes QRC and ran that. During that; the captain elected to turn on the APU and shut down both engines as we didn't have any abnormal flight deck indications and assumed the smoke was engine related because the noise we heard got louder as power increased. After the QRC was completed; I informed ramp and ops we needed a tow back to the gate due to the event. I also informed maintenance of the smoke event and gate return. The captain handled coms with the cabin until his radio panel quit working and he was unreadable over the mic. I then handled all coms inside and outside after that point. A few minutes after engines were shut down we received a PACK 2 OVHT ECAM but we were unsure if that was related to cutting out all airflow into the cabin. We were also receiving a nuisance  RMP 1 FAIL ECAM that would chime every few seconds leading to the failure of the captains coms. After a few minutes; I checked back in with ops to determine the time for a tug to show up because it was getting extremely warm in the cabin with zero airflow. They indicated no more than 5 minutes. Maybe 2 minutes later the tow crew arrived and hooked up to the aircraft. Once they established communication with me; I queried ramp for clearance back to the gate. Once cleared; I gave the clear to tow to the ground crew. I then informed ops that we would like the paramedics to meet us at the gate in case any passengers or crew experienced any symptoms from the smoke inhalation. We returned back to the gate and deplaned the aircraft.

column121: We took off from ZZZ normally; and climbing through 13;000' or so we both noticed the secondary engine instruments screen turn on; which only happens when an engine parameter has been exceeded. Upon seeing the #1 engine vibrations exceeding 4.0 and varying between .3 and over 4.0 I called for my aircraft and the captain began working on the QRH for the high engine vibrations.  We never felt any vibrations from the flight deck. I reduced thrust in the #1 engine until the vibrations remained within limits; as called for by the QRH. He had me continue to fly the airplane while he talked to dispatch; ATC; the flight attendants; and the passengers.  While he did this I accepted vectors to a STAR and set up for an RNAV approach to runway XXL.  We discussed an overweight landing; briefed the approach; and landed normally. No further abnormalities.Cause: It seemed like just a maintenance issue.  A couple of years back we changed procedure to blank out the screen with the secondary engine instruments with the idea being that when one is exceeded the screen suddenly turning on would get the pilot's attention.  I have personally flown with captains that both like and dislike this idea. In this instance the screen popping back up worked very well and immediately got both of our attention.

column121: On Day 0; I was the pilot flying on Aircraft X from ZZZ to JAN. On the visual approach for Runway 16L; we started configuring the aircraft with flaps 8 and 20 at about 10 NM on a right base leg. We slowed to the maneuvering speed for flaps 20. We then intercepted final in white needles (RNAV) at about 7 NM from the runway. Then we put the landing gear down; configured flaps 30; and slowed to the straight in speed. We started descending on the approach using vertical speed 0.2 NM prior to the fix HARAG. We then noticed that the PAPIs for 16L were not visible. This caught us off guard because there wasn't a NOTAM saying they were inoperative. The captain tried to turn the lights on using the radios without success. We decided to continue the approach since it was visual conditions and we had an electronic glideslope from the ILS. Reaching 1000 feet; I called out one thousand;" and the captain replied "stabilized; cleared to land." On short final; at about 300 feet above ground level; we got a "terrain" Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System (EGPWS) callout; which confused us since we were on the glideslope. A couple seconds later; we got a flaps aural alert; which made us realize we were still at flaps 30. We immediately initiated a go-around. We were then vectored back to a 10 NM final by Approach Control. We continued to a landing without further incident. At the gate; we debriefed the reasons for the go-around.The primary contributing factor for the unstabilized approach was fixation / distraction by the unexpected inoperable PAPIs for 16L. This caused us to forget the final flaps configuration and the before landing checklist. A secondary contributing factor would be complacency with the 1000 feet stabilized call. It can become habitual to say the callout without fully verifying all of the stabilized approach criteria.Going forward; I will focus on preventing distractions and fixation during critical phases of flight; and I will verify all of the stabilized approach criteria at the 1000 foot call. A helpful tool would be to use the "1;2;3;4;5" memory aid to verify proper aircraft configuration. 1 is cleared to land; 2 are the two thrust reversers; 3 is down three green; 4 and 5 are flaps 45."

column123: After pushing back off the gate (XX) at ORD; we contacted Ramp for our taxi clearance and were told to taxi SP line hold short A; contact Metering. Upon contacting Metering the controller sounded confused as to where we were and then seemed to take a second to affirm our position. He then told us to monitor Ground. We believe we may have inadvertently taxied slightly onto A without the proper clearance from Ground. We were instructed to taxi to 22L via A A13 V. The rest of the flight continued on with no issues.The cause of this event is due to poor signage; markings; and construction at the ORD airport. The instructions were clear; however it is very difficult to see where the SP line turns into the A taxiway as the construction to the southwest blocks the signage and the taxi marker lines are not painted very well. Before we even started taxiing we could hear another airplane on the wrong taxi lane (SE) when they were supposed to be on the SP line. I believe that the poor signage and construction with little indication of where Taxiway A begins is the main contributing factor.I think the best course of action would be to include more signage or markings to denote where Taxiway A begins and SP ends. Another way to fix this may be for Ramp to give a clearance to hold short of A6 rather than A; as that is much more clearly visible and denoted on the taxiway. column121: I am writing this to explain the series of events that led me to run off the left side of the runway on XXL at ZZZ airport on Day 0 at approximately XA:00 and strike a taxiway sign in Aircraft X.Weather at the time of airplane dispatch was 310@13G18. I decided to do a landing lesson with a PPL student pilot to prepare him for his upcoming prog check. Winds throughout our instruction had been variable; gusting up to 24 during our laps in the pattern. During instruction; I was teaching the student how to execute crosswind correction during landing.On the sixth lap in the pattern; while we were in the downwind; the weather conditions at the airport deteriorated rapidly. At this point; ZZZ tower released a weather report stating severe low level windshear; winds 250@20G35; and a dust storm at the departure end of the runway.At this point; ZZZ tower had cleared us for the touch and go; and I instructed my student to turn base for runway XXL. While turning onto the base for XXL; I saw the massive dust storm that ZZZ tower had reported quickly approaching the departure end of runway XXL; blowing left to right. At this point; my student dropped flaps 10.Turning base to final; I instructed my student to come in at 70kts due the excessive wind. He dropped flaps 20. After this; I instructed him to maintain flaps 20 and emphasized coming in at a higher approach speed.Now on short final; I could feel the crab angle required for our ground track to run parallel with the runway increasing as we were descending. The idea for a go around had entered my head; however looking down the end of the runway; I could see the dust storm; at least 800ft tall; moving toward the approach end of runway XXL. Seeing this; I knew going around at our current trajectory would involve penetrating the dust strom at a low airspeed and altitude; and I immediately took the controls with the understanding that I needed to get the airplane on the ground.I was able to use a crosswind landing technique to touch the airplane down on the centerline of runway XXL. I immediately initiated flaps zero and instructed ZZZ tower that this was going to be a full stop. As I was attempting to slow the airplane down on the runway; the nose of the airplane began to drift from the center line to the left at a rapid rate. I immediately acted by exercising full aileron correction left; and full rudder deflection to the right in an attempt to prevent the airplane from weathervaning into the wind. I had reached the control limit of both the aileron and the rudder while still on the runway; but I had lost complete directional control at this point.Now completely at the mercy of the wind; I could see that our direction of movement was veering us off the runway and into a taxiway sign. I initiated full back pressure to reduce as much kinetic energy as possible; causing the airplane's nose to rise. We struck the taxiway sign with the underside of the airplane.Now at a reduced airspeed; I was able to get the nose of the airplane pointed back toward the runway. I allowed the airplane to coast back in the direction of the runway. I did not apply toe break pressure for the sake of preventing the nose landing gear from digging into the grass. We came to a full stop with the right main landing gear on the runway; and the nose wheel and left main landing gear in the grass.The first thing that I did was turn to the student and ask if he was okay. He told me he was. I called up to the tower and told him that everyone on the airplane was okay. I asked tower if we should taxi onto a taxi way. He told me to shut down and stay where I was; and I complied.

column121: A complex go-around created by an ATC landing/take-off conflict led to an undesired aircraft state in which the PM perceived safety was in jeopardy and took control of the aircraft.The flight began eventfully with a passenger and service animal issue that caused a delayed departure. Once resolved; the taxi out through initial approach was unremarkable. The workload and complexity began during the latter stages of the arrival and clearance for the approach.The weather was approximately OVERCAST010 to FEW050 and there was a NOTAM for our landing runway (XXR) that advised 'Special Authorization Cat 1 (ILS) procedure Not Authorized; unless advised by ATC that cranes are down.' As we were cleared for the approach and above the glideslope (~2000' AGL); I directed the PM to inquire on the status of the cranes. We were informed multiple times that the 'cranes are up' and there was an unfamiliarity from ATC about this NOTAM; but eventually a declaration that 'we are authorized for the approach.' Meanwhile; I had disconnected the autopilot and autothrottle; accelerating about five knots; but intercepted the glideslope configured gear/F15; slowing from 165kts to target speed at the FAF/1500' AGL. We briefly discussed that we felt safe continuing the approach; completing the landing checklist prior to 1000' AGL and entering IMC. This phase was the first element of complexity during this approach.Upon breaking out of the weather at approximately 800' AGL; I observed an airplane on the runway and queried the PM if he saw the same thing. He confirmed there was an airplane there; followed by ATC providing instructions to it and the preceding aircraft. Next; we verified stable at 500' AGL and were discussing the probability of a go-around as the aircraft was slow to begin the takeoff roll. ATC instructed us to go around at approximately 300' AGL; but with noticeable closure on the impending lift-off of the other aircraft. I initiated the go around in accordance with the SOP; while offsetting to the right (away from the other runway) and remaining under the weather layer; keeping the departing aircraft in sight. I was unable to verify any of the PM go-around actions as I was primarily concerned about flightpath deconfliction with the other aircraft and verbally said 'what does he want us to do' as I estimated our distance to the other aircraft nearing 3000' nose-tail separation. ATC then gave us a left turn to 060 (nearly across the taking off aircraft's flight path) and climb to 3000' MSL; and after a slight delay; I complied with that instruction; beginning the climb back into IMC. This phase was the second element of complexity during this approach.As we climbed into the weather and I transitioned to instruments; I observed the aircraft passing through approximately 1200' MSL at approximately 12 degrees nose high pitch; but with an airspeed of approximately 190 KIAS and decreasing rapidly with the trend arrow approaching 160 KIAS. I immediately lowered the nose towards 5 degrees nose high as I scanned across the other side of the cockpit to analyze the poor aircraft performance. During this time; I believe I said '(check) Flaps' or possibly 'level change; set Climb Speed (CMS); Flaps 5;' but more attention was narrowly focused on determining the throttle setting/engine performance and aircraft gear/flap configuration. I continued to lower the flight path towards level flight; advanced the throttles slightly; and did observe increasing airspeed; as well as a momentary sink rate of approximately 500' FPM. There was comm from both ATC and the PM during this point that I did not fully interpret while focused on precisely controlling the flight path; while also still attempting to diagnose the performance degradation. At this point; without any Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System (EGPWS) aural warnings; the PM perceived 'red terrain' on the Navigation Display and said 'climb' and then 'I have the aircraft.' Obviously; this was also startling; but I released control of the aircraft and tried to make the mental shift to gain Situational Awareness (SA) as the new PM. I did not immediately notice any 'red terrain'; but did perceive a significant increase in pitch attitude. Still without certainty of the flap position; I begin moving the flaps to a lower setting; neither the FO nor I can definitively say who moved the flaps to 5; though we know he did press LVL Change and set CMS at some point in this immediate sequence of transitioning PF/PM roles. While still gaining SA; I observed 'yellow terrain' on our nose starting at approximately five nautical miles and made a request to ATC that 'we need a turn away.' ATC subsequently provided a frequency change; the new PF also said things during this time that I did not fully comprehend. I observed the aircraft continuing to accelerate; nearing 250 knots and I raised the flaps to UP; the 'FLAPS; FLAPS' aural warning also sounded at some point during this sequence of me functioning as the PM. The PF at some point engaged Command B and we cleared the weather back into VMC. This phase was the third element of complexity during this approach.Now on top of the weather with a stable aircraft and on a good vector and altitude; we were able to restore normal CRM; and executed the after take-off checklist. We double checked each other and the aircraft; returned to the original PF/PM roles; completed a descent check; and uneventful landing and taxi-in (though there was still concern/uncertainty regarding the NOTAMs referencing the cranes; but we had not noticed any on the previous approach).  Due to being late; we only very briefly debriefed in the airplane after completing the parking checklist and I said we would discuss prior to the next flight. The FO left the jet as I stayed to wish passengers farewell and apologize again for the inconvenience. Upon exiting; I saw the CA of the next flight on the jetbridge and we discussed the passenger service animal and NOTAM issue for several minutes. I arrived to the next aircraft and began a deliberate debrief with the FO; recognizing that we will probably be late departing. During our discussions; it became apparent to me that we may have oversped the flaps; I then left the middle of our debrief to go back to the other aircraft to inform the Captain of our suspicion; stating that it was less than 10 knots; for less than 10 seconds; at Flaps 5 or less at ~2000' MSL. I returned to satisfactorily continue our debrief; double checking on the fitness of both the FO and my own fitness for duty for the next flight. He stated that he was; I agreed with his assessment; and did not have concerns regarding my fitness. The next flight was conducted uneventfully.To recap and summarize; the slightly varied and out-of-sync SA among the PF; PM; and ATC resulted in multiple missed/delayed comm and lack of shared mental model on the flight deck (degraded CRM); ultimately producing a poorly executed go around.

column121: Descending on the ZZZZZX approaching ZZZZZ AT 26000 ft Pressurization page presented itself showing cabin altitude 9000 blinking. Noticed DELTA P was around 5.2 less than what it should have been and outflow valve open. Became distracted didn't cross ZZZZZ at required altitude distracted with conversation about emergency status with Captain. We realized depressurization was happening. I expedited descent as I noticed DELTA P descending and cabin altitude climbing which peaked at 11150. Once established on vectors for XXR and at 10000 ft with cabin altitude mirroring ambient conditions I removed my O2 mask donned my headset; transferred controls to the captain for a CAT 3 approach with a subsequent uneventful landing and taxi to the gate.
column123: While descending through FL260 the FO noticed the pressurization page popped up. As we looked at that page; we noticed that the cabin altitude was at 9000 feet. We also noticed that the delta p was around 6.1 and the outflow valve was slightly open. We immediately donned O2 masks and advised ATC to start the emergency descent. As we descended the cabin altitude continued to climb. The highest we saw the cabin altitude was 11100 feet. The cabin O2 masks never dropped. ATC vectored us while we descended for new runway XXR. We reset FMGC for new approach and finished briefing CAT 3 Autoland. At 10000 feet we removed our O2 masks and continued the vectors to ILS XXR CAT 3 approach. ATIS was reporting 1/4 visibility heavy snow. Completed the Autoland to XXR and taxied off runway to gate XX.

column121: Company Chart 10-7 for BCN in the Jeppesen manual is no longer correct and requires an immediate update. It should read as follows:All current 24L RNAV SIDs state; Maintain runway heading to 410... The initial turn shall begin no later than upon reaching 500." The State Rules and Procedures; 10-1 pages no longer include any of the verbiage referenced in 10-7.I would further recommend the entire section under "Turn Compliance" be deleted or completely rewritten. The current wording states we "must" violate our OpSpecs and begin the turn below 400 feet. ATC does not require this and this circumstance does not meet the other 2 exceptions to our minimum turns after takeoff (FOM).Furthermore; there's a superfluous statement: "Hand fly or autopilot engaged (minimum of 200 feet)." Is there another way to fly an airplane?As one who has regularly flown this departure; it is unnecessary to fly this departure in heading if hand flying. By leaving LNAV engaged and beginning the turn at 410 feet; LNAV magenta path will automatically update directly to the first fix on the departure. It's far simpler and less likely to be flown incorrectly. A far more useful suggestion would be to verify all speed and altitude restrictions on the SID. I have yet to load any of the SIDs at BCN that didn't require manually entering at least one speed restriction not coded in the database. In addition; at the weights we usually depart BCN some of the altitude restrictions are difficult if not impossible to make; especially at higher ambient temperatures. Under these conditions use of Noise Abatement Departure Procedures 1 (NADP1) is required. Lastly; this station frequently publishes variable wind direction in the body of the METAR; often resulting in a tailwind component that prevents us from using the shorter Runway 24L/06R. Many crew members seem unfamiliar with the calculations necessary to ensure Performance Data performance. Perhaps a training module would help?I assume the information on the page was written some time ago and never updated resulting in low altitude turns and overly complicated and unnecessary departure "technique.""

column121: I was flying at FL350 with FL370 as final. ZZZ Center was the controlling sector during this time. I was given a climb to FL370 at 1;000 FPM or greater. I set the FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) to VS +1000 and told the FO that we will monitor the airspeed and bleed off as much as we feel comfortable with or make it to FL370-but not going to get too slow or be dangerous. We started the climb with an indicated mach of .752At approximately 36400 I was 10-12 knots above 1.3VSO and decide thats enough. The FO told ZZZ Center that we can no longer maintain 1;000 feet per minute but can take a turn. We were given 10 degrees left. Then told to turn RIGHT 090. We start the turn and almost immediately told then turn LEFT 300. When turning left the FO goes oh thats because another plane is right below us. I then look at the MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) and see they are 400 feet below. Immediately we get a TCAS RA to climb. I disengage the automation; go full power and comply with the RA per the procedure in our 737 AOM. When we were clear of conflict I reengaged the automation and continued our climb to FL370. The other aircraft also got a TCAS RA to descend. Then given clear back to ZZZ [VOR].Cause: The climb to 370 was not that imperative-we could have just waited for the other aircraft to pass and climb then. Also there was a SIGMET on the weather app for MOD turbulence up to 350 shortly after Top of Climb. To get above it faster for flight attendant safety and passenger comfort I flew the climb at max rate on the VNAV page which was 256 indicated and that become .752 MACH when we started our climb to 370. Typically we fly 280-300 and then .76-78 so if the conditions allowed a faster climb perhaps I could have had more speed to bleed off to get to FL370. Also with the price of fuel I know we are really paying attention to ECON speeds and everything where our usual 300 and .78 may not be the more desirable speed anymore-but that could have given me more speed to bleed off.

column121: PA30 was approaching the airport and announced a 5 mile final. Cessna proceeded to Runway XX Hold short line and completed final checks for departure. The Cessna crew scanned the sky for traffic but did not see the PA30 on final.  The PA30 announced a 2-mile Final; the Cessna pilots visually scanned the final approach; did not see traffic and immediately proceeded towards the runway for departure.  The Cessna pilot made a radio call 'taking Runway XX for departure'.  The PA30 pilot shouted 'Hey we are on short final; what are you doing!'  The Cessna pilot immediately stopped the aircraft approximately 150 feet from the runway edge but beyond the hold short line. The left seat pilot looked again; saw the PA30 and judged the aircraft to be about 1 inch wide on the windscreen. The pilots exchange dialogue for a few moments to verify positions; and eventually the PA30 executed a go-around  which seemed to be several hundred feet above the threshold; Contributing factors: Overcast; grey sky; and Cessna was position perpendicular to the departing runway.  Lessons Learned: Angle the aircraft prior to the hold short line as appropriate to get a clear view of the final approach course. It may have been possible to see the PA30's landing lights.Human Factors: Cessna crew was alert; fatigue was not a factor. Cessna crew used pre-takeoff checklist; and briefed the takeoff prior to departure. The crew heard the distance calls and judged and concurred the separation to be safe and sufficient for departure.

column121: While performing a normal take off for a flight to ZZZ1 oil sprayed onto my windscreen. At the time I was unsure of what the issue was so I began to prepare to land straight ahead. My passenger; another pilot; assisted me by stating that we still had good oil pressure and that perhaps we should go around and land on the same departing runway XX. I agreed; increased power to full; climbed to pattern altitude and told tower that I'd like to land XX. They asked me if I was requesting priority handling and I responded that I was; and that I had oil spray across my windscreen. I was cleared to land on XX; and I landed on XX. Other traffic on final to XX was directed to clear out of the way. I landed; exited via Taxiway 1 to the ramp and taxied back to the hangar. I was met by airport fire / rescue. Upon inspection after shutdown it was found that the oil filler cap wasn't secured or came loose during takeoff / flight. SOP procedures are currently being updated to stop the practice of taking the cap off after flight to allow the crankcase to exhaust. The positives of this practice seem to me to be far outweighed by the negatives. I also have altered my procedures to never fly an airplane that I haven't physically checked that the oil cap and any other removable caps are secure. I've also discussed with CFIs to update my abort briefing to be adjusted that I only land straight ahead or turn back to land in the event of a power plant failure. If I am able to still safely climb; I will do that and return to land on the departing runway.

column121: We were flying along the top of some stormy weather at FL 390; as the cloud tops began to rise we asked to climb to FL 410 to be above the clouds and weather. Once we did that we were VMC above the weather with pockets of occasional light chop. We saw on the radar that we were approaching a cell ahead of us; however there was no cloud build up that we could see and it was indicating that the building cell was beneath us. We decided to ask for a deviation to the right just to make sure we wouldn't fly directly above it; even though continuing straight or turning would have remained clear of any clouds and we be above the cloud tops by at least a couple thousand feet. In our turn to the right we encountered turbulence that began to build rapidly and ultimately pitched the aircraft up and down so violently; that the autopilot disconnected and the aircraft pitched down losing about 300 feet rapidly; by the time I was able to regain control of the aircraft; apply power; and pitch up; we had sunk below our cruising altitude to about 40600 feet. We reported the loss of altitude to ATC and then stated that we were back on course; completed with our deviation. Besides the continuation of moderate chop we continued on to our destination with no other events

column121: I was working the R-side with a D-side training team with me as well. At sectors XX/XY combined. Aircraft Y Called requesting their clearance from MKT to ZZZ. My d-side coordinated the approval request with M98 Approach and with their approval I read Aircraft Y Their Clearance and released them for departure. During this time; I was having a discussion with the D-side Trainee and Trainer about the coordination they just did. I also had to have my D-side Coordinate and Altitude with M98 as well as point outs that were required for another aircraft. During this time Aircraft X called airborne off of MKT and I thought they said they were 3 miles northwest of the Airport. The flight plan they had to ZZZ1 airport. With what I thought I heard for their distance from MKT and the airport they were flying to being roughly a 320-heading vs Aircraft Y's route which was roughly a 360 heading. I used the code for Aircraft X they were below the MIA when radar Identified them. So my clearance was 'Aircraft X climb and maintain 6;000 leaving 2;800 cleared to the ZZZ1 Airport via direct. At this time the D-side trainer said you probably should have just told them to maintain VFR. But it was too late. MKT is a class E airspace; and they were less than 3 miles from the airport. seconds later Aircraft Y called airborne. As soon as their tag came up I turned Aircraft X to a 270 heading and amended their altitude to 4;000. I did not radar identify Aircraft Y but asked them is they could maintain VFR I know this legally doesn't change a thing; but it was the first thought that came to mind. When Aircraft X was at 2;800 and Aircraft Y was at 3;100 their courses were diverging; however the separation was only 2.02 miles apart. once Aircraft Y was level at 5;000 feet I radar identified them. Then switched them to M98 approach. After this I cleared Aircraft X back on course. I told my supervisor and had him pull up the replay. Then got out of position to fill this out.Recommendation: Ensuring the separation could have been done by simply not issuing a clearance to Aircraft X and telling them to maintain VFR. This scenario happens Often at MKT being a busy airport while several aircraft will call up airborne picking up IFR. I should have done what I did in the past and not issue the clearance. I misjudged the distance Aircraft X was from the airport and misheard them. The aircraft type difference was a large factor in performance; and I should have known better than to issue the Clearance. A tower at MKT has been in the talks and would greatly improve the safety of the Aircraft going in and out.

column121: This narrative is regarding the events that occurred on the morning of Day 0 at approximately XA:28. This report is being filed to bring awareness to a potentially dangerous situation. It is my hope that a more detailed analysis will be conducted to help alleviate any further issues.On the morning of Day 0; at the non-towered AXH airport for a repositioning fight to ZZZ; the crew was issued an ATC clearance from Houston Approach. The clearance was issued on the ground and is as follows: Aircraft X enter controlled airspace heading 220; climb and maintain 2000." Before departure the crew referenced the obstacle departure procedure for Runway 9 instructing a climb to 2000 feet before turning LEFT. Crew briefing included the ATC instructions; Obstacle Departure Procedure (ODP) procedure; and nothing indicating an other than standard traffic pattern direction. There was no mention of obstacles on the airport chart and after completing the briefing the crew elected to continue with normal operations and depart IFR. The crew complied with the listed ODP by climbing to 2000 feet and then turning left to then comply with the ATC issued heading of 220. Radio contact was initiated with Houston Approach; questioning why we had turned left. ATC went on to indicate the proximity of the aircraft to an antenna farm on the left downwind leg that had an altitude of 2000 feet. ATC instructed a climb to 3000 and a turn to a new heading. There were constructive discussions regarding omissions of chart data and misleading ODP instructions. In conclusion; the crew followed all directions; to the best of their knowledge and attempted to operate the aircraft in the safest manner possible.Suggestions: It is imperative that the AXH Jeppesen chart 10-9 reflect obstacle departure instructions to climb to 2000 before turning right and not left. In addition; conduct an analysis and change the direction of Runway 9 traffic to the right for obstacle avoidance. Going forward; when ATC issues a clearance off of Runway 9 they need to specify; turn right heading - - -. If a right turn is not specified the crew assumes a left turn is expected as indicated by the left turn on the ODP and direction of the standard left traffic pattern. Dangerous obstacles exist north of the airport and there needs to be a modification to either the chart or the ATC procedures when issuing clearances."
column125: Fractional Captain reported AXH departure procedures should reflect ODP and instruct to turn to the right and not to the left for obstacle avoidance.

column121: Arriving into GSP with no arrival routing at a top altitude of 10;000 feet; Atlanta center handed us off to Greer Approach. Greer approach then instructed us to maintain present heading and descend to 4;000 ft and expect runway 22; our heading was going direct the airport. We noted in Jeppesen charts that the tower closed at 0445z. However; that time is wrong for daylight savings time and it really closes at 0345 Z and is the consistent closure time year round; locally.After leveling at 4;000 feet a couple minutes passed and we needed further instruction. We queried Greer approach a couple times for further instruction and received no answer. Greer approach and tower had closed. We were still on an IFR clearance and we had no turn to intercept or anything. They just left us hanging on a heading at 4;000 ft. No further clearance. We switched to tower frequency; also CTAF; and announced our intentions. It was VFR and continued forward with an approach to runway 22 while announcing our position on CTAF. After landing we cancelled IFR with Atlanta center. No further events noted. Radios operated just fine the entire time. Greer approach and tower just signed off without notice.Cause: Greer approach closing and leaving us on a heading and altitude for approach without any further clearance or instructions prior to closing. Just silence. The charts publishing tower closure time incorrectly during daylight savings time. This is true of all our charts; not just GSP; for tower closures. Publishing Zulu times does not account for daylight savings time.

column121: During decent onto arrival into Havana Cuba we received NAV FM/GPS POS disagree ecam. The message kept popping and disappearing throughout the decent. We suspected GPS jamming going on in the area. We were able to check the position of the aircraft and continued on. We were set up for the visual approach backed up by the ILS to runway 06 in Havana. The GPS position began to drift more and we got terrain warning message during landing close to the runway. Since we were on a visual approach in a stable position to land we continued and made a normal landing. By the time we taxied the position error had fixed itself. We wrote up the discrepancy in the log book. Everything went back to normal and we continued on the next leg with no issues.Cause: I think if Cuba is jamming GPS signals they should let us know ahead of time. I think multiple flights were having position errors that day into Havana. We shouldn't fly there during the times they are GPS jamming.
column123: During decent for arrival; ECAM 'NAV FM/GPS POS DISAGREE' message appeared and cleared itself several times; we suspected GPS jamming. Flight crew was able to validate aircraft position using ground base Navaids. Since we were visual; we determined that the best course of action was to continue with approach and land. Due to the distance to airport we weren't able to complete the follow up items in QRH. Therefore; GPWS TERR was not deselected; which created an additional distraction; however; approach and landing was uneventful. After gate arrival; we looked at the QRH for guidance; called dispatch to let them know as well as ZZZ Maintenance. We were advised that we were his 7th call he received with regards to GPS anomalies the day of event. We entered information in the logbook as well as a report to company. As precaution for the departure for our return to ZZZ1; we decided to perform a full IRS (Inertial Reference System) alignment as well as to request HAV ATS for a conventional RNAV DEPARTURE (EMUPA3) using ground base navigation as a backup to mitigate any potential GPS anomalies. We reported the event to HAV ATS as well. During departure GPS worked as normal with no ECAM or IRS position disagreement.Cause: GPS jamming within Cuban airspace. Add note to release to inform crews so we are better prepared for an event like this within Cuban airspace.

column121: ATC cleared us for the RNAV RWY 19 into SGU. We were given the frequency change and everything was normal. There were numerous aircraft around SGU including on the ground; in the traffic pattern; and inbound to the traffic pattern. When we were at about a 10 mile final; Aircraft Y turned base. We immediately started discussing the possibility of a go-around because of the proximity and probability that we were going to catch up to them. Once we confirmed the aircraft wouldn't be clear of the runway; we initiated the go-around. We made left traffic and landed with no further issues. When on the ground I remembered that we were cleared for the RNAV and I believe we technically should have flown the missed approach. I believe we made the safest decision flying the traffic pattern as we did because of the amount of traffic in the area and because it was VMC below 10;000 MSL. Cause: Large amounts of traffic on and around the airport. Uncontrolled airport. A pilot who may not have understood how fast we would catch up to them turning base in front of us.Suggestions: In the future; I plan on talking to aircraft which I believe will possibly cause a conflict so we can coordinate arrivals more effectively. We could also cancel IFR when we know we meet all requirements to stay and operate in VMC in accordance with company policy

column121: We were flying along trying to navigate through thunderstorms in which our radar was not depicting very well at all. While in some of the roughest bumps; our radios were overcome with static screeching and we were able to hear ATC maybe 1x5. This bout of turbulence was likely the worst I have encountered thus far as a pilot.While in the midst of this we received a CAB EMER call from our FA. She explained to us that a older male pax was on our emergency O2 since his personal O2 was depleted. With the distraction of the radio and heavy turbulence we herd that the O2 bottle has a 15 minute supply on it. With these factors in play I decided to immediately request priority handling and proceeded to ZZZ asap. We advised ATC as well as Dispatch and requested EMT personnel to meet the aircraft at the gate.ZZZ approach cleared us for a visual approach to RWXX. However; they them advised us to turn in order for them to squeeze in one aircraft ahead of us. This did not make me happy to say the least. During this approach we received a Terrain followed by Pull up GPWS which is described in my previous report. Upon landing we quickly got to the gate and the EMT came onboard to check on the PAX before the rest of the plane deplaned. I was told the PAX was ok and he was take into the terminal via wheelchair. After this event ended; I called maintenance and MEL'd the portable oxygen bottle as it was used and still indicating 1000 psi.Once we returned to ZZZ1. I had enough time to talk with our flight attendant. She described the situation and told me how the passenger had two portable oxygen (batteries) that are personal. The first tank was depleted on his previous flights and the tank used for our flight became depleted because of the turbulence and his heavy breathing during the flight. our flight attendant described the actions she took and I think she did a fantastic job in addressing the situation. She was filling out her medical form to provide us. However; the turbulence was so strong. It was not feasible to complete that task or for us to reach out to medlink. There were no medical professionals onboard the aircraft.During this flight we had previously requested priority handling. We had the field in sight and cleared for the visual to RW XX. I had selected 2100 which was the faf altituded and was pointing the plane towards the fix to land asap due to situation. ATC gave us traffic to follow and instructed us to turn right an additional 15-30 degrees. We were in a decent at 1000fpm and the 'Terrain Terrain' caution alarmed followed by a warning 'Pull Up'. We were visual with the ground so I disconnected autopilot and climbed to 3000. The alert went away. This occurred about 10 miles east of the final approach course. I then hand flew the rest of the approach and landed without any further issue.Cause: PAX O2 supply became depleted due to heavy breathing with associated turbulence. The actual descent rate exceeded the planes threshold for issuing the warning.Suggestion: Inform pax requiring O2 to come with a greater supply if possible. Priority aircraft should have priority to the field; especially medical in nature. PAX was on O2 with a breathing issue.

column121: We were holding short of runway XX at ZZZ on the east side of the runway. We had just received an IFR release from air traffic control who gave us a three minute void time. There was one aircraft on downwind for runway XX. We made a radio call to the common traffic advisory frequency to advise that we were going to take the runway for departure. As we began to power up past the hold short line; the first officer said stop stop. I stopped the aircraft with the nose just passed the hold short line for runway XX at the approach end. As I looked over the shoulder of my first officer towards the 3 o'clock of our airplane; I saw a C130 approaching low and fast on a severely short approach. The C130 operator had not advised us of his intention to make a short approach. Due to the close proximity and high approach speed of the C130 I chose to stop and remain where we were and advise the C130 our nose was just passed the hold short line. The C130 made a radio call on the common traffic advisory frequency to say they were on left base. In the interest of safety and out of an abundance of caution; I chose to allow the C130 to execute his procedure first before taking the runway. The C130 accomplished a touch and go in front of us and then afterwards we departed without incident.Suggestions: It's incredibly important; especially in an uncontrolled airport environment to be aware of the type of aircraft sharing the airspace. This particular C130 was a firefighting tanker out doing practice maneuvers. The aircraft commander of the C130 never indicated to us the type of aircraft they were or the nature of their fighter pilot type of approach that they were planning on accomplishing. The aircraft descended very quickly from 1600 feet above the runway on a downwind in a hard left bank straight to the runway threshold. This type of approach caught us off guard as we assumed a normal approaching landing which would have given us more than enough time to depart safely without conflict. I'm thankful to the first officer for having his head on a swivel and calling out the closure rate of the surprise maneuver.
