column121: The First Officer was the PF. CA was PM and had just finished transition training a few weeks ago. We departed runway XXR in ZZZ; APU Bleed On takeoff. Shortly after takeoff we received an EICAS message for L Bleed Fail. The FAIL light was also illuminated on the L Bleed switch. We continued to climb out on ZZZZZX departure; cleaned up the airplane and ran the after takeoff checklist. We decided to leave the APU on and start running the L Bleed Fail Checklist in case the APU would be needed. The FO continued to fly the departure and took over the radios while the CA ran the checklist. After closing the XBleed per the checklist and working through a few decision trees; the checklist asked if oceanic or high terrain is an issue. There was terrain along our route with the first critical point about 17 mins into the flight. Since we were not there yet; we took that into consideration and continued with the checklist. The next step had us reducing the L Thrust Lever to idle. This step took us both by surprise. The CA tried to scroll thru the checklist to see what the next steps would be and if the engine would remain at idle or be shutdown; but it was too difficult to tell thru the checklist. We determined the best course of action was to contact mx (Maintenance) via dispatch over satcom. We talked with mx to see what they showed and to verify that we needed to bring the engine to idle. They looked thru the QRH and verified the engine needed to be brought to idle; and the need to remain clear of icing conditions. They also showed that the PRSOV (Pressure Regulating Shut Off Valve) was showing failed open. Since dispatch was on; the told us a reroute would be needed to remain clear of icing and they were working with the duty pilot and chief pilot. While the CA was coordinating with mx and dispatch; the FO had pulled up the MEL for the L Bleed Fail. It had a long note about the possibility of a duct burst that could cause a major event." The CA confirmed with mx that a duct burst was a possibility. We were now approaching the first terrain area. There was a broken layer of clouds out ahead of us that would prevent us from remaining out of icing. We were also unsure if we would get engine thrust back. We were dispatched Method 2 and not yet at our cruise altitude. Taking all of this information into account; CA and FO decided the best course of action was to return to ZZZ so we could continue the checklist. The CA informed mx and dispatch of our intentions. Mx agreed and dispatch worked on amending the release. The CA asked dispatch to notify ZZZ ops. The FO notified ATC of our intentions and we were cleared back to ZZZ. Once workload permitted; the CA continued the checklist; reducing the L engine to idle. The checklist permitted use of the left engine upon completion. We were overweight so the overweight checklist was also run. ATC worked us back into the arrival flow and we landed uneventfully in ZZZ. Since ATC provided us with priority handling; CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) was standing by but not needed. We taxied to the gate and wrote up the Bleed Fail and overweight landing."

column121: Departed XXR on the ZZZZZX; FO flying; bleeds off take off.  The usual turbulence in the climb.  Uneventful initial climb out.  After passing ZZZZZ he called for the after take off check about the same time as initiating the right turn in LNAV/VNAV.  Seeing that the aircraft was turning north away from terrain and meeting all vertical path requirements first (flight path forward priority here) thus far I diverted my attention to reconfiguring the bleed panel and ensuring we were pressurizing.  All normal thus far.  Approaching ZZZZZ1 I completed the after take off check list and at the same time the controller called and said we were off course and asked if we needed assistance.  This was both alarming and confusing; but at this time I did notice we were slightly left of the magenta line by maybe one half mile (.5) but he was correcting back.  I checked our altitude to be 6;200 feet - within vertical path limits.  I responded with 'negative he is turning back.'  Controller came back with 'you are below the MVA'.  At this point we were passing ZZZZZ1 and on or above vertical path and returning to the magenta line heading east.  Normal ops at this point handed off to ZZZ center.  I work a fair amount of flights out of ZZZ; I was surprised to hear this from the controller.  We were absolutely never in any position of being in danger of terrain.  It was day VMC and all vertical path criteria were met and as I said maybe 1/2 mile left but pointing where we should be.   I will say this:  in cruise the FO and I de briefed this and he said to me 'maybe it's because I didn't use all the bank' to which when I queried this he mentioned we were heavy it was bumpy he didn't feel comfortable with 25 degrees of bank so he used less.  Intent to fly safely was there; but possibly this contributed to the controller seeing on his radar a slower rate of turn and slight track deviance.  I told the FO that unless we are single engine and below the shark tooth and in VNAV/LNAV we are protected for 25 degrees bank.  The FO is a stand up guy and has time in both seats at two other airlines previously but I do think the lower bank contributed possibly to this.

column121: Incorrect Hardware Stack-Up on LH Engine FWD Upper Mount BoltWe were performing a scheduled engine change and upon removal of the LH engine we found that the FWD Upper Mount Bolt was missing one of the two washers. AIPC (Aircraft Illustrated Parts Catalog) 71-21-01-01 calls out for 3 washers to be installed on this bolt. Shortly afterward; I observed an undervoltage indication on COM 2; and the ammeter showed a discharge condition consistent with a possible alternator or electrical system malfunction. Immediately after observing these indications; I lost two-way radio communications with ATC.I attempted to reestablish communications with ATC and squawked transponder code 7600 for lost communications. Due to concern over a potential alternator failure and possible continued degradation of electrical systems while operating in IMC; I elected to begin a descending left turn toward known VMC conditions; which I knew existed below approximately 2;800 feet. At the same time; I accomplished checklist procedures to reduce electrical load by turning off nonessential electrical equipment in an effort to conserve battery power and restore communications capability.At approximately 3;500 feet MSL; I was able to reestablish communications with ATC. ATC subsequently cleared me back to ZZZ via visual approach and assigned 3;000 feet. Shortly thereafter; I exited IMC conditions. I advised ATC of my intention to cancel IFR in the air; however; full communications were lost again immediately afterward. I again squawked 7600 and proceeded to enter the traffic pattern at ZZZ; landing without further incident.In hindsight; I recognize that the published IFR lost communications procedures could have been followed after the initial communications failure. However; during a high-workload; single-pilot IMC situation involving a suspected alternator failure; I prioritized returning to VMC conditions and landing as soon as practical. Additionally; after communications were briefly restored; I believe it would have been beneficial to request priority handling and request direct routing back to ZZZ. At the time of the initial communications failure; I attempted to request priority handling but was unable to confirm transmissions were being received and therefore selected transponder code 7600 under the assumption ATC would recognize the abnormal situation.

column121: During a recent cross-country flight; I departed with full fuel and conducted fuel tank changes approximately every hour after the initial 30 minutes of flight. En route; I continued monitoring fuel burn and engine operation; and no abnormal indications were observed during the flight. However; as the flight progressed and fuel levels decreased; I did not adjust my fuel management strategy to a more conservative approach. Specifically; I should have switched tanks more frequently at lower fuel levels and should have more seriously considered making an additional precautionary fuel stop.While complying with ATC instructions during the arrival and landing phase into ZZZ; I began noticing engine roughness. Recognizing the potential seriousness of the situation; I immediately contacted the tower and requested an immediate landing. ATC accommodated the request; and the aircraft landed safely without further incident. After landing; it was determined that approximately 10 gallons of fuel remained onboard.The issue arose primarily from inadequate conservatism in my fuel management decision-making. Contributing factors included over-reliance on planned fuel burn calculations; confidence that the remaining fuel quantity was sufficient; and failure to fully appreciate the reduced margin for error as fuel levels became lower. Although the aircraft landed safely with approximately 10 gallons of fuel remaining; I later recognized that my operational decisions unnecessarily reduced available safety margins.The concern was identified during post-flight reflection and review of the flight. After evaluating the circumstances; I realized that while regulatory fuel requirements may still have been met; my decisions did not reflect the level of conservatism and risk management expected for safe aeronautical decision-making. In hindsight; an additional fuel stop would have significantly improved the safety margin and reduced operational risk.From a human performance standpoint; several judgment and decision-making factors contributed to the situation. My perception during the flight was that fuel status remained acceptable based on calculations and expected fuel burn; however; this perception reduced my willingness to make more conservative operational choices. Plan continuation bias and confidence in the original flight plan likely influenced my reluctance to stop for additional fuel. Additionally; I recognize that I did not sufficiently account for the increased importance of proactive fuel management as usable fuel decreased.Corrective actions taken since the event include additional study and review of aircraft performance data; fuel burn calculations; and fuel management procedures. I have reevaluated my personal minimums and fuel reserve standards and will adopt a significantly more conservative approach moving forward. In future operations; I will switch fuel tanks more proactively when fuel quantities become lower and will not hesitate to make additional fuel stops whenever they improve operational safety margins.This event served as an important learning experience regarding aeronautical decision-making; risk management; and fuel planning discipline. I take full responsibility for my decisions and will continue working to improve my judgment; situational awareness; and operational conservatism in order to become a safer and more professional pilot.

column121: Summary:  I experienced a low speed runway excursion on landing; in a lightweight tailwheel airplane without differential brakes; due to the airplane weathervaning into the crosswind against a full opposite rudder input.I went for a 1.3 hour personal flight in a Sonex Waiex airplane out of ZZZ airport.  Due to preparations for an upcoming airshow; runway XX/XY was closed; and the airport was operating on runway XZL with winds from 200 degrees at 8 kts.  When returning for landing; the ATIS stated the wind had increased to 12 gust 19; creating a significant left crosswind condition.The Waiex is a tailwheel (conventional landing gear) airplane without differential brakes.  It has a single hand brake; and the tailwheel is steered with a pushrod link to the rudder.  It is an experimental amateur-built airplane.As I began the landing flare; I was using nearly full right rudder to align the aircraft heading with the runway; but was able to align it and opted to continue the landing.  The landing roll initially stayed straight; then the airplane began to weathervane left into the crosswind as I slowed; and the airframe began to shudder due to the rightward deflected tailwheel skidding on the pavement (the crosswind on the tail surfaces overpowered the traction of the tailwheel).  The airplane rolled off the edge into the grass at 20-25 kts and came to a stop about 30 feet from the edge of the runway; nearly aligned with runway heading.I notified tower that I had departed the runway into the grass due to crosswind gust exceeding my control authority; had not hit anything and would like to taxi clear; and tower cleared me to taxi back onto runway XZL and then exit at Taxiway 1.  From Taxiway 1 I contacted ground control and taxied back to the hangars.  There was no damage or evidence of the runway excursion on the airplane.

Tower asked if there were any injuries or damage; we replied negative and that we could re-enter the runway and taxi to the next intersection and exit. As we taxied by the windsock I noticed the direction appeared to be northerly or northeasterly than the tower had reported. Another factor was that I have limited time flying from the rear seat. The majority of my 7AC time has been from the front; this was only my second landing from the rear seat in several years.In retrospect; I should have requested runway XY or XZ to mitigate the crosswind and tailwind components. I do not feel a go around would have been appropriate; as the speed at the initiation of the ground loop was very low.

column121: On Day 0; at approximately XA:45; I (the remote pilot) was operating a DJI Mini 5 Pro small unmanned aircraft system (sUAS) from my residence. Although I hold an active FAA Part 107 Remote Pilot Certificate and have approximately 150 hours of small UAS flight time; this flight was conducted recreationally as detailed in the LAANC authorizations. The drone was equipped with the required anti-collision and navigation (NAV) strobes: one top-mounted Firehouse Technology ARC PRO (flashing white on top) and four additional ARC PROs (flashing red on the port side and flashing green on the starboard side). These strobes and mounts increased the takeoff weight (TOW) of the drone to 352 grams. I maintained visual line of sight (VLOS) with the sUAS throughout the entire flight. My home is located just outside the controlled airspace of both ZZZ and ZZZ1.I was flying under two active LAANC authorizations (ZZZ) (ZZZ1). Both authorizations were valid from XA:00 to XM:00 and authorized a maximum altitude of 300 feet AGL.Purpose of the flight: I intended to take photographs of Aircraft Y that was on approach to Runway XXL at ZZZ. The approach path passes almost directly over my house. I had not set the drone's maximum altitude limit to 300 feet AGL before takeoff because I originally planned only a very short flight to capture the photos; land; and possibly fly again later (the LAANCs remained valid until XM:00. I climbed to approximately 385 feet AGL. Aircraft Y was approximately 0.25 miles west of my location at 2175 feet AGL when I was taking the photos. After taking several photos; I continued southeast to perform a loop. During this maneuver; I crossed into ZZZ1 airspace while still at 385 feet AGL (where the authorized maximum was only 300 feet AGL). I immediately turned north after crossing the highway and entered a grid with a 400-foot AGL maximum; but I remained at 385 feet AGL (still above my LAANC clearance of 300 feet). Continuing north; I then turned west at Road X (crossing into Class G airspace) and proceeded to the intersection of Road X and Road Y. While circling south near Road Y; I realized I had been operating above the altitude authorized by my LAANC. I immediately returned to my residence; landed safely; and began preparing this report. I am submitting this report voluntarily to promote aviation safety. I will provide my complete flight log and any additional information or data requested.

column121: I was training a trainee on sector XX. The sector wasnt super busy but for him at 25% hours; it may have felt slightly busier. The complexity turned fast when Aircraft X went missed at ZZZ on the ILS Z Rwy XX because of wind shear. Aircraft X was a chinese speaker and definitely didn't understand english perfectly nor did he understand approach procedures correctly. More on that in a minute. After going missed; we vectored Aircraft X and another aircraft toward Rwy XY at ZZZ. Aircraft X was then giving instructions to fly to ZZZZZ direct ZZZZZ1 direct ZZZ for the RNAV X Rwy XY. Procedurally; if you do the approach over ZZZZZ; then there is no procedure turn authorized. Well; Aircraft X did the procedure turn! And as we had another aircraft right behind him; the complexity shot through the roof. I tried to handhold my trainee because I think I have a solid amount of experience and could help him through the situation. I think I did a pretty good job. So I was speaking to my trainee during most of his transmissions. I told my trainee to cancel the back aircrafts approach clearance; maintain 130 thousand; and make him do a left 360 for spacing. As soon as my trainee gives that clearance; Tower calls us to switch the runway again! Which in turn; brings more complexity to the situation. My trainee cancels the approach clearance of Aircraft X. Once that happens; the back aircraft requests something that we dont quite hear; and thats when I step in. I tell the back aircraft that Tower just switched runways on us; and to fly back to Runway XX; and climb him to 140 thousand knowing that my next move would be to climb Aircraft X. Then Aircraft X asks if he should be on a heading. He was currently climbing through like 123 thousand; and flying through a 120 thousand MIA box; but was going to momentarily be in a 129 thousand MIA box. My Trainee told Aircraft X to fly heading 070 which I knew wouldnt be good in a moment. So I keyed up and told Aircraft X reaching 130 thousand to fly heading 270 which would get him away from the other aircraft and be good with terrain. Aircraft X never turned to the heading my trainee gave; and technically did go into the 129 MIA box at 128 thousand briefly before reaching 130 thousand and turning northwest bound. The aircraft never turned below terrain and I felt that we handled the situation very well and the trainee and I both learned some things.RecommendationMy trainee thought he was doing the correct thing by terminating the approach clearance for Aircraft X; when in retrospect; we should have told him to fly the published missed approach and climb to an appropriate altitude to stay separated from our other aircraft and terrain. I think once we did cancel the clearance for Aircraft X we had our hands tied and I think the next course of action we took was the correct one; except we should have issued a low altitude alert as well!My only other recommendation would be for Aircraft X and that would be to correctly learn that procedure turns have to be authorized from a controlled if they are charted non-authorized in the pubs. We never had a chance to talk to Aircraft X again about that as we needed to finish cleaning everything else up from all the missed approaches and runway changes.

column121: Descent into ORD via BENKY6; just past MONKZ given lower altitude by approach control.  Level at 6000; we were told to slow to speed 210; fly heading 360.  Just as we began to slow; we encountered wake turbulence.  We both called 'upset' I was PM; my FO was PF.  He disconnected auto pilot/auto throttle and we recovered with approximate 30 degree roll in both directions.  We gained about 100 ft in altitude; and continued on downwind heading.  Once stabilized; we turned to heading 360.  We called ATC with a wake turbulence encounter; and ATC responded with 'there is no aircraft near you' which was incorrect because we could see the heavy jet turning base in front of us.   In fact we even used VVM (Verbalize; Verify; Monitor)/CRM/TEM (Threat and Error Management) skills to say careful for potential wake behind the large aircraft.  No mention of potential wake turbulence by ATC however.  After encounter; upset; and recovery we told ATC of our wake turbulence encounter.  ATC asked how much roll we had; and if there were any injuries.  Below 10000 ft/sterile it's kinda hard to get an instant injury report.  We said no injuries; roll of 30degrees left/right.  We continued approach landing 28C.  By now heavy jet was 7-8 miles in front of us.  Approach handed us off to tower at SEIKA;  Tower advised cleared to land 28C; caution wake turbulence.  That was the first time ATC mentioned we were following a heavy jet.  I acknowledged landing clearance and copy wake turbulence that we already encountered.   Landing/ taxi/parking all non-event.  Once parked; I was then able to ask Flight Attendants if there were any injuries/upset passengers.  There were none.

column121: Departure and climb were routine. I was the Captain/PM and the First Officer was PF.After leveling off; we received an L HYD RESV EICAS message. We accomplished the applicable QRH non-normal checklist; which did not resolve the issue. A review of the status page indicated left hydraulic quantity decreasing; suggesting a system leak. Based on indications; we anticipated progression to L HYD SYS PRESS.The leak appeared slow; and after reviewing the L HYD SYS PRESS non-normal checklist; we assessed that continuing to destination was acceptable. We contacted dispatch via SATCOM; requested Maintenance be advised; and asked for concurrence on continuing. Dispatch confirmed preference to continue to ZZZ.We advised Dispatch that we would likely request priority handling in the terminal area and anticipated the need for a tow off the runway. Requested they notify ZZZ operations.Approximately 30 minutes later (about 90 minutes from ZZZ); we received L HYD ENG PUMP. We accomplished the associated non-normal checklist and secured the engine-driven pump within approximately 90 seconds of the EICAS message.Approximately 5 minutes later; we received L HYD SYS PRESS. We accomplished the associated non-normal checklist and secured the electric pump within approximately 60 seconds.  Dispatch was updated and confirmed all parties had been notified.We requested priority handling with ZZZ Center upon check-in and were vectored toward ZZZ. We requested direct ZZZZZ (final fix on the ZZZZZ arrival) to support our configuration planning.The First Officer and I developed a configuration plan; including Flaps 1 at ZZZZZ. Subsequently; ATC issued a STAR change to ZZZZZ1 arrival; and we requested direct ZZZZZ1; which supported our plan.We were initially advised to expect the ILS XXL and completed the approach setup and briefing. Approximately 20 NM from the airport; ATC reassigned us to ILS XXR. I initially declined due to workload; but advised ATC we could accept XXR if doing otherwise would disrupt the ZZZ operation. After being cleared for the ILS XXR; we were unable to obtain a valid localizer ident or glideslope. Upon query; ATC advised the ILS was out of service and offered the RNAV approach. Due to proximity to the airport and workload; we declined the RNAV and advised we would need to execute a missed approach with the gear remaining down the rest of the flight. ATC issued a  heading and climb to 3000 ft. ZZZ Approach then offered the ILS XXL; which we accepted. The remainder of the approach was uneventful.The First Officer performed the landing. I assumed control at approximately 100 knots for rollout. Rollout was uneventful. A company tug met the aircraft and towed us clear of the runway to parking.The CRM training we received was extremely helpful to us in navigating the challenges we faced as a crew. We were task loaded with a complicated non-normal checklist. We had multiple changes by ATC  on the arrival.  Specifically; reviewing the checklist before executing it; developing a what if plan such as considering an unanticipated missed approach with the landing gear down and the flaps in the alternate configuration; and using our resources such as ATC and dispatch to obtain support in the terminal area.  The company procedures also prepared us well for this challenge.  A recent intensified focus on fuel planning led to an enhanced awareness of our fuel status; which became critical on the missed approach. We both experienced this situation in the simulator many times so we felt very well prepared for this event and felt we; as a crew; maintained good situational awareness.For an aircraft operating under distress with a complex non-normal checklist; the number of late changes (arrival and runway assignment) significantly increased our workload. Minimizing changes in the terminal area would improve safety and reduce crew task saturation.

There was a jolt when the airplane banked. I tried to gently climb back to altitude so I did not over stress the wings.  We told approach that we had a wake turbulence encounter. We were assigned 210 knots before Scole. After we were back at altitude we continued the arrival. We had a second wake turbulence encounter later in the arrival after transitioning to the local altimiter setting. Now I'm trying to remember the exact altitude of the second wake turbulence encounter  I think it was around 15000. It was not as severe as the first one. After the second wake encounter we were told to slow to 180. The PIC looked at his MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) and saw that there was no wind. One passenger was not seated during the first encounter.Suggestions: I will review the unusual attitude recoveries. I should have requested a slower speed. We should have checked on the passengers but we were both concerned with flying the plane.

column121: On flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ; I was the PF and the Captain was the PM. Departure; climb; and cruise were normal. We were cleared to descend from 4;000ft to 3;000ft. While descending into ZZZ at approximately 3;500 feet; we were cleared for the visual approach to Runway XX. During the approach; the left engine fuel flow indication displayed 0 PPH. The PM notified Operations of the indication issue and potential write-up; and requested Runway XY. ATC cleared us for landing on Runway XY.At approximately 3;000 feet; left engine roughness was noted. The PM selected the auxiliary fuel pumps to LOW. Following an RPM drop; the PM selected the auxiliary fuel pumps to HIGH. Engine roughness continued. Ran memory items. Reduced thrust from the left engine was observed and additional right rudder was required to maintain coordinated flight. Airspeed was maintained above Vyse. The PM accomplished the engine inoperative in-range and approach checklists in the QRH. The crew briefed continuing the approach in the current configuration due to the left engine continuing to produce partial power. At that point the aircraft was turning base to final. The approach and landing on Runway XY were otherwise normal. A positive exchange of controls took place and the Captain assumed control of the aircraft during the landing rollout.After landing; I briefed the passengers regarding the presence of vehicles approaching the aircraft. The left engine subsequently lost all power after exiting the taxiway. The aircraft was secured without further incident.

column121: First flight since annual and also my first flight in months. Pre-flight checks were perfect so I proceeded onto runway XX. I took the runway and powered up half way well holding brakes to make sure engine data was good before releasing brakes and going full power. Plane had lots of power and took off as expected with all engine data as expected. I turned cross wind at pattern altitude 2400 feet; raised the flaps and started reducing manifold pressure to 25'. I then started to reduce RPMs as I started the downwind turn as I had climbed to 2600 feet. At this point the engine went to idle and fuel pump alarm came on. I turned on vapor suppression pump and switched tanks from left to right. This made no difference so I turned off vapor suppression and pressed the primer button. This brought the power back temporarily; at this point I announced aircraft in distress and intent to land runway XY and asked traffic starting on runway XX if they could clear runway XX. They were able abort takeoff and vacate . During call I had pressed fuel primer again this added power again and put me a little higher than expected and over XY. I did a S type descent deploying speed brakes and landing flaps to runway XY and engine died on rollout. I believe this because I forgot to turn on fuel vapor suppression on rollout.My first move should have been to turn back for runway XY and 2nd move to turn on backup fuel pump instead of vapor suppression and switching tanks. I need to review my emergency flight procedures well sitting in airplane so I can 'dry' practice as part of keeping current. I believe I did well. I had delayed this flight many days due to not feeling up to par; busy traffic pattern and sub optimal weather.

column121: Pilot Flying - Person A (PIC)Pilot Monitoring - Person B (NFP/First Officer)Event:On Day 0 LR 60 at approximately at or about XA:00 Person A (PF) and NFP (Person B; PM) executed an emergency descent from approximately FL270 for the smell of electrical fumes during climb on the ZZZZZX SID direct to ZZZZZ1 intersection.While climbing in heading mode and deviating for weather; we were given direct ZZZZZ1 on the ZZZZZX SID. PF and PM noticed FMS1 was not working properly. PF/PIC exchanged flight controls to First Officer to continue climb direct to ZZZZZ1 intersection since his FMS 2 was working properly and while PIC troubleshot FMS1 and took the radio communications with ATC. We were then cleared to climb to FL310; when F.O's PFD (Primary Flight Display) FAILED and immediately followed by the smell of electrical fumes. PIC Requested Flight Controls from FO; PIC took over the flight controls and requested priority handling for smoke or fumes in the cockpit and performed an emergency descent to assigned ATC altitude of 11;000 and requested FO to run the Smoke and Fumes EMERGENCY CHECK LIST. No smoke was observed at any point in flight or in the cockpit. Passengers were informed there was a maintenance issue by the PM and told to remain seated with their seatbelts on.PF and PM donned oxygen masks and began the appropriate checklist and emergency descent. PF then requested vectors back to ZZZ. The 'Smoke and Fumes in the Cockpit' checklist was completed up to the first decision point where PF and PM then determined the fumes had dissipated. ATC provided vectors and altitudes for the emergency descent and return to ZZZ. PF continued flying the airplane; while PM set up the cockpit for the ILS XXL. The descent; approach; and before landing checklists were completed. PF then executed a safe landing on runway XXL and taxied via 1; 2; 3; 4 to the ramp. PIC decided additional emergency assistance was unnecessary. The airplane was then parked by the PIC at the ramp; PM de- powered the aircraft and then PF opened the door for our 7 passengers. One female passenger received brief medical attention from emergency personnel and left the airport under her own power. After taking a moment to evaluate our performance both PIC & FO in this situation; we felt we handled it well. However; we could have been more thorough with the appropriate emergency checklists. This was a highly stressful situation; and we were mainly focused on getting the aircraft on the ground as quickly and safely as possible.

column121: At just past XA:00 on Day 0 I was returning from ZZZ to LOM and requested RNAV 6 from PHL Approach Control (123.8) for practicing my IFR flow (the field was visual). A request that was accepted by PHL Approach. I was directed to the LASBE (IAF-RNAV 6) and cleared for the approach. On turning to the final approach course; I told PHL approach that I had visual of the field. They advised me that there was no traffic observed. At this time; I canceled my IFR. I switched to CTAF and made a 9-mile final call on the CTAF; followed by a 5-mile final call; followed by a short final call. I did a quick scan of the runway on short final; and everything looked good to land.As I touched down; I see a plane on 24 at the opposite end of the runway; and that is the first time I heard him. His call was to warn me of his presence on the runway. He had just rolled on to 24 and was fortunately stationary at that end. There was no danger of any collision since I stopped within 1500 feet or so of touchdown and taxied off the runway. Once the runway was clear; the other plane departed as soon as I was off the runway. When I walked into the FBO (there is a speaker tuned to CTAF); the people there told me that they heard my 3rd call - the short final call; but not the first two (or did not pay attention). They said they never heard the other plane till he piped up to warn me of his presence when I had already touched down and I was on my landing roll. What did I learn? When I am on a short final; I am generally focused on the touch down point; typically the numbers at LOM; and once I pass the threshold and begin my level out and flare is when I raise my eyes to the end of the runway. I think that is what I did on this landing as well and by the time the presence of the plane at the other end registered with me; I was on the ground and slowing down. It was too late to go around. I should not assume that the runway is mine even if I have been making calls; scanning and hearing nothing on the radio. I should always be more watchful and continue scanning the entire runway environment; including at this late stage in my landings.

column121: On Day 0; I accompanied another drone pilot to conduct operations at a project site for Company A. The other pilot has been operating at this location for approximately two years and had previously coordinated flight activities for the site.At the time of the operation; I was under the understanding that the required authorization/ Certificate of Authorization (COA) obtained for the project site applied to multiple pilots operating under the same organization. Once I recognized that my understanding of the authorization requirements may have been incorrect; I immediately terminated the flight operation and informed my manager of the situation. Following internal discussion; we decided to voluntarily submit this self-report in the interest of transparency and continued operational safety.No incidents; injuries; property damage; loss of control; or unsafe interactions with other aircraft occurred during the operation.To help prevent similar situations in the future; our team is implementing additional internal drone operation procedures and training measures. This includes the development of a structured drone training program for new pilots; with emphasis on:FAA authorization and airspace requirementsPilot-specific operational approvals and responsibilitiesPre-flight compliance verification proceduresFlight safety protocols and operational best practicesOur intent is to strengthen awareness; standardize compliance procedures; and reinforce a proactive safety culture for all future drone operations.

column121: Aircraft X had been cleared direct to ZZZZZ intersection (a transition fix to ILS XX ZZZZ).   We were descending to cross ZZZZZ at or above 5000'.  Descending through 8500  and slowing to clean maneuvering I called for flaps 1.  The flap needles on the flap indicator did not move.  We continued the descent to 8000' and I selected ALT HOLD.  The FO and I both confirmed a flap malfunction.  I gave the aircraft to the FO and I requested priority handling with ZZZZ approach and asked to maintain 8000'.  This was approved and approach clearance was cancelled and was issued a radar vector.  I then stated fuel in minutes and pounds and souls on board.  As we were vectored in the terminal area we agreed the we had a trailing  edge flap disagreement issue.  I ran the checklist; tested the  flight attendants; made a PA and coordinated with approach control to head to the airport.  I then took the airplane back to perform the landing.  We coordinated with tower to stop the aircraft on a taxiway to have Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) visually inspect the tires and brakes and any other abnormalities they could see.  None were observed and we continued to the gate.  We entered the abnormality in the aircraft Electronic Log Book.  Upon completing the parking checklist we discussed all the details with maintenance personnel. Next I completed the mandatory calls to Chief Pilot AND Dispatch."

column121: On final approach into ZZZ while the FO was flying the Autopilot disconnected and the RA flag on the FO side displayed. He then lost his flight director and ILS guidance.  This is also when he noticed that the electric trim stopped working on his control column.  The CA then took control and was unable to have any success with the electric trim on his control column.  Since we were already flaps 5 and on the ILS we decided the best option was to continue the approach and request priority handling as to mitigate the chance of a go-around which would have been harder to control while manually trimming.  We continued landing with a normal approach and taxied off the runway to the gate with no further issues.  We then remembered that the previous crew had seen an RA flag on their flight but they did not write it up as it did not come back.
column123: Previous crew told us they had seen a RA flag on previous flights but did not write up because it quickly disappeared. Our preflight and taxi was normal. On takeoff the controls were excessively heavy during rotation but normalized during initial climb. Autopilot was engaged and flight continued normally. On approach into ZZZ at approximately 3000 ft the FO side RA flag came up on the Primary Flight Display (PFD) and the autopilot disengaged. Then I lost flight director guidance. We chose to continue as the plane was stable and we had the runway in sight. I tried to trim the plane but electric trim was not working. I told the captain who took control and also could not operate electric trim. He continued flying while I manually trimmed the airplane for him. We requested priority handling out of an abundance of caution and elected to continue the approach since we felt a go around with no trim could put us into an undesired aircraft state. We landed normally and without incident and taxied to the gate under our own power. The maintenance discrepancies were noted and we contacted the Chief Pilot.

column121: Flying the visual approach backed up by the ILS 3. Prior to commencing the approach; it was briefed with knowledge of terrain and obstacles; and I had my terrain display present on my MFD. I was PIC and PF.ATC provided us with a descent down to 3000' at midfield downwind; and then provided us with an initial base leg vector; prior to receiving clearance for the visual approach. Being approximately 5 miles from the FAF SIPME and already on a tighter base leg; I requested 2600' to beset in the altitude selector; which is the minimum altitude at the FAF SIPME. After being cleared for the visual approach; the plan was to continue the descent down to the minimum altitude at the FAF and capture the glideslope.At about 4600' and recognizing that we were slightly high turning into our base leg; I increased the descent rate briefly in order to trend towards the glide slope intercept altitude. After I recognized that we were trending towards it I began to intermittently shallow our descent out; ultimately setting less than -1000 FPM as the final vertical speed setting. At no point did we descend below the minimum segment altitude prior to the FAF of 2600'.At approximately 3 miles from the FAF SIPME; and approximately 2700 - 2800 feet; we received Terrain Terrain Pull Up." I initiated the escape maneuver; but almost immediately after initiating it and having a pitch up attitude; the terrain caution concluded. Since this message cleared almost instantly with a slight pitch up attitude; and no visual obstacles were in our path; it was determined that we were clear of the terrain threat. Being in complete VFR; and back to a desirable aircraft state at an appropriate speed prior to the FAF; I determined we were in a safe position to continue and execute the approach. We proceeded inbound to complete the approach; having no exceedances or other events occur.Afterwards; we had noted on the Jeppesen Approach plate that the approximate location just prior to receiving the terrain caution has terrain listed at 1785'. I had briefed terrain and the highest obstacles; but what could have been done better is to emphasize this specific point as it pertains to my descent plan for the approach. Being in VFR conditions; we had maintained a visual on the terrain prior to the base leg; and it wasn't until we were above it that it was out of sight.In hindsight as PIC and PF; recognizing that we were high and having been turned onto a shorter base leg; this could have been preemptively resolved by communicating with ATC; and potentially even requesting vectors to provide more time to descend.As a crew we debriefed this event on the ground; and talked in depth about exactly how this could've been prevented. We concluded that more in depth briefings on the terrain we will encounter at specific points; a more clear and shallowed descent plan; and avoidance ofcomplacency in VFR conditions could've worked to prevent this from occurring."

column121: Taxing on SP; and we were told to hold short of the boundary line. Listening to traffic ahead; they are switching over near FW/A7. Got clearance to go onto SE and then told to continue SP and contact Ground. Contact ground and cleared to A13 with hold short V(this is the 3rd change to our clearance in about 3 minutes). At this point; Ground tells us to hold short A7 (we're turning onto Alpha). Talked to Tower and Tower advised that we had missed an instruction to hold short of the boundary line. Advised tower that we thought the boundary line was the communication boundary line abeam FW/A7(Chart 20-9B). Tower advised me that no the Boundary line referenced is for the Non-Movement Area on SP with implied instructions to hold short of Alpha(Ground Markings Not on the Chart). Asked for clarification on where the boundary line was they advised SP and Alpha intersection. Contributing factors was construction and taxiway lines barely visible at the intersection with construction on the north side of alpha taxiway. Unfamiliar with where the non-movement boundary line starts; and Taxiways begin; because we were on a taxiway (SP); we incorrectly assumed the communication boundary line on Chart 20-9B was the non-movement boundary line and not a taxiway marking. Suggestions: In chart 20-B; reference the boundary of where the non-movement area starts; it is not clear on any of the taxiway charts where the non-movement area ends. Ramp control should also use standard phraseology. 'Taxi SP hold short of Alpha' instead of telling us to hold short of a boundary line that is marked on the taxiway and is faded from construction and aircraft movement.

column121: At 31k feet approximately 50 Nm north of flagstaff we had the auto pilot disengage as well as the ventral rudder and yaw damp. We had several red and amber CAS messages and red X's on both PFD's (Primary Flight Display). I immediately hit the quick disconnect and then Person A grabbed the yoke as he was the one flying. When we realized what we had lost I contacted ATC (LA Center) and informed them we had lost autopilot and some other systems and needed to descend to 25k which is what our memory items are for the loss of systems mentioned. He asked if we were declaring an emergency and I advised ATC so we could get the priority handling. Once we started I reminded Person A of the possible Dutch roll and then grabbed the QRH; Person A said he felt vibrations in the thrust levers which I also felt. By this time most messages had cleared. Around 25k I engaged the yaw damper. I then asked for lower at which point they gave us shock at 12k. We determined the system was back online and engaged the autopilot. At this point the system was still only using GPS 1 and AHRS 2 was in backup GPS and AHRS 1 was not online. We then told Albuquerque we seemed to be back online and things seemed ok. We got cleared to YOLOW at 7k and I called the airport in sight and got cleared the visual. Person A then hand flew the airplane the rest of the way in in case we had an autopilot issue again.Suggestions: Better information on GPS jamming locations and do not use on known flight routes.

column121: Was conducting a repositions flight for Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1 after dropping off a different diamond in ZZZ that same day. Everything was routine/ normal / in limits until about 300 ft - 400 ft AGL in the upwind. Noticed an abnormal noise/ slight vibration/ engine roughness coming from the left engine. A few seconds later probably around 500agl received a Left hand engine ECU (Engine Control Unit) A and B caution. No change in performance or engine output/ engine indications noted. Immediately after this communicated a decision to come back to land as a precaution. First coordinated with Pilot Monitoring (Person A); then Communicated to ATC that we were turning back to land XXR due to abnormal annunciation. Person A then was helping run/ find checklists while I continued flying. They cleared us to land in the upwind. Everything was normal until reaching midfield/ approach end of the downwind; when ATC advised that they potentially had seen a puff of 'smoke.' We then scanned and noticed in the left engine that we were leaking fluid pretty heavily. Initially was thinking it was coolant due to location of leak (fins on the inboard side of the nacelle). Other than ECU Annunciations engine page looked normal and engine output felt normal. Continued to setup for landing and focused on flying the aircraft while there was still available engine power. During the turn from downwind to final; we both realized that it smelled like fuel was potentially leaking. I continued to fly the aircraft and focus on landing when PM suggested we secure the engine just in case to negate a fire hazard. We then ran secure items and engine was feathered by about 300 AGL on final. Left gear down; but brought flaps back up to APP in order to not lose airspeed; maintained approximately 85-90 knots down to the runway and landed safely. Attempted to make turn off of runway; however was unable to continue due to asymmetric thrust overpowering steering. Stopped on taxiway and requested a tow.Suggestions: Keep two pilots on reposition flights. It was infinitely helpful having a second set of eyes and hands assist with the problem.
column123: On takeoff from ZZZ I was pilot monitoring (PM). Pilot flying (PF) was Person B. In the upwind; approximately 500 AGL; two CAS messages appeared; followed by slight engine roughness of LH engine. CAS messages were: LH ECU A FAIL & LH ENG ECU B FAIL. I verbalized the non normal in the flightdeck and PF called ATC requesting landing back on rwy XXR at ZZZ. No emergency was declared at this time since the engine appeared to be running mostly normal - load and RPMs were unchanged; thrust seemed stable; and PF did not report any unusual control pressures. Tower cleared the aircraft for right traffic and cleared us to land at that time. As PF turned crosswind I performed the landing checklist to the line; verified that the PF was in control of aircraft; and let him know that I was pulling out AFM for simultaneous ECU (Engine Control Unit) A&B failure. As the aircraft began the initial descent to land; tower called and let us know that they might have momentarily seen smoke; but it was no longer observed. At this time I noticed that the LH engine was leaking fluid from the cooling fins. I verbalized this to PF; and initially thought that it was coolant; but as we turned onto final i began to smell fuel and suspected a fuel leakage. ~500 AGL verbalized this to PF and suggested securing the engine to mitigate fire risk. PF agreed; I asked him to pull the LH throttle idle so that his control wouldn't be compromised and then I performed the remainder of the engine securing checklist as published. Landed XXR at ZZZ and taxied off the runway but was unable to continue further taxi with the LH engine secured. Tower coordinated a tow off of the movement area back to the maintenance hanger. Dispatch & maintenance were notified; I wrote out the aircraft squawk; and then this report was submitted.Suggestions: Keep two pilots on Maintenance ferry flight pickups.

column121: Situation 1:While operating from Location X at the intersection of the 50 ft and 100 ft LAANC grid; we moved the Landing Zone (LZ) for safety reasons but failed to properly reassess the new location. I didn't account for the offset of the new LZ being farther east than we originally calculated; and I failed to make the necessary adjustment in the field after relocating. After moving; we were positioned under the 50 ft grid but did not adjust our operational assumptions accordingly.Situation 2:Because the change in LZ was not fully accounted for; we continued the flight using the 50 ft operating plan without adjusting for the offset. This resulted in operating at 100 ft when the correct authorization for that location was 50 ft.Main cause:The primary issue was not fully re-verifying the updated LAANC grid after relocating the LZ. The offset shift was not recalculated in the field; leading to the incorrect assumption that we had exited the 50 ft grid when we were still inside it.Going forward:Anytime the LZ is moved during operations; I will stop and fully reassess the new position before continuing flight. column121: During a review of my UAS records; I discovered that I had inadvertently conducted commercial small UAS operations while my recurrent training was overdue by approximately two months. As a corrective action; a new UAS credential and training verification SOP was introduced. This SOP requires confirmation of Remote Pilot currency before accepting or conducting any commercial UAS mission; periodic review of pilot credentials; redundant calendar reminders for recurrent training deadlines; and documentation of credential status in the mission file.Additionally; as an extra safety and compliance measure; we will complete the FAA ALC-515 recurrent training course annually; even if the regulatory recurrent training interval allows a longer period. This annual review will help ensure continued familiarity with current Part 107 requirements; operating limitations; airspace procedures; and UAS safety responsibilities.This issue was unintentional and was corrected immediately upon discovery. The lesson learned is that currency requirements must be verified through a formal process; rather than relying only on memory or a single automated reminder.

column121: I was working Aircraft X on final. I had previously handed off Aircraft Y who was inbound from the west for pattern work to the Local Control (LC2) controller. I had cleared him to land and told him about traffic on the downwind for the parallel runway. I told Aircraft X that traffic had him in sight and would maintain visual separation when Aircraft X was about 4 mile final and there was about 2 miles between him and Aircraft Y. I had heard the controller working Aircraft Y tell Aircraft Y to maintain visual separation and caution wake turbulence which is how I knew that Aircraft Y reported Aircraft X in sight.I noticed that Aircraft Y was flying a shallower downwind than was usual and was doing about 120 kt. on the downwind which is considerable faster than what similar aircraft do on the downwind. I told the controller who was working Aircraft Y to 'watch for the slop over' because of the way Aircraft Y was flying. I then observed Aircraft Y turn base wide and 'slopped over' or veer into the path of Aircraft X. I could not tell who was in front or behind from my perspective; but I then saw Aircraft X turn sharply to the right as if he was afraid that Aircraft Y was going to impact his left side. I then told the controller that Aircraft Y was too close to Aircraft X. The controller then proceeded to instruct Aircraft Y to start a climb and go around. Aircraft X then said that Aircraft Y was way too close to which I just replied 'Roger.' About 30 seconds later Aircraft X said he was executing missed approach so I issued the standard missed approach instructions which is heading 195 and climb and maintain 3000.I would strongly recommend to suspend all flight training at SNA. The runways at SNA are 500 ft. apart which is extremely close. We are depending on low time or student pilots to turn the base in such a manner as to avoid colliding with airlines and jet traffic inbound on Runway 20R. The AFD instructs pilots to do a 15-degree offset dog leg for base to final turn. That is a lot to ask a pilot who is training or who just got the license. It's a complicated maneuver to begin with but it is a vital necessity due to the proximity of the runways.I see it constantly where the pattern workers on Runway 20L will slop over and veer into the final for Runway 20R. It happens constantly and no matter how many times we tell pilots not to do it or correct the pilots; it happens on a regular basis. Luckily when there has been slop over; either nobody is on final for Runway 20R or the inbound traffic is far enough in front or behind the pattern worker to take enough corrective action. It is my own personal belief that someday a small aircraft will slop over and collide with an airliner or business jet inbound on Runway 20R. In my mind; if flight training is allowed to continue; it's not a question of 'IF' but a question of 'WHEN' a catastrophe will occur. Mixing commercial jet traffic and VFR pattern workers who are either learning or have low time at SNA is a recipe for disaster that will cost a lot of people their lives. There are a number of neighboring airports where the student pilots can go and do their flight training without putting the lives of airline passengers at risk; I believe that right to live of 200 plus passengers on an airliner supersedes the right of a student pilot to learn to fly at SNA.
column123: Aircraft Y; in the traffic pattern and on the downwind leg; reported Aircraft X in sight. Pilot stated that he would maintain visual separation from Aircraft X. Aircraft Y was then cleared for the option" on Runway 20L. Aircraft X was on short final; arriving Runway 20R; which is 500 ft. laterally separated from the parallel Runway 20L.Runway 20R is the air carrier and primary IFR runway here at SNA at 5;700x150 ft. Runway 20L is the primary traffic pattern / light GA runway here at SNA at 2;887x75. Aircraft Y turned final to Runway 20L off the left wing of Aircraft X; but overshot the centerline of Runway 20L; flying too-wide of a turn; and nearly cutting off Aircraft X; who had to take an evasive turning maneuver to avoid an NMAC. Aircraft X executed a go-around. John Wayne Orange County Airport (SNA) is a very busy Class C airspace air carrier airport in Southern California. The airport handles about 11.5 million passengers per year; while handling a high volume of arrivals and departures daily between XA:00 and XQ:00. The airport has two parallel runways (see above); and is situated on a 500-acre plot of land. The airport has a large terminal that has 22 regularly used airline gates. It also has a ramp just south of the terminal used for air cargo operations. The airport has 3 FBOs on the field with a very high volume of corporate and private jet traffic.Through the years; there have been several close calls between pattern working light GA aircraft and airliners. There have been many light GA airplane incidents that have been attributed to wake turbulence. In my years at SNA; I have witnessed several very close calls between airliners and small aircraft conducting flight training. As a controller; and as one who worked this high volume of traffic daily; I am baffled by the pressing need by these local flight schools to conduct flight training here at a busy air carrier facility. It is not uncommon to have 6 or 7 low time student pilots in the traffic pattern; right next to arriving and departing large and heavy aircraft. The airspace and airfield is so limited in space that it is a requirement for departing GA aircraft off Runway 20L to conduct an immediate left 15-degree offset turn to avoid "drifting" into departing jets off Runway 20R. The margin for error here at SNA is virtually none. Airline pilots and passengers should not be put in this dangerous situation day to day. It is a common occurrence here to see student pilots soloing for the first time; in close quarters with airliners.I rarely feel the need to file a report regarding anything that will hinder the flying public in any way; but I've seen enough here at SNA to prompt me to do something to look out for peoples' lives. I highly recommend that SNA suspend flight training indefinitely. VFR itinerate traffic; no problem. Furthermore; to increase safety here; I recommend that Runway 20L be permanently decommissioned and recommissioned as a taxiway. Furthermore; I recommend that an EMAS be installed at the departure ends of Runway 20R and Runway 02L. I would also recommend that a displaced threshold be built at the approach end of Runway 20R in order to increase the length of takeoff rolls for larger aircraft. The current 5;700-foot runway; in my opinion; is not enough of a safety margin when the land space currently exits for a displaced threshold for departures."

column123: I was acting as a safety pilot for my friend who owns a Cessna 182H after getting fuel and doing a thorough preflight we departed on a cross country flight to an uncontrolled field. We were close to a taxi way and did not see or hear any other traffic in the area so we shut the engine down and pushed the aircraft off the runway and on to the taxi way as to not damage the tire and to get it clear of the runway. We then walked to the FBO where the manager of the airport who was also a A&P offered us some air so we could pump up the tire and see if it was leaking. We pumped up the tire and inspected it and did not see or hear any leaking. We then taxied to the end of the runway and departed to our home airport and landed safely. When we were taxiing in on our arrival we could feel the front nose wheel felt slack again and after we parked on the ramp we could see that it had definitely lost more air. Once we tied down the aircraft we discussed what we should have done differently. We should have had a mechanic take the tire off and inspect it for leaks or just replaced the tire all together. Ive learned from this event that it's never a good call to takeoff with a tire that's in question even though we thought it just needed air.

Gear handle appeared down; but hydraulic pressure was indicating zero.  I turned the switches back on and pressed the gear handle down (it moved slightly further down) and saw hydraulic pressure coming back up.Upon further investigation at the maintenance shop; it was discovered that the landing gear handle detent stop was misaligned and the gear handle was free to move up and was not held down by the mechanical stop as it should be. By design; the landing gear selector valve vents pressure back to the hydraulic reservoir if the handle is between detents. They were able to re-rig the mechanical stop to restore proper function.The benefit of being a Lake with the engine on a pylon is that damage was minimal and limited to the wing float and scrapes on the lower fuselage keel where it also contacted the runway.

column123: Aircraft X had an MEL 21-XXX for One Auto Cabin Press Control.  Logbook; placard; mechanics; and crew complied with the MEL instructions and verifications. During the climbout; the flight crew felt increased pressure in their ears.  ATC cleared us to FL120; and somewhere between 10;000 and 12;000 feet; we received the EICAS Master Warning red lights and aural alert.  I was the pilot flying; so I took control of the aircraft and radios; disconnected the autopilot; stopped the climb; and informed ATC we needed an immediate descent to 10;000 feet.  The FO announced the type of aircraft condition; and all pilots donned our oxygen masks and established communications. I requested priority handling; requested a 180-degree turn back towards the ZZZZ airport; and a lower altitude.  We held in our present position below 10;000 feet and completed all required checklists; briefings; and reports.  Then we proceeded to ZZZZ [VOR] and held while we briefed the plan for an overweight landing.  We landed on runway XXL; Airport Rescue and Firefighting checked our aircraft on the taxiway; and followed us back to our parking spot.  I made two logbook entries for the pressurization problem and for the overweight landing.  I stayed on the flight deck to confer with the maintenance about the aircraft's issues.  ZZZZ ATC was very professional and helpful throughout and should be commended for their prior preparation and calm demeanor.Cause: Aircraft X had an MEL 21-XXX for 'One Auto Press Control;' a Technical Standby Instrument (TSI) to monitor a component in the pressurization system; and a yellow placard for a mechanic to check before every flight.   I am surprised this aircraft was approved for ETOPS service across an ocean.  Our failure could have occurred in the middle of the Ocean at 36;000 feet at night.  IF that had occurred; we could have had multiple injuries due to extreme pressure changes; an emergency descent to 10;000 feet; and then a diversion.During our in-flight pressurization failure; while we were running our checklist; we received several interruptions on the COMM page from Dispatch.  I am not sure whether these were sent manually; automatically via automatic function; or by rescheduling the aircraft for its next takeoff.  One message was sent to us with our new flight plan; and I believe the other concerned crew duty legalities.  These messages pop up; and my FO must verify them and then cancel them because they concern another flight that we are being scheduled for.  Suggestion: Don't send non-essential messages to aircraft during their procedures that should be conducted in a sterile cockpit.  Don't send any scheduling messages below 10;000 feet during the sterile period.  Let us land the aircraft safely; then we can consider reassignment; rescheduling; or a new flight plan.ZZZ ATC asked us if we needed speed relief during the approach.  Instead of 160 KIAS until a 4-mile final; we needed 175 KIAS due to our heavy landing weight.  The autothrottles worked as normal; but I had to override their normal idle timing.  The Overweight Landing checklist in the QRH addresses this; but it's regarding 'using throttles manually'.  Suggest a note about being ready for the autothrottles to move to idle after 30 feet; because this isn't always the best scenario.  I had not considered this during the brief.  I was fortunate to feel the autothrottles reduce before I wanted them to; so I overrode them very slightly; resulting in a normal touchdown.

I was already in the air; committed to completing the takeoff; and under the instructions of very short turn clearance. I continued the climb and planned on identifying the issue and dealing with it once stabilized on the climb; after the turn; however; at that point I turned left instead of right. The Tower directed my attention to the issue but gracefully said that there was no need to correct.The irregularity turned out to be higher than normal oil temperature indication. Once that was clear; I performed a precautionary landing. It was an incorrect indication problem.Lessons and conclusion: The initial hold short line crossing was irregular and got me a bit unsettled; and worried about consequences. In conjunction with the irregular indication; I made the second mistake. The conclusion is that I must make sure that I am 100% back to myself before accepting a clearance.Another lesson is that the markings (throughout the field) in LHW are truly bad; and in my mind at an unacceptable level. Signs are unlit; pavement markings are very faded; and the location of signs is improper. I would like to suggest that placing hold-short line locations on taxi diagrams is a good idea; especially when the hold-short line is so far from the actual runway (I estimate at least 250 ft.). I think that the average pilot will look for a hold-short line much closer to the runway and when the line is so faded will easily miss it. This however clearly does not release me from missing it.

column121: The Jeppesen 10-26 new revision for AWO 10-9 Chart" (dated Day 0 effective Day 6) now has potentially hazardous misleading information note depicted and published; reference the Runway 16/34 GRASS RUNWAY. However; note that the misleading information note may not necessarily be due to any Jeppesen error; and may instead be traced back to either misleading airport published information; or misleading FAA published source data? Nonetheless; the depiction and related note may contain potentially hazardous and misleading information. The problem: The three Runway 16/34 grass runways to the east of main Runway 16/34 referenced by Jeppesen in the note on the 10-9 diagram are actually 3 separate colinear grass runways that CANNOT be used as a single runway. It is NOT a single 3450 ft. x 145 ft. runway. Note that there are deep terrain grading depressions now located between each of the three separate runways... due to (the arguably inappropriate) surface re-grading that was conducted years ago at AWO. Those grading depressions now preclude any aircraft from rolling at high speed from one grass runway to the next. It is only possible for any aircraft to transit those depressions at very slow taxi speed; as with a glider towing behind a golf cart. Some powered aircraft; could now even risk a prop strike. Note that the original Navy design of the AWO airfield since WWII (before the arguably inappropriate grading between those grass runways) was a much safer design; and actually originally allowed for aircraft contingency use; to safely roll across the crossing taxiways; in any non-normal situation; such as an overrun or underrun. However now; any grass runway overrun or underrun between those three grass runways would likely cause a serious accident. Further; the new (inappropriately) revised geometry of the Runway 34 departure threshold taxiways now places pre-departure holding-area aircraft obstructions in the immediate pre-threshold area of the first Runway 34 grass glider runway when landing to the north; further shortening that grass runway's usable length. The usable Runway 34 grass runway available distances and locations for each of those three separate grass runways should be depicted; and published; separately and individually."

I always land at the start of the runway in a short distance -- since I always make the first turn-off -- so I did that; but did get a nasty comment from a pilot flying overhead. But I didn't like how it played out really; and I said at the time that it was probably my fault to mollify him.If you go by who is in front; well yes; he's a helicopter and he turned in front of me. If you go by who is lower; then I was. I think that I should have gotten a direct answer from him instead of just assuming that he was waiting for us both to land; but I was working with the Cirrus so closely on the radio that I didn't think he would try to get in between us.The safety lesson? Be careful around students? I'm not entirely sure; since I'm still thinking about it. I have always held that the helicopters have just as much of a right to be here as we do; but then again; they've been very considerate too. The AWOS was reporting winds variable from 260-330 degrees 8G15kts. With that in mind; we decided to utilize runway XX. After rotation the airplane climbed to 20-30 ft at which time the airspeed did not increase nor did the vertical speed. With the departure end of the runway fast approaching I elected to abort the takeoff and to descend back to the runway. The aircraft floated down past the 1;000 ft markers on the departure end of the runway and eventually touched down. I applied max braking and maintained directional control and announced to the student/passengers that we would be rolling into the grass. column121: This was a scheduled cargo flight between ZZZZ and ZZZZ1 with two operating crew and two company jump-seaters.  This event occurred within ZZZZ FIRWhile operating ZZZZ-ZZZZ1 as First Officer and PF we were established at initial cruise at 31100.  We were continuously in and out of cloud tops during this portion.  After a few minutes the wing and nacelle anti-ice systems automatically turned on.  Almost immediately we had a bleed #2 EICAS alert with associated inop light in #2 bleed air switch.  The PM ran the bleed #2 checklist; after complication we got L; R EICAS msgs.  While working that checklist we received bleed's 1;3;4 EICAS alerts as well.  This was followed shortly by the return of bleed 2 EICAS alert. We noticed cabin altitude climbing and at an altitude of 5700' we elected to put on O2 masks and activated supernumerary o2 switch.  The captain ran those checklists and managed to get two bleeds back on but we eventually lost all 4 bleeds a second time.  Unable to maintain cabin pressure; we advised ATC and coordinated a rapid descent to 3000 meters.  During rapid descent the highest cabin altitude noted was 12000' and highest rate of cabin climb was 2000 fpm.  Once below 10000 we removed masks and continued running the litany of EICAS generated non-normal checklists (Cabin Altitude; Bleed 1; Bleed 2; Bleed 3; Bleed 4; Packs 1+2+3; Cabin alt auto; Outflow valve r/l; Suprnmry oxy on; Pack mode 2; Pack mode 1; Pack mode 3). Once below 10000' we struggled to maintain communications with ZZZZ Control even using XXX.X; we required multiple relays with other aircraft.  Also during this low altitude cruise with center AP (Auto Pilot) engaged and no other crew engagement; power began to increase with a corresponding climb commanded by AP.  PF disconnected auto-pilot and auto-throttles and returned aircraft to level flight at 3000 meters.  We also noticed lights in MCP (Mode Control Panel) flickering continuously bright to dim.  Once stabilized the left AP was selected and auto-throttles were re-engaged.After evaluating options and communicating with dispatch we elected to continue the short flight to ZZZZ1.  Once in terminal area we requested short delay vectors to allow for flaps to extend in secondary mode due to lack of bleed air to actuate leading edge in primary mode and landed safely off ILS-Z to runway XX.  We maintained our ATC handling status until landing due to abnormal aircraft condition.This was a fairly challenging situation.  Time of day; complexity of system failures; communications with foreign controllers; cabin altitude and use of oxygen mask all contributed to high workload.  I was surprised how much the O2 mask decreased our ability to effectively communicate and maintain a high level of situational awareness. I recently completed annual training which involved use of oxygen mask which definitely helped in this situation.

column121: Before heading to the property; I checked the property and what restrictions there were at the property. Weather was clear and wind was mild. I drove out to the property; and started my flight around the home. I went to the furthest distance to the south of the property to get the entire property in the shot; and made it to the 118m flight altitude. At that time; I noted that there were lots of birds in my flight area. I took the last picture at that farthest south position. I made the decision to avoid coming back through the birds circling in my flight area; and circled to the west to avoid them; crossing the road (no cars were present at the time of my crossover). I continued to fly north for less than .2 miles; and circled back over the road to the north (again it was empty). I continued my flight path around the property and safely landed. After landing I adjusted my position and did one more flight around the home at a lower flight altitude. The Restricted area started at the west side of the road and led north; with the road being the red line. At the time when making that decision to go west; I was more concerned about avoiding the birds; that in that moment I mistook where the restricted area started. Only after uploading images; and mapping property lines with aerial maps did I realize my error.   For future flights; I need to recheck the AirControl app when arriving at the location to visually see the lined areas in person; and set those reminders. When set to close restricted lines I need to visually run through scenarios and a plan of action of areas I can fly to in case I need to avoid issues like this in the future. I should have either turned east; came down in altitude to navigate around the birds; or returned home to wait  until the area was clear.

column121: Aircraft X filed ZZZZZ. ZZZ to ZZZ1 and was level at 090. They were a P28A and not a jet or high-altitude aircraft so they should not have been on jet airways; which don't have an MEA through the terrain around ZZZ2. They should have filed a victor airway as they were not technically capable of flying jet airways. I had just taken over the sector from the previous controller. About 5 minutes later the MSAW for Aircraft X started flashing as they were about to hit an increased area of terrain where the MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) went up to 095.Neither myself or the previous controller had noticed the aircraft was on a jet airway with no MEA/MOCA and was headed towards higher terrain. I gave a low altitude alert and the aircraft climbed to 100.At the time this event happened I was completely task saturated. I was working 5; YES FIVE; sectors combined over 3 different frequencies ALL BY MYSELF.  I had multiple calls from approach; the missile range; FSS clearances; ZZZ [Center] calls; and other sectors. At one point an aircraft started broadcasting 'in the blind' because I was so busy answering other aircraft several hundred miles away from his position that he thought ATC was gone. I had numerous low altitude aircraft that I was providing approach control services for; 2 IFR drones that were hovering over the western arrival/departure corridor for ZZZ1; and weather deviations; and high altitude overflights. In order to do all this I was essentially on a MID configuration and super zoomed out so I could see all the airspace under my control.  I replayed the Falcon.  I had 23 data blocks on the scope at the moment the MSAW started going off. I should have had a D-side just to help with all the data block separation; not to mention the phone calls.The CIC (Controller in Charge) was planning to split off 2 sectors whenever someone came back from break or the XA:00 am people showed up; but that didn't happen fast enough. The TSD (Traffic Situation Display) was obviously showing that my sectors were ready to get stupid busy. I told the CIC I couldn't wait any longer and that they needed to abandon the CIC desk and split off sectors X and Y. They agreed and did so. It took probably about 5 min afterward for me to fully regain control of the sectors I had left: Z; A; and B. Safety was compromised without question.The combined configuration of C; Z and A was already deemed unsafe for day shift operations and requires manager approval since we have had numerous safety events with that combination. The MAP number for when those sectors are combined is only 14. YET STUPIDLY if you add EVEN more sectors and complexity and combine up C; Z; A; D; and B all together the MAP number jumps up to 20 and is not an illegal day shift combo.  So we are actually incentivized not to split sectors. If we think it is unsafe to have more than 14 aircraft in the combined low sectors in what world does it make sense to allow 20 aircraft if we do all that plus add two additional high altitude sectors into the mix?!!This event 100% happened because myself and the controller before me were trying to do the job of 3 people and couldn't keep up. The manager was super busy dealing with all the other stuff and didn't notice we hadn't split anything off.We had a controller on break when this event happened; they should have been recalled. Trying to provide approach control service to aircraft when you are looking at 300 miles of airspace is not safe on anything other than a slow MID shift.  Working 5 sectors combined on day shifts should not be allowed unless the volume is like 14 or lower like it is when only 3 of the sectors are combined.I should have shut off ZZZ [Center] and ZZZ1 approach until I could get the sectors split off and safely take on more airplanes. I prioritized efficiency over safety.CICs and FLMs (Front Line Manager) need training to understand that the TSD (Traffic Situation Display) is a predictor; and that it is not accurate tothe exact minute. Sectors are not split in a timely manner because they wait because the TSD says the volume doesn't happen until XB:03am and will say I have someone coming back right at XC:00 am.  Ignoring the fact that it takes several minutes for a briefing to occur; but also not understanding that the TSD time is an estimate; a prediction; and can be of by 5-10 minutes; is a common problem is my specialty.Due to staffing; we rarely have a supervisor in the morning.  CICs tend to take more risks and prioritize breaks and don't like to page someone back early because it is one of their peers and people complain.  A supervisor in the area would have reduced the chance of this event happening..

column121: An untethered balloon was launched from Rio Rancho; NM.  ZAB was told when the balloon was launched and was given a website to track the balloons path and altitude. There was no flight plan filed through the NAS and there was no transponder.  The ZAB supervisor was trying their best to update where the balloon was and the altitude.  However on the radar controller scope nothing was official.  We could not see any target or altitude readout and had no official information on the balloon.  Aircraft Y was at FL360 and westbound to PHX at level flight.  The Aircraft Y pilots reported seeing the balloon only 1000ft below them and just off their left wing.  This is so unsafe that balloons can launch with no flight plan; no transponder; no way to track a target.  I believe this could lead to a collision with an aircraft causing a loss of life.  Balloon should have a transponder with mode C and have a flight plan filed with the NAS.  There is no reason that in today's busy airspace we should have balloons flying through flight levels with no way of tracking the balloon.  If the balloons have transponders with verified mode C altitude we could vector aircraft away from the balloon.
