column121: We were scheduled to operate from ZZZ-ZZZZ in an aircraft with an inoperative Hot Air Valve per MEL. After engine start the air conditioning system appeared to operate normally. We departed from runway XXR and passing 8000' the inflight crew contacted the flight deck with a report that the air is blowing very loud; all passengers are turning off gaspers; the air is surging and there is a loud whistling sound. They indicated it was not normal and something was wrong. At the same time the cockpit became uncomfortably hot and the air was not blowing from any cockpit vents. I briefed my FO and we decided to level at 10000' enter into holding and troubleshoot the issue; for concerns of pressurization. After transferring control and radios to the FO; the CA reviewed the system pages of the Bleed Air; which did not indicate any faults and reviewed the system pages of the Pressurization which did not indicate any faults. The CA then contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control and discussed the malfunction. Maintenance Control could not find any issues on their end; however we clearly had a malfunction on our end that was not producing any ECAM messages. After consulting with Dispatch and Maintenance Control I advised them that we felt taking an aircraft into mountainous terrain; would not be the safest course of action. They both supported my decision to return to ZZZ. All checklists and procedures were conducted at this time; including diversion and overweight landing checklist. The CA setup a return to ZZZ and throughly briefed the FO on our approach. The crew was briefed and passengers were advised. There were no issues with the return. Once we completed parking checklist the CA made a logbook entry for the malfunction and overweight landing. The Chief Pilot and Assistant Chief Pilot then made their way to the cockpit and asked for a detailed explanation of what occurred. A offline commercial pilot was in the cabin and commented as he deplaned that he knew that something was wrong with the system. We debriefed the inflight crew and they all heard the same loud noise; whistling; surging of air; and abnormal air pressure coming from the gaspers. We then debriefed with the Chief Pilots at the gate in the terminal.

column121: Flight ABCD was scheduled for departure at XA:40Z from ZZZ to ZZZZ. Departure occurred 44 minutes behind schedule due to cargo loading delays in ZZZ.During the takeoff roll; the flight crew observed abnormal aircraft acceleration performance. Additional thrust was applied in an effort to improve aircraft acceleration. The First Officer was the Pilot Flying during departure.At rotation; crew experienced unusual handling and flight characteristics. The aircraft remained controllable and recovery actions were effective. No EICAS messages; cautions; or warnings were generated during the event.After departure; the crew coordinated with Dispatch regarding the abnormal takeoff performance. Dispatch subsequently advised that the aircraft was approximately 56;000 kg overweight. This information was later confirmed with ZZZ Operations.The flight continued to ZZZZ without further incident and landed safely.Dispatch and flight crew coordinated effectively in flight after identifying abnormal aircraft performance. The faulty load sheet and resulting overweight departure condition created a potentially hazardous situation that required immediate operational assessment and risk management.Captain A was DH (Dead Head). He assisted us through out the flight and sure be full paid for working the flight.Cause: Preliminary FindingsAircraft departed significantly above allowable weight limits. Initial indication of the issue was abnormal acceleration during takeoff roll. Abnormal handling characteristics were experienced during rotation and initial climb. No onboard system warnings or EICAS indications alerted the crew to the overweight condition. The issue appears related to an incorrect or faulty load sheet and/or load planning process.This event presented a significant operational and safety risk. An overweight takeoff condition of this magnitude could have resulted in: Reduced takeoff performance; Inability to meet required climb gradients; Runway excursion or rejected takeoff complications; Structural exceedances; Loss of aircraft controllability during critical phases of flightImmediate coordination between the flight crew and Dispatch was essential in identifying and managing the situation safely.Suggestions: Recommended Follow-Up Actions1. Conduct full investigation into load planning and load sheet generation procedures.2. Audit cargo weight verification processes in ZZZ Operations.3. Review dispatch release validation procedures for overweight detection safeguards.4. Evaluate communication and cross-check procedures between load control; dispatch; and flight crew.5. Determine whether additional automated protections or alerts can be implemented to identify extreme weight discrepancies prior to departure.

At around 700 feet AGL; the LH engine began having RPM oscillations of around +-200 RPMs; including going into the overspeed multiple times. At the same time; power of the left engine was reducing on its own and the yaw from the asymmetric thrust was setting in. During all of this; the engine was making a grinding noise; best described as it sounded like a handful of marbles were thrown into the prop. Flight Instructor (IP) took controls as soon as practical; and reduced the power setting on the left engine to 70%; where the roughness ended. After determining the engine was healthy enough to stay on; IP requested from tower to make a lap in the pattern and land back on runway XX. Tower cleared us to land and asked if we were declaring an emergency; IP replied with negative"; since the engine was operating normally at low power settings; and the flight was otherwise safe at this point. The rest of the traffic pattern went normally; SP helped Flight Instructor run checklists and the landing was normal. I'm currently unaware at this time if ATC provided priority handling on our behalf; as they never asked for fuel or souls on board; rather only asking what the issue with the airplane was. However; as we were turning base leg for runway XX; the Airport Rescue and Firefighting trucks were sent to meet us at the runway; and one would follow us back to parking. Upon post-flight inspection of the aircraft; nothing seemed visually wrong; and we never got any annunciations at any point from the Primary Flight Display (PFD). Airplane is now safely parked and secured on the ramp at ZZZ."

column121: At 2500 ft; instructor was talking a student through emergency landing profile (ELP). While scanning instruments and then looking at the Ipad for traffic to safely conduct the ELP the instructors eyes then transitioned to the right and at this point observed a high wing aircraft at the same altitude; going the opposite direction; within 500 ft of the instructor's aircraft. Instructor performed evasive maneuvers while the other aircraft maintained their original heading. No calls were made by the other aircraft on CTAF and the aircraft was not on ADS-B. Instructor had been making calls advising of the intended practice emergency landing. The rest of the flight was uneventful with the instructor and student landing safely. Corrective actions would be requiring all aircraft to be on ADS-B. Most mid air collisions happen on clear days below 3000ft within 5 miles of an airport. All participating aircraft using ADS-B-out would vastly aid in collision avoidance. The only other corrective action is using the see and avoid doctrine and diligently scanning in a figure 8 pattern 60 degrees to the left and right and 10 degrees up and down of the aircraft. A lapse of the scan pattern for 10 seconds while talking to a student and glancing at an Ipad can mean the difference between a collision and an NMAC.

column121: Arriving at ZZZ flight following was used with ZZZ1 and ZZZ Centers and ZZZ CTAF and ASOS prior to arrival and landing. Turbulence was a factor in all operations for landing; taxing and departure during the XA:45 landing period on RWY. XX (wind 260@26G36) and the departure on Rwy XY at XC:00 (wind 280@21G33). During our time on the ramp at the FBO; the ground crew chocked and tied down the plane due to the extreme turbulence on the surface. While landing; taxing in and out and departing we had the CTAF in the active position on the GTN 650Xi and the Center frequency in the standby position. Conditions seemed to favor a departure on Rwy XX; but at that runway hold line a recheck of the weather strongly indicated that XY had less of a crosswind component. I taxied to the 1 hold line of RWY XY and did pre takeoff checks and setup the GTN 650Xi for the departure route. On the takeoff I noticed over the intersection of Rwys XX and XY that I was passing several hundred feet above a jet that had departed on RWY XX.In analyzing the situation I discovered I had not heard any calls for the jet and that during my setup of the GTN 650Xi at the runway hold line. I must have inadvertently touched the standby frequency block which brought the Center frequency into the active position as the aircraft was rocking in the ground turbulence and thus not allowing me to hear the calls from the jet and the jet not hearing my departure calls either.The learning experience for me is recognizing how close the HOME and Direct buttons are to the active and standby communication frequency selector on the 650; and to recheck the communication setup while at the hold line. This piece of navigation equipment is a relatively new addition to my aircraft. My previous radio equipment had a button which would exchange the standby and active frequencies. Another thought would be to have the CTAF frequency in both the active and standby positions; and the Center frequency on the number 2 COM/NAV unit.I fully understand how this kind of a human failure can cause a devastating accident and I will be more attentive to this detail.

column121: I decided to land at the ZZZ airport while enroute. I had never landed there before so I gathered the airport information from my phone enroute.  The runway is fairly short. There was another aircraft in the pattern as we were approaching and it was on the ground before we entered the pattern.My first mistake was with my radio calls. I was making calls stating the wrong runway end.  I believe I was confused based on the calls the other pilot was making and the direction he said he was coming from. I should have verified with my chart. I didn't. I mention this because I realized that I was making the wrong calls on final and I think that the realization of this mistake just added to the situation.    My pattern was a little tight and I ended up coming in fast. I was in landing configuration with 40 degrees of flaps. I felt I might not be able stop in time due to the short runway and decided a go around would be appropriate.  However with a short runway with trees on the end and 40 degrees of flaps I ended up struggling to climb to clear the trees. I didn't want to start removing flaps as I was fairly slow and fairly low over the trees and didn't want to settle into the trees if I lost any lift. Once clear of the trees I milked off the flaps as I began to accelerate and decided not to make a second attempt.I was too slow and too close to the trees for my comfort level and due to the short runway with obstacles really didn't feel I had many options other than keep the nose down and allow speed to build. Had it been a warmer day with less aircraft performance it could have ended badly which is why I am filling out this report.There are several things that could have helped avoid this situation: 1. I should have done a more detailed review of the airport prior to landing there for the first time as printed resources don't always tell the whole story.  Perhaps I should have looked at some aerial photos or maps. 2. I should have made a better approach; because my pattern was tight I ended up high and ultimately too fast.  A slightly wider pattern would have provided for a more stabilized slower approach.  3. I should have made the go around decision earlier. I ate up too much of the short runway trying to 'save' the landing. 4. I do think that some complacency and perhaps over confidence in flying a familiar  airplane contributed to getting too far down the road before calling the go around. I did some additional go-around practice at a local airport with a much longer runway later in the flight and intend to do more specifically focused on seeing if letting some flaps out particularly in a 172 with 40 degrees would be more helpful or harmful in this scenario as the flaps are almost all drag at 40 degrees and provide very little if any additional lift.I did discuss this situation with some pilot friends to debrief the flight and brainstorm ways to improve and was given some helpful insight.

column121: On returning from a part 61 training flight in the practice area to the west of ZZZ; I instructed my student to pass to the south of the right downwind of runway XXR; in order to set up for a 45 degree entry. While sufficiently far enough south the downwind leg; I noticed an aircraft turn an early right crosswind and cut in front of another aircraft already on the crosswind. The traffic; a Cirrus SR-22; announced via CTAF that they intended to depart to the south. They began tracing straight towards my aircraft; and at this time I took flight controls from my student. I attempted to reach the other pilot to coordinate via CTAF but was unable; or my calls were not acknowledged. At this time I began a descent and a turn towards the airport to allow the traffic to pass off my right side; to my south. The departing traffic; which originally was headed southwest bound; began a turn towards the west; again tracking towards my aircraft. Seeing the other aircraft's ground speed of approximately 180 knots; and knowing my ground speed was approximately 100 knots; I knew it was only seconds until we would collide. At this time; both aircraft had descended to approximately 800 feet MSL. To avoid the collision; and to avoid turning into other traffic established on the downwind to my north; I initiated an aggressive descent to pass beneath the opposite direction cirrus. During this descent; my altitude dropped to approximately 480 feet AGL. After passing the cirrus; I resumed a climb back to pattern altitude of approximately 1022 MSL; and conducted a normal 45 degree entry to the right downwind. The landing was uneventful. To avoid another near miss in the future; I will emphasize to other pilots the importance of departing the pattern in a manner consistent with the AIM's guidance (downwind; then depart) instead of flying on course immediately.

It is unthinkable to me that an airport participating in commercial jump operations does not have its primary working frequency listed on the sectional. If you look up the airport in airnav.com; you can see the multicom frequency of 131.5; but it is not clear whether the parachute operations use this or perhaps use the LHZ CTAF frequency instead. The inability to see the NOTAM; an inability to view the jump operations in the same layer as a TFR layer; and a parachute operation not having their working frequency listed on the VFR sectional all seem like areas of potential improvement to avoid a midair collision with either a parachutist or the jump airplane.

column121: While operating a passenger flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 we planned a departure on RW XX with a right forward quartering headwind /crosswind. We taxied to runway XX and announced our intentions on the Unicom frequency. We received our IFR clearance on the ground via ZZZ CTR on the radio as well.We heard no other traffic on the Unicom frequency of XXX.XX We saw no visible traffic during our taxi; in the air or on the ground. The Cessna 182 had taxied much earlier than us so assumed he had departed on his flight to ZZZ2. There were no radio transmissions from the Cessna 182 and that was confirmed via the FBO audio recorded during that time period.Our transmissions were on the recording stating our intentions to taxi to RW XX. We completed our taxi check and were holding short of RW XX. The Co-pilot transmitted our departure intentions for ZZZ RW XX and we began our normal takeoff roll. The aircraft accelerated normally and the Co-Pilot called V1 and Rotate; At that moment the C182 appeared at about 11 o clock in the windshield and approximately 50 to 75 ft. in the air. It was too late for an aborted takeoff as it appeared we would pass barely underneath the the C182. A rotation at that instant would have caused impact with the C182. I felt the safest option was to delay the rotation and remain on the runway for a couple of seconds as the traffic passed over us. It happened very quickly and we rotated and resumed the climb away from the runway. The remainder of the flight was normal and uneventful. The incident occurred due to lack of situational awareness resulting from a lack of radio communication. I was unaware visually of another aircraft positioned at RW XY prior to beginning the takeoff roll. This incident could have been avoided by pilots verifying correct Unicom/ CTAF frequencies in use at uncontrolled airports. Visually verifying other aircraft when possible and the use of all available appropriate aircraft lighting to enhance visibility.
column123: Our aircraft was departing on runway XX. I made CTAF calls taxiing out of the FBO via 1 and made a call once on runway XX ready for takeoff. Another aircraft was seen taxiing on the other side of the airfield via taxiway 2. No radio calls were heard from that aircraft. Visual contact was lost as it blended in to the airport environment at the approach end of runway XY. We started our takeoff roll and as we passed V1 speeds we visually saw the other aircraft departing runway XY. It was approximately 75-100 ft. AGL as it passed directly over us at the intersection of Runway XX and Runway XY. We elected to stay on the ground/runway at takeoff speed until the overflying aircraft was not a factor overhead. We then executed our takeoff with sufficient runway left to safely get airborne.Once airborne at approximately 1000 feet AGL I made another call on CTAF that we were turning northbound and departing the airport environment. No response was heard from any other aircraft in the area; including the aircraft we narrowly missed.Once landed at our destination in ZZZ1 we called airport personnel via cell phone to determine if they could hear our calls on the radio. They returned our call the next morning and stated that they heard ALL of our radio calls but none from the other aircraft. We had briefly talked with the other aircraft's pilot/occupant and knew that they were heading to ZZZ2. We called company at ZZZ2 and determined the aircraft's identification to be Aircraft Y. We did not make any contact with the crew of Aircraft Y as they had left the airfield.We believe that Aircraft Y may have been on the wrong CTAF frequency in ZZZ which is why we did not hear any radio transmissions from them nor did airport personnel. If true this directly caused the problem. To prevent this from happening again; we should have attempted to make direct radio contact with the other aircraft we saw taxiing either on CTAF or Guard frequency. If no contact made; we should have delayed taking our runway until we could absolutely confirm that other aircraft had taken off from their runway and was no longer a hazard.

column121: In regards to the incident of a hard landing at ZZZ.This report is being written by the Pilot in command of Aircraft X at the time of the accident. The trip was intended to be a day trip into ZZZ; we had departed earlier that morning with a VFR request from ATC to give us vectors in route to ZZZ1. This request was canceled shortly after the plane was no longer under control of ZZZ1's Class C Airspace. The intention behind this action was simply to take a more well defined route down the coast which we would follow south to ZZZ.The exact time of the event is not clear to me; I know that when I was roughly 25 miles to the North East of the field I had received the ATIS and information 1 was in effect. It stated that the active runway was Runway XX and the winds were coming from 060 at 11kts; gusting to 18kts.Upon contact with ZZZ Tower; it was communicated the active pressure in inches of mercury and that I was to advise when I was established on a right downwind for Runway XXPrior to my advancement into the downwind the controller in the tower had called asking if I was setting myself up for a straight in approach into Runway XY; as far as I was aware I was not only far east to the runway but also east of the tower that sits on the east of the runway. The tower communicated that from their perspective; I was in position for the unactive Runway XY; however I was still at pattern altitude and at least a mile away from being lined up with the centerline for Runway XY. I continued my approach into the right downwind and advised with midfield; everything seemed in order and even still; turning to base appeared normal; it wasn't until I had turned to final that it was clear to me that I had not adequately accounted for the wind correction due primarily to the gusts at 18kts. I was blown off to the west by roughly 0.5sm - 1sm; and with the gusts now coming in on the headwind; losing attitude on final proved itself to be a challenge; to the degree where this first approach resulted in missed/go around actions being taken. ZZZ Tower at this point advised me to turn back into the right downwind for Runway XX; however it was not advised that this turn was to be made while midfield with the runway; this required a sharper turn of of the runway heading; while working against the gusting 18kt headwind. My initial plan through this missed approach was to clean up the plane's flaps and trim while maintaining the runway heading until 700ft AGL. This request from the tower; while not the primary cause of the hard landing; was in some key details a reason behind the unstable final approach that lead to the events regarded to in this report. I made the needed adjustments to clean up the plane; however I was only up to 800ft AGL throughout the pattern instead of the pattern altitude of 1000ft AGL. upon this second attempt at a right downwind I extended my downwind to allow for more room for adjustments on base and final. The turn to base was standard and by this point I had only applied 10 degrees of flaps and no trim. Upon my second attempt for a final approach I had started off with 10 degrees of flaps but soon realized that I needed to lose more altitude than anticipated. This is because I knew I was below pattern altitude so I held off on the 500ft decent following the plane being abeam the runway numbers. By my approach into final the plane was still roughly 800ft AGL; this prompted me to add in 20 degrees of flaps; however the trim stayed neutral. The plane was well pitched for 65-70kts on the decent because of the heavy use of flaps and everything was steady on the approach until around 150ft - 200ft AGL the turbulence and gusts had rapidly gotten more intense. This pushed the plane back and while I was able to maintain a steady angle of attack until around 100ft AGL; I was just barely crossing over the runway threshold when a final gust pushed the plane on an uneven angle and slowed it into a stall; the final airspeed I rememberseeing was 38kts right before the stall. This happened so close to the runway that I was unable to go around again or glide comfortably to the runway. Aircraft X impacted with the runway and rolled in the grass between the runway and taxiway 1. It stopped in the grass and the mixture was leaned to idle before pulling out the throttle and turned off all electronics to the plane. The plane was swiftly evacuated and rescue crews arrived on the scene. No damage to property or injury to any body involved was found. The only known damage to be found was a chip to the front wheel's rim which was still able to hold air and the windshield had shattered leaving only half of the glass remaining in frame.

column121: I was parked on the terminal ramp at HWY and loading a passenger in the front seat of my Stearman when a solo parachute jumper was observed heading right toward the front of my plane from the right and he then landed on the ramp just in front of my right wing. His parachute lines and chute were blown over the top wing of my biplane and the jumper came to rest right in front of my right wings. I asked him if he was OK and he replied he was. I then got the passenger out of my plane and asked him to gather the chute together so it would not blow in the wind and possibly cause the lines to pull more on my wings. I then climbed on the nose of my plane and removed the lines that were stuck on my top wing and we were able to free the parachute and lines from my wing by walking it toward the wing tip. The jumper collected himself and was exiting the ramp when I called to him and asked if he was an instructor. He said no; he was a student. I met with the airport manager after this to make sure she knew what had happened and asked her to follow up with the jump operation who operates at the airport. My concern is my safety and the safety of my plane and passenger. column121: During a routine training flight; my student and I were conducting closed traffic work at ZZZ focusing on landings and crosswind correction techniques. Wind conditions were around 8 kts crosswind component on runway XXL. During our final landing of the lesson; the student applied the incorrect crosswind control and utilized the wrong rudder to align us with the runway centerline. This resulted in us deviating from the paved runway surface. I recognized the developing situation but was unable to correct it in time before the runway excursion occurred. The aircraft continued through the grass onto the next available taxiway and came to a full stop. I inspected the landing gear and propeller and found no apparent damage. No airport lighting; signs; or airport property were struck. The ground was solid and grass was short. I returned the aircraft to ZZZ where maintenance personnel inspected the aircraft and also didn't find any damage. In retrospect; several human factors likely contributed to the event; including possible student fatigue and frustration after repeated difficulty maintaining aircraft control in crosswind conditions. Additionally; my instructional coaching and intervention were not sufficiently timely or effective to prevent the excursion. A go-around should have been initiated once the unstable landing and developing loss of directional control became apparent. This event reinforces the importance of an early go-around when landing stability becomes questionable. In the future; I will emphasize a greater importance on early go-arounds during training for myself and my students.

Unable to maintain cabin pressure; we advised ZZZZ ATC and coordinated a rapid descent to 3000 meters. During rapid descent the highest cabin altitude noted was 12000 and highest rate of cabin climb was 2000 fpm.  Once below 10000 we removed masks and continued running the EICAS generated non-normal checklists (Cabin Altitude; Bleed 1; Bleed 2; Bleed 3; Bleed 4; Packs 1+2+3; Cabin alt auto; Outflow valve r/l; Suprnmry oxy on; Pack mode 2; Pack mode 1; Pack mode 3). Once below 10000 we struggled to maintain communications with ZZZZ [TRACON] Control even using 121.5; we required multiple relays with other aircraft. It took multiple attempts to verify our final altitude and confirm QNE vs QNH. PF disconnected auto-pilot and auto-throttles and returned aircraft to level flight at 3000 meters. We also noticed lights in Mode Control Panel (MCP) flickering continuously bright to dim. We had a restriction to cross EBGAL below 14;000' and TIDUK at 9;000.  I felt that descending in managed descent would have been more appropriate; but did not articulate that notion; because the altitude of 9;000 was in the altitude preselect window; and the FMS showed that we would cross EBGAL below 14;000. We requested the RNAV Y 35R with approach control and they cleared us for it via the TIDUK transition.  At that point the PF set 5200' in the altitude preselect window; and I reminded PF to select APPR mode. When PF selected APPR I noted that column 3 on the Flight Mode Annunciator (FMA) annunciated APPR NAV in green and column 2; line 2 showed ALT FINAL in blue. What I did not notice was that we were still in Open Descent in column 2; line 1.The PF chimed sterile at 13;600; and got the exterior lights at 10;000.I was reviewing my charts when I looked up and realized that we were at about 5;800'. I immediately instructed PF to climb back to 9;000' for the crossing restriction at TIDUK; which we did make.  We were not in dangerous proximity to the ground at that time; and in fact were in VMC; but we actually were between 200-500 feet below MEA on that segment of the approach. After climbing to 9;000'; the remainder of the approach was flown correctly and we landed safely at CYYC.Cause:  I feel that while checking the FMA was appropriate; my missing the Open Descent annunciation in my scan is what allowed this event to occur.  I understand that Open Descent ignores constraints; but I did not realize that selecting APPR would not cancel the Open Descent and capture the vertical path as I anticipated it would. We should have selected managed descent before arming APPR.

column121: I was contracted to photograph the property at Location X.The property was at the lateral border of class D airspace over ZZZ [Airport]. That border cuts through the parking lot of the property I was photographing. My research in advance had showed the area as LAANC enabled for instant approval up to 400 feet; and only part of the potential operation zone was in restricted airspace. I didn't request that authorization in advance because I was conducting four flights across a 100 mile radius that day and didn't think I could accurately predict my arrival time.This was my fourth and last property of the day for this client; most of which were smaller portions of larger building complexes. The actual amount of land owned by the client at Location X ended up being much smaller than I had anticipated; and so was my operating zone. I picked my takeoff location and pulled up the Aloft air control app; which said that LAANC was not enabled for my operation. I misunderstood this to mean that my operation was outside of the zone requiring authorization as long as I stayed below the legal ceiling of 400 ft.I took off and conducted the flight; and halfway through I received a notification from DJI that I had entered a warning zone. I used the DJI map to navigate away from that area; take a few more shots outside of it; and land a few minutes later. I checked the Aloft map again after landing and realized that there was a temporary flight restriction in place for the entire class D zone around ZZZ; and that I had entered that zone for maybe 1-3 minutes.Primary cause is Pilot Error (Hazardous attitude; inexperience and misinterpretation of maps and restrictions)-The operation zone I discovered when I arrived differed somewhat from what I had researched and planned in advance. -I was licensed several years ago; but I've only conducted about 6-10 commercial flights since then; and none in controlled airspace until Day 0. I had submitted my first LAANC request in Location Y earlier that morning. I wasn't familiar with how the map displayed temporary flight restrictions; I failed to reference the legend; and I misread the situation.-I covered multiple properties in a 100-mile radius that day; and this was the last of the day; leaving me somewhat fatigued and impulsive. I should've rescheduled the property when I realized I was confused instead of proceeding with my best; most convenient guess.Secondary cause may be LAANC software ambiguity. The language for LAANC authorization not being available vs not being required is similar with the app I was using.This was my first experience with LAANC and I have enough first-hand knowledge of the procedure now to significantly reduce my confusion in the future. I won't hesitate to reschedule in the future if I can't be sure I'm in compliance.

column121: Flight ABC from ZZZ to ZZZZ. Flight was late off the gate because of a tire change in the hangar then cleaning and catering once it got to the gate. Pretty chaotic off the gate; so much so that someone mentioned it felt like a training exercise. There was also a delay in our final weights as we were taxiing due to an error with the initial weights we were pushed. Something to do with an electric wheelchair.Captain's leg; I was pilot monitoring. Climb and level-off were normal. Relief pilot calculated breaks and left for his rest period. Received and OK'd ETOPS WX. We had sent a message but were waiting on reply.Almost exactly two hours after takeoff at XA:38; cruising at 35;000 feet; about 110 miles almost due north of Location X; the amber R ENG OIL PRESS caution popped up and I pointed it out to the captain. Looked at oil indications and right pressure was red; showing pressure of 0. I pulled up the FM Non-normals for ENG OIL PRESS L(R). Pressure indication at or below red line limit: Go to the Engine Failure or Shutdown checklist." What!? A little bit of disbelief and surprise as I process the fact that this is an actual problem. The captain pulls up the non-normal emergency checklist on his side and verifies the issue. He directs me to request priority handling with ZZZ center and request lower altitude.I requested priority handling and get receive descent to 290. Captain then directs me to take over flying duties so he can work the checklist engine shutdown. We transfer controls and I start down in VNAV. I inform ZZZ of 170 SOB and 7+48 fuel on board while CA shuts down right engine. He then calls FA to wake relief pilot and have him report to the flight deck immediately. I am speaking with ZZZ; descending; and receiving vectors to the south while the relief pilot joins us and CA works checklist and coordinates with Dispatch and FAs. I notice the R Engine Temperature indicator in the red. I feel the yaw in the plane but; admittedly; took too long to remember that I needed to step on the left rudder pedal since the right engine had been shut down. Now in trim.A report from the cabin let us know a passenger noted flames coming from the right engine; though we had no indication of fire in the flight deck. The fire handle was decidedly pulled out of sequence from checklist but no extinguishing agent was discharged.I was working the radio and descending. I was trying to VNAV down to 290; then 200; then 6;000 feet; when I realized that was too many steps. I chose V/S out of FL200 because it was right in front of me on the panel. I realize after that I should have done FLCH; but it did what I needed done at the moment. Kind of a frenzied blur of a descent but at some point coordinated for divert to ZZZZ1; put it in the FMC as alternate; CA activated ILS approach RWY XX; coordinated with dispatch; and FAs; and Control for ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting). Through 10;000 feet I was fast but recognized it and started slowing to 250 knots while continuing down. I was aware of but not focused on my distance from the airport and knew that I was high and fast. I was coming up on 6;000 feet; but I was still at 250 knots and high. I was cleared to 3;000 feet and direct to ZZZZZ (IF) for straight in to RWY XX; and shortly thereafter cleared for approach to RWY XX. Still high and 250 kts; though. The single biggest mistake of the night was my not arming APP mode here when cleared for the approach. This led to me being below glide slope on final which was trapped at 1000 feet but could have been avoided had I armed when cleared for approach.We completed the checklist and had a quick brief. There was a question if I felt comfortable performing the landing. I was comfortable but offered if the captain wanted to take it. We stuck with SOP; and I was going to make the landing and he was going to continue monitoring the situation. Relief pilot was an invaluable extra set of eyes and mind offering timely advice and mental support. We were coming up on 3;000 feet but hadn't fully restored our PM and PF rolls. I was worried about ALT CAP at 3;000 because I misinterpreted the approach chart thinking the glideslope started at ZZZZZ. This error was not trapped and 700 was put into the altitude window because we were at ZZZZZ and cleared for the approach. Altitude should have remained at 3000 since it was a level segment until GS intercept but definitely not lower than 1900 per the approach plate. This error when unrecognized and I ended up below GS with the runway in sight. Gear went down around 3;000 feet to help slow the plane and flaps were configured as we slowed through the flap speeds. The "Glideslope" EGPWS warning went off and I shallowed my descent to catch the glideslope. At 1000 AGL it was caught that I needed to level off to intercept the glide slope. I disconnected the AP; leveled off; and armed the approach. LOC was captured right away; I stayed level and moments later intercepted the GS and then continued to follow it to the runway. I got right of course initially with A/P disconnect but worked my way back to the left for a stable approach at 500 ft and a 'buttery' landing; if not a little left of center line.Pulled off the runway; got checked out by ARFF; and coordinated a gate. All cleared and taxied in for an otherwise normal shutdown."

column121: Scheduled flight was ZZZ1-ZZZ. The Wi-Fi was discovered to be inoperable on this flight and was not previously written up. Dispatch was notified about this and did an excellent job of keeping us informed with the changing conditions and helping build our situational awareness. Enroute to ZZZ; the flight experienced a rapid onset of moderate clear air turbulence which caused the airspeed to rapidly increase above VMO by 10-15 knots for about five seconds. The captain told the flight attendants to be seated immediately. The PF maneuvered the aircraft further away from enroute storms and the turbulence became consistent moderate. Once the turbulence died down; the captain told the flight attendants to take their jump seats; followed by a check in. There were no injuries. ZZZ was calling for thunderstorms; hail and tornadoes at the ETA. Flight held over ZZZ [VOR] at FL310 in smooth air to allow the storm to pass. After about an hour of holding; once the extreme precipitation was north and east of the field as reported by ATC and verified by the weather radar; the crew decided to begin the approach to runway XX. On the descent; at approximately 11;000 ft MSL the aircraft was struck by lightning and immediately showed an Eng 1 Reverse unlocked ECAM message. The approach was aborted; the PF leveled off at 10;000 and made a right turn direct to ZZZ2. Priority handling was requested and the ECAM was actioned; resulting in bringing the eng 1 thrust lever to idle; where it remained for the rest of the flight. There was no buffeting so the engine was not shut down but it was treated as a single engine approach. The captain accomplished the brief with the flight attendants. The crew received vectors for the ILS XYL at ZZZ2. On approach; with flaps one selected; a momentary overspeed occurred due to gusty wind conditions. The overspeed lasted less than five seconds and exceeded VFE by approximately five kts. Emergency equipment was standing by. A normal landing was accomplished followed by an uneventful taxi to the gate. Postflight inspection revealed lightning strike damage to the left engine nacelle; right inboard trailing edge flap; and right sharklet and static wick.
column123: We departed ZZZ1 for ZZZ anticipating the need for holding due to lots of severe thunderstorms enroute and near our destination. We had no WiFi on board which limited our ability to monitor everything; but we notified dispatch of our limitation so they could help keep us informed. Our first issue occurred at 37;000 feet enroute to ZZZ. We hit instant moderate-severe clear air turbulence and our airspeed increased by 25-30 knots and we oversped the jet for about 3-5 seconds. The ecam appeared for less than 1 second. After the initial entering of the turbulence; it stabilized to continuous moderate. We coordinated with center to descend and turn away from the storms to try and improve our ride; which worked. When hitting the turbulence the captain told the flight attendants to be seated immediately. After we exited the turbulence; he had them check in and confirm there were no injuries. We relayed that to ATC and continued on to ZZZ.Getting closer it became apparent that we would be unable to continue our approach into ZZZ due to the severe storms. We coordinated for holding at ZZZ [VOR] for about an hour while we worked with dispatch and center to monitor ZZZ. The WiFi was inop on our aircraft so our situational awareness was limited on what was going on at the airfield and around it. We received reports that the conditions were improving and with dispatch made the decision to shoot the approach. We were informed that the area had light thunderstorms with light to moderate rain and up to moderate turbulence. A RJ had gone in 15-20 minutes prior and had reported lightning and moderate chop before discontinuing the approach. We checked the weather again with approach and conditions still appeared to be improving. The 319 weather radar showed only light-moderate rain around the airfield as well. We were told the airfield still had gusty winds but high ceilings and we were told to expect the visual approach to runway XX. This clearance reaffirmed our belief that conditions were improving; so we elected to continue the approach. Around 11000 feet we were struck by lightning. We instantly got an eng 1 reverser unlocked ecam. We leveled off at 10000 feet and coordinated with approach to turn away from ZZZ and head to ZZZ2. All engine conditions were normal; so we started the turn and then ran the ecam. It directed us to pull the power on 1 to idle and leave it there. We then treated it as a single engine aircraft and declared an emergency. The capt did a brief with the FAs and informed the passengers that we were diverting to ZZZ2. We set up for an extended final for the ILS to XYL and ran all Checklists. ZZZ2 also had gusty winds and light to moderate rain; and on approach we oversped the slats at flaps 1 by 2-3 knots for 2-3 seconds. Aside from that we landed normally and emergency vehicles followed us into the gate where we shut down engines and terminated the flight.

column121: While operating Flight ABCD from ZZZ1 to ZZZ on Day 0; at approximately XA:22; we were cleared direct to the Final Approach Fix (ZZZZZ) by ZZZ Tower for the visual approach and cleared to land on runway XX. Visibility at the field was reported to be 10 statute miles and weather was VMC. We verified the ILS frequency and course were tuned for Runway XX at ZZZ. With preview selected on the guidance panel; the First Officer selected Approach mode with the autopilot still coupled and while still in magenta lateral and vertical modes. Prior to the aircraft intercepting the localizer; the lateral and vertical modes both turned green and with the autopilot not yet captured on either the localizer or glideslope; autopilot performed an uncommanded descent from the assigned altitude and what appeared to be a smart turn inside the final approach course. The aircraft descended to approximately 800 feet AGL. We heard the 'one thousand' aural altitude alert; which prompted immediate disconnect of the autopilot and the First Officer climbed back to the charted altitude of the ZZZZZ (1;600'). We suspect the aircraft may have inadvertently captured a false glideslope and the combination of PREV mode active with APP armed prior to localizer/glideslope capture may have caused the autopilot to respond to spurious vertical guidance.Upon hearing the 'One Thousand' alert; the pilot flying disconnected the autopilot and initiated an immediate climb back to FAF altitude (1;600'). Shortly thereafter; Air Traffic Control issued a low altitude alert. As PM; I acknowledged and noted that we were correcting.No terrain conflict; obstacle contact or loss of separation occurred. The remainder of the approach was well within company standards and the landing was completed uneventfully.Cause: APP mode selected prior to localizer and glideslope capturePotential false glideslope signal in the vicinity of the FAFPossible smart turn intercept prior to localizer captureEmbraer 170/175 autopilot susceptibility to spurious ILS signals prior to valid course captureAutomation dependency Automation responded to vertical guidance signal before established on the published ILS pathSuggestions: Consider company training emphasis on delaying Approach mode selection until fully established on both localizer and glideslope; even when cleared direct to FAF for situational awarenessConsider training emphasis on direct-to-FAF clearances where autopilot and localizer/glideslope anomalies are most commonplaceConsider encouraging RNAV approaches whenever cleared for visual approaches to avoid mode confusion (both on the part of the aircraft automation as well as on the part of the pilot)
column123: During arrival into ZZZ; the visual XX backed up by ILS approach was briefed and the aircraft was configured in preparation for a stabilized visual approach. The aircraft was about 5 miles out navigating toward the FAF at a 70 degree angle to intercept with the published FAF altitude set and protected in the altitude selector. approach guidance was properly set up and verified prior to selecting APP mode. the autoflight system unexpectedly captured both localizer and glideslope indications despite the aircraft being outside a normal intercept profile. The aircraft then initiated an automated smart turn toward the localizer while simultaneously beginning a descent with a potential false glideslope capture while we were fully deflected from the localizer; Due to the close proximity to the approach and not being required to intercept outside FAF on a visual; the automated behavior was not immediately recognized as a problem. After a few seconds of monitoring what was happening and getting the 1000 foot call while still fully deflected; the autopilot was disengaged and corrective action was taken to return the aircraft to the appropriate FAF altitude and flight path towards FAF. at the same time at which we received the 1000 foot callout; a low altitude alert was given to us by tower. Once reestablished on profile; the remainder of the approach and landing were completed without further issue.Cause: Aircraft capturing localizer and glideslope when not established on final approach pathSuggestions: Wait to engage APP mode until fully established on final

column121: We were assigned Aircraft X to fly from ZZZ. When we arrived at the aircraft l was met by the FO that had flown it in. He advised me they had received an EICAS message about the Cargo Fire Extinguishing system and that line maintenance was onboard working on the write-up they had made for the message they had received on landing. We continued to complete our preflight duties while line maintenance cleared the message and the aircraft was cleared by maintenance. We departed and all was normal operations until approximately 30 minutes into the flight at 34;000 feet when we received a EICAS message CRG AFT FIREX HI ARM" Advisory. The message was displayed for just over a minute and then extinguished. During that time we referenced the QRH for direction and it stated this was a "Crew Awareness" message. Immediately after the "CRG FIREX HI ARM" message extinguished a second advisory message briefly appeared "CRG FIREX LO ARM" and was quickly replaced by a "CRG FIREX HI DISCH" status message. The QRH states that this message means that the "Cargo high-rate discharge fire extinguisher bottle has been discharged." We did not see any other indications of a Cargo Smoke warning (lights or EICAS messages). At this point in the flight I opted to send an ACARS message to dispatch to advise maintenance control that the Cargo high-rate bottle had discharged into the cargo compartment and asked them (dispatch and maintenance) if they wanted us to return to ZZZ. Our thought being that we still had over 90 minutes remaining to fly to our destination; but we were now only approximately 30 minutes from ZZZ. I opted to establish a SELCAL phone patch with dispatch shortly after sending the ACARS message to expedite the communication that we needed to have due to the complexity of the possible decision to divert. While establishing the phone patch through Company radio we received the message "MAINTENANCE SAYS ITS CREW DIFEREABLE".Once the phone patch was established with dispatch we discussed the message we received; what I thought was now the state of the compromised cargo fire suppression system; and some possible options with our dispatcher. The dispatcher again restated that maintenance said that we could continue to our destination and defer the cargo fire suppression system there. I told our dispatcher that this would mean we probably would not be able to carry cargo out of our destination. When a Cargo bottle is used to respond to a "CARGO FWD (AFT) SMOKE" warning message and the contents are discharged the QRH states to LAND AT THE NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT. While we DID NOT have a CARGO SMOKE indication (Cargo Smoke push lights; or EICAS messages) our high rate bottle had been discharged and our ability to respond to any future CARGO SMOKE messages during the flight was compromised. Upon further discussion I opted to return to ZZZ to address the issue.My concerns regarding this particular in-flight event are the lack of safety minded real time decision making support from the team (dispatch and maintenance control) on the ground. A statement like "Do what your QRH directs" does not help in this situation. Especially considering the fact that the EICAS messages we were referencing in the QRH did not expressly state what to do given this particular set of circumstances. If we had opted to continue to our destination we would have flown for over 90 minutes with a compromised Cargo compartment fire suppression system to a destination that could probably not service (repair the system or replace the halon) on the aircraft while dealing with contract maintenance in a foreign country. According to the FAA; inflight lithium battery fires and smoke incidents on domestic flights now occur at a rate of roughly two incidents per week. A fact that I was made aware of while attending recurrent ground school less than a month ago. We were carrying cargo and according to the EICAS messages present we did not have a high rate bottle option available to fight a fire in either cargo compartment. Guidance to continue to a foreign country destination and overlook the possible inflight risks; as well as deferring equipment that removes or seriously impacts the ability to carry cargo is at a minimum a bad business decision; or worse; our company is left trying to explain to the families of our passengers or the FAA why we opted to continue if we had an actual cargo fire happen without the possibility to fight the fire in the remaining flight. The decision to RETURN TO ZZZ should have been made as a consensus by all parties involved. After returning and landing safely in ZZZ we were advised by line maintenance that this aircraft has a history of these types of messages occurring. A side note to this incident; after being reassigned another aircraft and completing the flight several passenger thanked us for getting them safely to their destination; despite arriving a couple of hours late."

column121: Upon blocking in at gate XX; I set the Parking Brake In Accordance With (IAW) SOP's and the Triple Indicator showed normal Brake and Accumulator Pressure.  I then took my feet off the toe brakes and the aircraft began to roll forward.  The FO promptly called 'We're Rolling!' just as 'Brake System Fail' and multiple other ECAM messages populated with aural alerts.  I immediately applied maximum braking to stop the aircraft and noticed that the Brake Pressure indications in the Triple Indicator were at Zero; with normal accumulator pressure.  The airplane stopped abruptly as the ground personnel ran away from it.  Thankfully; the airplane stopped prior to impacting ground equipment; the jet bridge; or personnel.  I estimate we were a MAXIMUM of 5' from impacting equipment in front of the airplane.  I held the brakes until communications were established with ground personnel; the aircraft was chocked; and the tug was connected.  At that time; both engines were shut down and the aircraft was pushed back by the tug to the appropriate parking position.  Shortly after the aircraft was pushed into the appropriate parking position and after the last engine spooled down; normal Brake Pressure indications returned to the Triple Indicator and the ECAM faults cleared.  A detailed Discrepancy was entered in the logbook software. Maintenance was called and I personally described the problem to the responding mechanic.  NOTE:  I did discuss the situation with Union Safety and the Committee volunteer who handled my call stated that this same problem had occurred with another Airbus in the previous few days.Cause: I have no idea what the causal factors were - there was clearly some issue with brake system of that particular airplane and based on my discussion with union Safety; there MAY be an issue with the fleet. Regarding mitigation; I sincerely hope Maintenance; Union Safety; Company Safety; Flight Ops; and all other relevant departments investigate this situation THOROUGHLY.  As mentioned in my narrative above; the airplane was a MAXIMUM of 5' from impacting anything from ground equipment to a jet bridge; to a person.  Had the FO not immediately noticed the unexpected forward motion of the airplane; we would be dealing with an accident; a damaged airplane; and almost certainly injured personnel / passengers.
column123: After normal flight at gate arrival; crew taxi'd into gate XX.  After park brake set; each pilot started their flow for shutdown when as pilot monitoring I saw ground crew scattering and noticed aircraft was still rolling forward with the brakes set.  I said we're rolling forward and called for brakes as we jumped over the chocks and were picking up speed.  CA as pilot monitoring hit the brakes bringing us to a stop.  We noted no pressure in the hydraulic gage except for the accumulator and the brake handle was still in the set position.  Then a slew of brake failure cautions presented with no audio ding.  We held the brakes until ground crew connected the tug.  Once the engines were shutdown and the last engine stopped spinning. all cautions corrected themselves and the brake system returned to normal.we were tugged bake into position at the gate.Cause: Complete brake system failure. Recommend review of aircraft data and awareness to flight crews that this can happen during shutdown.

column121: Crew received taxi instructions from ramp control while positioned in the ramp area at ORD. During the initial transmission; the instructions were delivered rapidly and included multiple routing elements. The First Officer; who was relatively junior; missed portions of the readback; and the controller requested the instructions be read back again.The revised taxi instructions were understood as follow another aircraft; taxi on the east side of the Y; taxi via Taxiway SE; hold short of Taxiway A; and contact Ground Metering.While complying with the instructions; the crew encountered several aircraft positioned on Taxiway SP immediately ahead. Additionally; Aircraft Y and Aircraft Z were oriented southeast on Taxiway SP; limiting available maneuvering space and requiring the aircraft to continue further south on Taxiway SP.As the aircraft proceeded; the crew attempted to identify the hold short point for Taxiway A. However; the crew was unable to positively identify the transition point between Taxiway SE/SP and Taxiway A due to limited signage and the absence of a clearly depicted Taxiway SE on available company taxi charts.Uncertain whether the aircraft had stopped at the correct location; the crew contacted ramp control for clarification. Ramp control advised that the aircraft had proceeded too far and instructed the crew to hold position and contact Ground Metering.After contacting Ground Metering; the crew was advised they were not expected to be in that location and were instructed to contact Ground Control. The primary contributing factor was confusion regarding the taxi routing and hold short location in a congested and operationally complex ramp environment. Several factors contributed to the event:The routing issued differed significantly from normal and familiar procedures commonly used in that area in recent months. Historically; crews typically remained on either side of the Y and contacted Ground Metering prior to taxiing northwestbound on Taxiway SP while monitoring 131.3. The routing issued during this event differed substantially from that normal flow. Taxiway SE was not clearly depicted on available company airport charts available to the crew. Signage and markings in the area did not clearly identify where Taxiway SE or SP transitioned into Taxiway A.Multiple aircraft positioned in the area created congestion and reduced maneuvering clarity.Rapid communication cadence and repeated radio exchanges increased cockpit workload during a critical phase of taxi operations.Despite the confusion; the crew operated conservatively; taxied slowly; sought clarification when uncertain; and attempted to maintain clear and professional communication throughout the event.To help prevent similar events in the future; the following improvements should be considered:Improve airport signage and surface markings in the southeast ramp/SP/A taxiway transition area to better identify taxiway boundaries and hold short locations.Ensure all active taxiways and routing terminology used operationally are accurately depicted on company airport charts and electronic flight deck references.Promote standardized taxi routing practices whenever possible to reduce confusion caused by frequent procedural changes.Encourage clear; concise; and measured communication between controllers and flight crews; particularly during periods of high workload and congestion.Consider additional coordination between ramp control; Ground Metering; and ATC to ensure consistent expectations regarding aircraft positioning and routing in this area.The crew believes the event resulted primarily from unfamiliar routing; unclear taxiway identification; and a congested operating environment rather than any intentional noncompliance with ATC instructions.

column121: While enroute; we had a system 3 hydraulic malfunction that required us to land at the nearest suitable airport. We found a spot on the ramp after exiting the runway. We contacted operations to send a tow team to tow us to the gate. In anticipation of the tow team's arrival; we shut down both engines. After waiting about 20 minutes for the tow team; suddenly the aircraft started to roll forward and then stopped. Without realizing it; we had been parked in an area that had a slight pitch.In hindsight; we realized that by shutting down the number two engine; we lost hydraulic pressure on the brakes. Due to the non-standard configuration of the hydraulic pumps with the hydraulic three malfunction; the normal brake pressure applied by that system was not on. Keeping hydraulic two system on would have prevented this problem.Cause: The non-standard configuration with the hydraulic system and the high workload related to an unplanned diversion both contributed to this event.Suggestions: During non-standard operations with hydraulic system malfunctions; it would be great to have some kind of checklist or reminder to double-check the systems for any non-standard scenarios that might be anticipated. Due to the nature of an unplanned diversion; and all the details that come with that non-standard scenario; it was difficult to remember the non-standard situations to expect with system malfunctions.

column121: Severe turbulence encounter over OBK aboard Aircraft X; ZZZ - ZZZ1; XA:14 Day 0.Aircrew was aware of a large weather system along the route of flight and; on the previous flight (ZZZ1 - ZZZ); had coordinated a significant deviation from the originally filed flight plan due to this weather system. Prior to departure; we reviewed the flight plan filed by dispatch; and assessed that; as the route of flight took us to the north of the weather pattern (as opposed to going through the south of it; as we had been filed on the previous leg); we would safely avoid the weather.I conduct all of my welcome aboard announcements via face-to-face communication at the galley. During my PA; I stressed that we would be encountering significant weather during the first 1 - 1.5 hours of the flight; and that it was very important for the passengers to remain seated while the seatbelt sign was on; for their safety; and that I anticipated turning the seatbelt sign off during the remaining hour of the flight.In flight; Center (Chicago Center?) recommended that we add OBK to our route to avoid the northernmost boundary of the weather. We entered OBK into our weather application; assessed that this was a prudent route modification based on the developing weather; and accepted OBK. I also communicated the change to dispatch. We observed an area of moderate turbulence over OBK and did not see that as a significant threat; however it was enough for me to ensure that both FAs were seated while we penetrated the turbulence in accordance with the FOM.I initially directed the FAs to remain seated during the initial climb based on other turbulence I observed we would encounter early in the flight; then I released the FAs to perform service at their discretion. When I initially released them; I informed them that they would be able to be up for approximately 30 minutes; then they would need to be seated to penetrate an area of anticipated moderate turbulence (over OBK). After approximately 30 minutes; and about 5 minutes until we reached OBK; I called them to direct them to return to their seats.We had been operating in full IMC for about 20 minutes prior to reaching OBK. (The weather at OBK was visually embedded from our perspective.) ATC advised that there was an area of moderate to heavy precipitation around OBK; I was tracking this area via both the weather application and the onboard aircraft radar. I noted (via onboard radar) that there was an area of heavy precipitation depicted just south of OBK; and that our route appeared to slightly bypass that area to the north. Weather application still showed moderate turbulence.We encountered substantial turbulence as we reached OBK. Altitude and airspeed deviations were so violent that it was nearly impossible to keep up with them; I estimate that we had +- 500 ft. of altitude loss/gain at one point. FO as PF slowed from Mach .77 to .75; and I engaged both Continuous Ignition and the Turbulence Mode on the FCP.Based on the information displayed on our weather application; I believed that we would not be in the worst of the turbulence for very long; so it was in our best interest to continue in our direction of flight instead of turn around. The event lasted approximately two minutes. After exiting the severe turbulence; I assessed that we had just experienced a severe turbulence encounter and called the FAs to assess the conditions in the cabin. The FAs reported no injuries or known damage. I then reported a severe turbulence encounter to ATC; consulted relevant guidance on the FOM; notified dispatch of the encounter and requested maintenance to meet us at ZZZ1.After reaching the Western Michigan area and exiting all turbulence; I turned off the seatbelt sign and the flight continued normally.In my opinion; the weather in the area around OBK simply progressed worse / faster than forecast; and there just was not a viable means available to any of the relevant actors (flight crew; ATC and dispatch) to detect that area of severe turbulence.Dispatch provided what appeared to be a safe route prior to departure (having immediately prior to that fight to initiate a route modification to that same departure point; I closely scrutinized the proposed route to avoid a repeat of that situation). ATC SPECIFICALLY recommended OBK to further isolate us from the weather. Dispatch was informed and did not object to the route modification. Flight crew was actively monitoring the weather during our approach to OBK via weather application and onboard radar; there was simply nothing to indicate an area of severe turbulence via the resources available to the crew; and likely dispatch or ATC.Risks to passengers and crew were successfully mitigated by direct and constant communication and ensuring cabin preparation for turbulence penetration.Suggestions: Information only.
column123: Severe turbulence in flight. During cruise flight at approximately FL340 the aircraft encountered severe turbulence while enroute from ZZZ to ZZZ1. column121: Aircraft was in cruise flight; 34;000 ft.; on a weather deviation approximately 35 miles east of route between the ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 intersections. Flight was proceeding normally; we were anticipating a turn back on course to rejoin before ZZZZZ2 (turning back approximately abeam position ZZZZZ1) as we tracked the weather via radar and satellite data from the Weather App. Aircraft was dispatched with 2 MELs - 21-XX-XXX Packs and A46-YY-YYY Domestic Enroute (USA) CPDLC Restricted. The first MEL meant that we were operating with a single PACK - #2. (Pack #1 was OFF per the procedure of the MEL.)Due to reported SatCom outages - Dispatch just happened to choose our flight to do a SatCom voice check. As the non-normal unfolded this fortuitous SatCom call from the company helped expedite communications to prep ZZZZ Operations for the divert. We were able to communicate our intentions and had both dispatch and Maintenance Control looped in on the issue as it was happening live. We received the following ECAMs: Air Pack 1+2 Fault. CAB PR Lo Diff PR. CAB PR Excess Cab Alt.We followed SOP in accordance with an aeronautical decision-making model and worked the ECAMs as they presented themselves. I called for priority handling on 121.5 (guard) - announced our intentions to divert to ZZZZ and we began an expedited descent to 10;000 ft. ZZZ [ARTCC] Air Traffic Control responded to our distress call - gave us a new frequency; established radar contact; and gave us a vector towards the airport (ZZZZ). We donned our O2 masks and established flight deck communications. Continued to work the non-normal while on the expedited descent. The situation continued to evolve as the associated ECAMs began appearing - i.e.; CAB PR Lo Diff PR & CAB PR Excess Cab Alt. I communicated to inflight via the call button - they answered right away. I told them that we were in a situation. Explained the reason (loss of pressurization system) and told them our time to landing. I also made a PA to the passengers letting them know that we would be making an unscheduled stop; giving them a non-technical explanation of the problem; and that we'd have more information for them on the ground for how they would continue their journey to ZZZ. I was told during the post-flight debrief with the inflight crew that I did a stellar job pushing and pulling the information to both inflight and the passengers. Inflight felt very calm about the whole non-normal as it evolved. (Aside from the ear-popping) inflight told me that the passengers were very calm and nonplussed the whole time. My PA from the flight deck diffused any cabin stress that would have led to an undesirable outcome once on the ground.We continued working aspects of the non-normal and transited into the arrival and approach phase of the flight. Our new destination was inputted; weather obtained; approach was built and briefed; charts and airport company pages reviewed. In this phase of flight - everything was stable. The cabin altitude was at a safe breathable level; we had removed our O2 masks and reestablished flight deck comms. Important to note; the passenger O2 masks DID NOT deploy from the Passenger Service Units (PSUs) during the non-normal. We were proceeding on a vector to our approach - RVAV XX into ZZZZ. I took the time to review the Overweight Landing QRH Checklist. (Our landing weight was 147.8 - a couple of thousand pounds higher than max for that particular weight variant.) Also; the divert checklist in the Manual. I wanted to ensure that we were covering all of our bases and not missing anything. I also reviewed the steps we took during the non-normal up to this point - I talked out loud" while FO and I discussed what got us from 34;000 ft. to this approach into ZZZZ and plainly asked; "Did we forget anything?" The aircraft was expertly landed in ZZZZ by FO. He followed the guidance in accordance with the overweight checklist. "Soft" touchdown and the brakes did not heat up above approximately 200 C. We taxied to the gate where we were met by Station Operations; Local Crash Fire Rescue (CFR); Local Customs and Immigration; and Local Maintenance Control representatives. Times were noted and passed to dispatch. I made the following write-ups in the logbook: AIR Pack 1+2 Fault Inflight - may have been due to OVHT condition. CAB PR Excess CAB ALT ECAM - associated with the above write-up. CAB PR LO Diff PR - associated with write-ups. Overweight landing due to divert - Landing Weight: 147;800 lb.; soft touchdown; temperatures less than 210 C. NAV Tuning LS Disagree Inflight - reset as per QRH - continued normally. The 5th write-up was not associated with the situation; non-normal; or divert. After that I talked with the Maintenance Control representative; Station Operations; and made a PA for the passengers talking about next steps. Passengers were deplaned and the non-normal was debriefed (informally) with all of the crew. Aircraft was taken out of service and a flight was dispatched. Any unintentional (or otherwise) deviations from SOP were done under Captain's Authority under the appropriate FARs. Any errors were trapped using our Threat and Error Management (TEM) model. I would like to commend (and sincerely thank) the crew - FO and FAs - for their professionalism and skill during the event and divert to ZZZZ. Their quick thinking; calm demeanor; and adherence to SOP made this a very easy problem to navigate. I may be the final authority and ultimately responsible for the flight; but we couldn't have done what we did without the support of the whole crew doing their jobs competently and without delay. They are all the best. I'd also like to thank the instructor pilots at Company. Every instructor that I interacted during every training event for the past years contributed to the safe outcome of this non-normal. In conclusion; we had a safe and successful outcome. I can tell you honestly that I will be debriefing this incident internally for the rest of my career - with many lessons learned. Our flight had a serious mechanical problem and we stayed off social media and out of the news. The passengers seemed genuinely not annoyed with the outcome - they still got to their final destination; albeit a little later than they hoped. Our training and the safety systems worked the way that they were designed. It wasn't perfect - no real world non-normal is. I'm very proud of my crew and it's ultimately because of them (and the whole Company support structure) that we completed the flight as successfully as we did."

column121: We were flying A220 into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ and had just leveled off at the bottom altitude of 5;000 ft. at ZZZZZ1. After passing the fix; the captain (pilot flying) selected heading mode and requested the route be cleaned up for the approach. As the pilot monitoring I cleaned up the approach by placing ZZZZZ2 as the from waypoint and executing. Shortly thereafter we received a clearance to descend and maintain 2;000 ft. The captain selected 2;000 ft. and hit FLC as usual. The plane initiated an aggressive descent trying to catch the Flight Director (FD) which was indicating a steep dive. The throttles also started to command a high power setting. The plane ended up in an accelerating nose low attitude increasing well above the bugged 250 kt. The captain attempted to troubleshoot the issue and confirm the selections on the FCP. As PM I was monitoring the rate of descent and our altitude and speed which was approaching 300 kt. and 2;000 ft. rapidly. The captain removed all automation by turning the autothrottles and autopilot off. The aircraft was returned to level flight at 2;200 ft. with a brief overspeed to 304 kt. We then proceeded to maintain our assigned altitude of 2;000 ft. as the aircraft slowed. There was no ATC recognition of the excessive descent or high speed as we leveled by the assigned altitude of 2;000 ft. Automation was re-established and initially it looked like the FD was indicating another dive. Automation was again disconnected and re-established and everything seemed to be functioning as usual. We completed the approach and landing without any further anomalies.

column121: On Day 0; I was undertaking flight training from my Flight Instructor in a Piper Super Cub Tailwheel aircraft; Aircraft X; to pursue my tailwheel endorsement. The flight started off as any normal training does; we departed ZZZ1 to the east towards a training area so I could get a feel for the aircraft. After getting a feel of the aerodynamics of this aircraft; we proceeded to ZZZ. There we proceeded to enter the pattern and start landing practice.Our first few landings were three point landings to get an understanding of the approach and landing of the aircraft. Then we transitioned to wheel takeoffs and landings. On the second wheel takeoff; we proceeded as normal in the pattern with myself flying and making calls over the CTAF. As we turned base; the approach was stabilized on centerline and with a good descent rate. A gust on approach moved us left of centerline but was quickly corrected.On short final as we were crossing over the threshold; I brought the power to a position that would assist the wheel landing. On touchdown we started a rollout when a gust hit us on the right side of the aircraft causing us to weathervane into it. The Flight Instructor quickly hopped on the controls and verbalized his aircraft as the tail swung left into my gusting wind. As the plane started to turn it quickly turned into a ground loop that the flight instructor tried to correct for. Suddenly we were pointed towards the grass on the edge of the runway. In an effort to stop the aircraft before rolling off my flight instructor tapped on the brakes in hopes of slowing us down but the plane instead stopped in its tracks causing the nose of the aircraft to fall over and onto the ground.After the aircraft stopped moving and the nose was positioned into the pavement I turned off the engine by cutting the mixture and throttle; turning off the fuel selector; turning off the magnetos and the electrical system. My flight instructor got out of the aircraft first and I followed getting away from the aircraft and assessing ourselves for any injuries. After confirming no injuries we proceeded to talk to the authorities.Contributing factors for this event would be the gusting conditions; my little experience in a tailwheel aircraft; and the sensitivity of the aircraft brakes. My flight instructor performed to the best of his abilities and was focused on my safety throughout the incident.

Everything normal on taxi from gate to runway XXL as well as a standard takeoff. Upon climbing through roughly 5-6 thousand feet the left engine started to cough with no TLO (Temporary Limited Operations) or CAS (Crew Alerting System) message. Initially assuming it was engine protection mode I reduced the power slightly. For a moment the coughing stopped but then while I continued the climb the coughing returned. While viewing the engine page I noticed the LH oil pressure was in the yellow (low 50's psi) and the LH oil temp was getting close to the red line sitting just above 230 degrees F. Once I leveled off I pulled the power to normal cruise settings which stopped the engine from coughing however the LH oil pressure stayed low and the LH oil temp stayed high. At this point I decided to ask ATC to return to ZZZ. ATC cleared me back to ZZZ and vectored me in for a visual XX. ATC inquired about the reason for coming back to ZZZ; which I informed them the left engine was not running properly at high power. ATC prioritized my aircraft and proceeded to get me back to ZZZ promptly. Landing was normal and upon landing I was asked if I needed any assistance which I answered negative. Engine did not cough after I asked to return to ZZZ. Taxied into the gate uneventfully and passengers were taken care of. column121: On Day 0 while operating Aircraft X the flight crew experienced an un commanded movement of the aircraft during the shutdown portion of the flight. After being guided to a complete stop at the gate; the parking brake was set and PARK BRK message verified along with normal pressure indications. The shutdown flow continued in sequence and during the portion of the flow while heads were down; the aircraft began to roll. Once the un commanded movement was realized; the Captain slammed on the brakes immediately. The aircraft came to an abrupt stop. At some point during the roll or just prior to toe brakes being applied the crew received a BRAKES PARK BRK FAULT ECAM message with zero pressure indicated on the accumulator. There were no injuries to ground crew; flight crew or passengers. There was no damage to either the aircraft or jet bridge. The crew followed standard operating procedures and maintained positive control of the aircraft to the best of their ability throughout the event. Once the aircraft was confirmed chocked; the toe brakes were released and the parking brake recycled which then cleared the ECAM and returned hydraulic pressure back to normal. The aircraft was subsequently repositioned via tug vehicle and secured. Maintenance was contacted shortly after.Cause: This event appears to be purely an aircraft systems failure. Per the logbook; the aircraft has a history of this very same problem and clearly needs to be fixed permanently. One recommendation that the crew can add to help mitigate the risk of injury to the passengers would be to relocate the seat belt sign off to one of the last items on the shutdown flow and checklist. The passengers were thrown forward when the brakes were slammed on bc the seatbelt sign had been turned off per the second step of the flow. Engines were still running which allowed the aircraft to move forward quickly. Had the engines been shutdown prior to the seat belt sign being extinguished; we may not have had the high risk of injuring a passenger.
