column121: Upon arrival at ZZZ we taxied to gate XX.  We kept the throttles at idle in/through the turn to parking per the company pages; however the aircraft momentum led us to stop short of the hold line and we required a tow in.  I announced to the passengers to keep their seatbelts on and we would be towed to the gate.  After brakes had been set the ground crew moved the tug in front of the aircraft beneath the line of sight from the cockpit.  After a pause; one of the rampers on the Captain side of the aircraft gave a hand signal quickly.  I interpreted this as the opening hands signal to release brakes and did so.  There was a short pause and the aircraft began moving.  I initially perceived this as tug movement on the aircraft.  The FO said something expressing concern; which I first thought was due to him not having seen the signal directly.  Within another second or so we both applied brakes and I reset the parking brake.  The aircraft had moved a few feet; but I couldn't give an exact distance.  Via interphone we resestablished positive comms with the ramper and the rest of the tow-in was uneventful.  No aircraft damage or personnel injury occurred.  I met with and debriefed with the rampers.  I don't believe any passengers were alarmed by aircraft movement.  I phoned the Chief Pilot and relayed the above information.
column123: During taxi in to gate XX in ZZZ; a miscommunication occurred and the aircraft moved without concurrence or expectation from the ground crew.  Gate XX is noted in the company pages as requiring idle thrust from the taxi lane into the gate entirely; and that the gate is upsloped. This was briefed prior to arrival and we discussed possibly needing a tow into the gate if the turn couldn't be successfully accomplished at idle thrust.  It could not in our case; and we stopped about 50 feet short of the stop bar. The tow  in procedure was initialized by us and the ground crew and we shut down the engines. The incident occurred during the hook up of the tug unit. The tug and ground crew approached the aircraft; and being under the aircraft only briefly; the captain said out loud; ok brakes released" and the captain did so; to which I was alerted as being too soon in the normal sequence. I looked up and around the aircraft and saw the aircraft quickly yawing to the left and said; "whoa; no no no"; and began to depress the brake pedals from my side as I was trying to confirm my belief that this was premature. The captain stated; "I have the brakes released hand signals! They're towing us!" And I responded; "no; no you don't!"; the captain joined me on the brakes and I saw multiple ground crew from my window with the now-visible tug giving us the 'stop' signal; and relayed what I saw to the captain. We realized the aircraft had swung nose-left uncommanded/unintended and put the ground crew at very high risk.  The distance the nosewheel rolled I estimate to be about 10-15 feet.  The ground crew plugged in their headset and they confirmed brakes were set; and the captain asked if everyone was safe and ok; which the ground crew confirmed.  We froze the scene; discussed what happened; and ensured and agreed we could safely continue.  We; the flight crew; realized the ground crew already had the nosewheel bypass pin installed when the aircraft rolled; and the reason the aircraft yawed was the nosewheel free castering under the weight of the unbraked aircraft.  The captain stated he mistook this movement as being towed. With the ground crew; we discussed how to move forward safely; including how to straighten the nosewheel to restart the tug connection. This was accomplished safely and the aircraft was pulled into the gate and proceeded normally after that.  We debriefed the event very thoroughly between ourselves and with the ground crew. We identified the primary cause of the event was the captain and one of the ground crew confused the "brakes set" vs "brakes released" hand signals between each other; either through expectation bias or vague signaling; and the parking brake was released prematurely prior to completing the tug hookup."

column121: A helicopter completed a search and rescue mission in the vicinity of Herendeen Bay. The helicopter was flying between 250-500' AGL through a mountain pass to get to Sand Point; Alaska (PASD) to drop off the survivor and to obtain fuel. Enroute to Sand Point; near 5537.37N/16051.08W; approximately 200'-250' AGL; two aircraft; described as high-wing; were traveling through the pass in the opposite direction. The helicopter took action and descended to the left. At the lowest point; the helicopter was at approximately 100' AGL. It appeared that the two other aircraft were flying in a loose formation and they were banking left. One of the oncoming aircraft passed on the left side of the helicopter approximately co-altitude with 300' of separation; and the other flew directly overhead approximately 150' above the helicopter. The helicopter pilots reported the incident to Air Station Kodiak as a 'serious near mid air collision.' There were no damage nor injuries reported to the helicopter crew. The crew is unsure if the other two aircraft were aware that they were flying through the area. There were no radio transmissions made or heard within the helicopter. Visibility was reported from 1/2 to 2 miles. Ceilings were reported as low as 500' within the pass.

column121: Good afternoon. During visual pattern operations for Runway 26 at Colorado Air and Space Port; I observed two traffic sequencing and communication issues from tower control that reduced safety margins and required pilot corrective action.While intercepting final from the south on an approximate 360-degree heading; my aircraft was sequenced behind another aircraft on base to final. Due to a significant closure rate; I assessed that spacing would become unsafe near or shortly after final approach intercept despite early speed reduction. I maintained visual contact and ADS-B awareness of the traffic throughout the event.Radio congestion limited the ability to clarify instructions with tower. To maintain safe separation; I offset slightly east of final approach course. Tower communications and sequencing during the event indicated reduced situational awareness and ineffective traffic management consistent with degraded Crew Resource Management and communication discipline.Following the touch-and-go; additional pattern instructions resulted in a second developing overtaking conflict on right downwind. Unable to safely match the slower aircraft's pattern speed and spacing; I extended upwind until constrained by the Denver International Airport Class B airspace; then turned crosswind and maneuvered north of the expected pattern track to maintain safe separation.In both instances; corrective action by my aircraft was required to maintain safe separation and avoid an unsafe traffic conflict created by sequencing; tower desired ground track and communication deficiencies within the pattern. Tower responses following both events suggested confusion and frustration regarding the evolving traffic situation. I departed the pattern VFR to the east without further incident.

column121: During the time of this event; I was the On-the-job Training Instructor (OJTI) for our Radar East position training Person A. We were on for about an hour already at the time. While traffic volume was not high; there had been increased complexity with Parachute Jump Area (PJA) happening; and multiple VFR and primary targets that were a factor with our traffic that we were not in contact with. There was a visual identification tagged aircraft flying over ZZZ airport at 056 and Local Control (LC) (training in progress at the time) called asking if we wanted their next departure capped at 040 for them; which we said yes to. That cap was to stop a TCAS-RA from happening. We were discussing at the time if the cap was necessary or not. Aircraft X was put on course direct to ZZZ [VOR]. We got distracted with other things; and Aircraft X leveled at 040 towards the 044 MVA and was not told to climb; by neither Person A nor myself. Aircraft X then requested higher as he was entering the 044 MVA; which then Person A told Aircraft X to contact ZZZ [ARTCC]. It was at that time I realized he wasn't told to climb to 090 and keyed up to have him climb; though I did not issue a Low Altitude Alert. He was 3 miles in the MVA at the time.We should've put a focus on that aircraft and had continued their climb.

column121: While in flight around ELP we experienced GPS jamming. After a while we received GPS and GLS FMC alert messages. I verified RNP value of .24 and referenced the Flight Manual (FM). Both left and right GPS were failed at this time. It was anticipated that once clear of the GPS jamming that all systems would return to normal. For some additional context at this point of the flight we had been navigating through thunderstorms and I had all the flight attendants seated. When approaching the portion of flight that was about to cross the gulf I reached out to Dispatch and Maintenance Control to try to recover our GPS as I was thinking about the GPS issue more and was concerned that being away from land base nav aids for such a long time would cause the ANP to drift to unacceptable levels for a long segment over water. Maintenance Control directed to pull the Multi-Mode Receiver (MMR) ILS-1 Circuit Breaker (CB) per FM. It was during this reset both FMC failed; autothrottle; autopilot; disengaged and the aircraft went into Control Wheel Steering (CWS). The first officer flew the aircraft and was able to recover and engage the CMD with Alt hold/CWS. We received radar vectors from ATC to stay over the Houston shoreline at FL330. At this time Chief Pilot also was on the line and together we walked through a recovery of the right FMC was accomplished with the return of the Control Display Unit (CDU) FMC functionality.  It was at this time the options were discussed about how to proceed and I made the decision to divert due to the amounts of threats with the current aircraft maintenance status and external factors such as thunderstorms; overwater operations; international operations; remaining fuel on board; and weather upon arrival.
column123: The night prior I hadn't slept very well; I laid down at midnight and got out of bed in the morning but spent a lot of that time unable to fall sleep and didn't feel very rested going into the day. I made sure to give myself time before work to rest. I was able to nap for roughly three hours before getting ready for work. There was some traffic so the drive took me longer to get to the airport. I felt relatively rested through most of the flight and ready to continue with no concerns. I think the workload involved with the GPS jamming which eventually let to the Dual FMC failure and divert; along with weather deviations for thunderstorms throughout the issue was very fatiguing; especially for a late all night flying flight. When we lost our FMCs we reverted to ALT HOLD and Control Wheel Steering (CWS) R; Autothrottles disengaged and wouldn't reengage; I was hand flying; and coordinating with ATC to deviate around thunderstorms. The captain was talking with Maintenance Control; dispatch; the Chief Pilot and keeping the flight attendants and passengers informed. With this particular event there wasn't really much guidance in our manuals or procedures on how to proceed. It took a lot of discussion; troubleshooting and decision making to come up with a decision. We ultimately diverted. After arriving at our gate; the captain and I talked about whether or not we should continue. We agreed that it would not be a safe decision to extend our duty day and accept another flight. I think the whole event was just fatiguing on an already late night. While debriefing on the ground and trying to recall the details of the issue; it was apparent we were showing signs of fatigue.

column121: The flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 started off uneventful. Everything was going smoothly and as expected. During our climb to FL330; at FL320 I noticed a faint amount of smoke coming from the PTT button panel. There was also a noticeable burning plastic smell. The smoke did not stick around very long and was gone in roughly 20 seconds. The burning smell did remain throughout the flight though. Captain was the pilot flying when we noticed the smoke and smell. Captain transferred controls to me and requested priority handling with ATC. It was a very small amount of smoke; but it was still smoke. So we did our smoke fire and fumes memory action items. We established communication but the Captain was slightly hard to hear with the masks on. Captain tried making another call to ATC but they could not understand anything he was saying due to the mask not being clear. We transferred controls back to him and I took over communications and checklists. I cleared up confusion with ATC that was present from Captain not being understood. We established we were a priority aircraft and would like to divert to ZZZ2. We were told to descend and we could expect vectors for the ILS XX into ZZZ2. While we started a fast descent; Captain sent a message through ACARS to dispatch that we were diverting. I got out our QRH after confirming our memory action items from the QRC. I started the Smoke Fire or Fumes QRH. While going through this checklist I did get interrupted a few times. I needed to relay to ATC our situation. I told them our fuel on board and the souls on board. I needed to make this call a couple times as they did not hear clearly the first time. Once that was clear we called back to the flight attendant that we were diverting and seeing if he had any smoke in the cabin. He could not understand the Captain and after a couple attempts; I told him we were diverting and learned he did not have any smoke in the back. While this conversation was happening ATC was giving us instructions to swap frequencies and to keep descending. I believe we got swapped to approach at roughly 14;000 MSL. Approach gave us a heading to fly as well for the ILS XX. While we were descending; and I was handling communications; the Captain got the approach loaded and frequencies set up. Communications were set up and the approach was loaded. I continued the QRH and got to the point of executing an emergency descent; at this point Captain said to pause that checklist as we needed to focus on preparing for landing. We were also at roughly 10;000 MSL so we did not need any more of an emergency descent as we had acted quickly about getting lower. On our descent I called the FA for a briefing. I told him there was smoke and we are landing in ZZZ2. I told him he had roughly 5 minutes or less until landing. No special instructions as we should be going to the gate as normal. No bracing signal. I had him report that back and he did so perfectly. Continued our descent; we broke out of IMC at roughly 8;000 MSL if I recall correctly; after having being in IMC up until this point through the issue. Captain gave a briefing on the approach. Afterward; I ran the Cruise; Descent; and Approach checklists. Both of us verifying items were complete and accurate. After running the approach checklists; I checked our weight and told the Captain we would be over max landing weight. We got swapped to tower and continued our approach. I ran the overweight landing checklist and we utilized the new landing distance that we were still in compliance with. We were cleared to land by tower on runway XX. With the landing; Captain came in slightly below glide slope to have some time to arrest our descent. He did so very well and we touched down very smoothly. Tower told us we could stop on taxi way 1 after exiting the runway but we elected to get to the ramp. While we taxied I gave a passenger announcement that we were in ZZZ2 due to a precautionary event and we would give them an update when we have one.I apologized about the inconvenience of the diversion and for not addressing them in the air as we were quite busy. Tower gave us instructions to cross runway XY on 2. We got to the ramp and a fire truck was parked in front of the intersection; 3; that we took. The Captain came to a stop as it seemed two firefighters were approaching us and wanted us to stop. The firefighters came up to the plane with both engines running. They did not appear to see anything abnormal as they were very calm. They wanted to communicate and gave us some hand motions to their ears. The Captain and I opened our windows and I tried shouting to them that we could still smell the burning plastic. I had the goggles and mask still on which made this hard. They handed up a note pad to the Captain and we coordinated to taxi to a gate with passing the note pad back and forth. I told the Captain that we can still smell the smoke and mentioned evacuating there. He said no; it will be much better getting passengers off at the gate and I agreed. We did not confirm with the FA that everyone was seated before we started moving again. Later; FA did tell me that everyone was seated when we started moving. We did not contact company ops in ZZZ2; which looking back could have made the ground operations a bit smoother for us. While we taxied to the gate I addressed the passengers and apologized again about the inconvenience and thanked them for their understanding. While addressing the passengers I did not use an alarmed tone or emergency terminology. We parked the plane and continued to run all of our check lists on the ground as normal. The passengers started to deplane and while everyone was exiting; they were very grateful for keeping them safe. Many expressed their thanks to our entire crew. No passengers reported any sort of illness or injuries. Firefighters came aboard and utilized their heat camera and said they did not see anything triggering it. We assumed the source of the smoke was confirmed to be out. We talked with dispatch and maintenance and got everything situated for the day. The crew took a deadhead back to ZZZ.Suggestions: I would suggest that during training there be a little more emphasis of what to do with issues when safely on the ground. Our situation was time critical but did not constitute an emergency evacuation that would have drawn much more attention to the situation. The communications on the ground were lacking as well. I had assumed tower would have gotten a spot set up for us to go to when on the ground but they seemed very laid back with the mentality that we can go wherever we want.

column121: Set up and departure from the gate at ZZZ1 was normal; however; I did notice that while taxiing the aircraft would veer to the left requiring right tiller and rudder inputs to remain straight. In spite of this I didn't consider the aircraft unsafe to fly with taxi and take off uneventful.Weather en-route was stormy with storms moving through the ZZZ area; WX in ZZZ low IFR. By the time we arrived in the terminal area the storms had moved through with only light rain; winds at 010/8 and runway code at 555. Flying the ILS to runway XXR at ZZZ; the aircraft touched down on the runway centerline; however; just after the nose wheel contacted the runway the aircraft immediately veered to the left. My immediate thought was the aircraft was hydroplaning so I released brake pressure and applied right rudder. It felt like we were sliding towards the runway edge and I was concerned too much right rudder would exacerbate the slide. The reversers deployed but I don't think reverse thrust activated. As the aircraft slowed; I was able to regain control; return to the centerline and exit the runway. There was no shuddering or shimmy from the gear throughout the event.I slowly taxied to the gate with the aircraft still showing the left taxi bias we experienced in ZZZ1. At this point the FO mentioned he thought we may have hit one of the runway edge lights. It turned out we indeed had hit one of the runway lights between taxiway 1 and 2. There was no noticeable damage to the nose wheel or the aircraft. The only evidence was glass in the right nose-wheel rim. Taxiing to the gate and once we started the APU the electrical system went haywire. Master caution warnings and the EICAS lit up like a Christmas tree. THE APU GEN bus was offline; which would not reset. My PFD (Primary Flight Display) and the FO's MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) went dark and it was like we were on essential power at the gate. An electrical reset completed under Maintenance supervision fixed that issue. The passengers disembarked without any comment regarding the landing or the power outage at the gate. Their only comments were regarding the turbulence enroute. My FO is a low time pilot with just over 100 hrs on type; however; he was excellent throughout this event and was a tremendous help supporting me while I was communicating with Maintenance and Operations.Suggestions: The event was typical of uncommanded steering and I probably should've disengaged the steering and called for a tow to the gate. I thought of this as I regained control however I think the startle factor played a role here. Noticing the taxi trend to veer left maybe I should've considered a gate return; however the aircraft was late to the gate and I had a similar condition previously with the aircraft not tracking straight; however; previously it was not an issue. I didn't consider the aircraft unsafe to fly.
column123: Flight ABCD ZZZ1 to ZZZ the flight preceded as normal with weather en route until the landing. The condition code for XXR was 5 5 5 at the time of landing with light rain. Upon touching down after a normal flaps 45 approach the aircraft began to veer left. The aircraft began to reach the runway edge and struck an edge light with the nose wheel. As the aircraft slowed down the captain was able to keep the aircraft on the runway and return to the centerline. Runway was exited at 2. Departing ZZZ1 the aircraft had a tendency to pull left during the taxi. This did not affect the takeoff roll when departing ZZZ1. Additionally; after crossing RWY XY at ZZZ the number one engine was shut down and APU started near the parking gate. This led to a cascade of EICAS messages filling the entire page with an additional 15 messages not displayed. Everything from ICE COND INOP to SPOILER FAIL to DAU1 B FAIL. FO side lost the MFD (Multifunction Flight Display) and Capt lost PFD (Primary Flight Display). A reset of the electrical system was performed with Maintenance after parking at the gate.Suggestions: From what I could tell the initial pull to the left experienced in ZZZ1 during the taxi is what led to the incident. After touchdown the aircraft veered right and was approaching the runway edge. After slowing the aircraft the Captain (pilot flying) was able to steer the aircraft back to the centerline. It seems that the speed made the left veering tendency worse. As the aircraft slowed the captain had more control to steer the plane.

column123: After contract maintenance completed work on an ENG2 REVERSER FAULT; which occurred on the previous flight; item was closed and CDL (Configuration Deviation List) was applied. column121: Shortly after retracting the gear on takeoff we received a HYD G ENG 1 PUMP LO PR ECAM.  Initially it was intermittent; with Green pressure showing between 100 - 1100 psi.  It shortly dropped to zero quantity.  I delayed running the ECAM until we had gained a little more altitude and completed the initial part of the ZZZZZX departure.  Climbing through ~ 7;000-8;000 ft; I called for QRC.  With no QRC; I transferred control to the FO with instructions to tell ATC that we'd stop our climb at 11;000 ft; which was our current assigned altitude.  ATC was informed of the issue and that we'd need a few minutes to run some checklists and talk to company…with a likely return to ZZZ.  I ran the ECAM; and once that was complete; I began the QRH.  Once that was completed down to the Emergency Gear Extension; we paused the QRH.  I then contacted company via Satcom (dispatch and Maintenance Control).  The phone patch from dispatch to Maintenance Control took a while; so while we waited to be connected; we started to run the Overweight Landing Checklist to make good use of our time.  I also spoke to the cabin crew to bring them up to speed on what was happening and told them I'd get back to them when I knew what we were going to do.  Once connected with Maintenance Control; they confirmed that we had lost all green pressure.  With thunderstorms forecasted for the ZZZ1 area; with the possibility of a divert; we agreed that the best course of action was to return to ZZZ.  Dispatch reminded me of the overweight checklist; which we had already begun.  Dispatch sent us the re-dispatch back to ZZZ; which we received via the printer as well as on the Operations Management System.  Once done with dispatch and Maintenance Control; we informed ATC with our intent to return to ZZZ; that we'd need about 20 minutes to finish checklists and to prepare for the return.  I also requested priority handling; requested Crash Fire and Rescue (CFR); and we notified ATC that once on the ground we would be unable to exit the runway due to the loss of nose wheel steering.  With the aircraft ready for the return to ZZZ and having spoken to the customers as well as cabin crew; we informed ATC that we were ready for the approach.  I briefed the cabin crew and made them aware it should be a normal landing with the exception of the CFR equipment meeting us and our inability to exit the runway/need for a tow to the gate.  Prior to returning to the airport we completed the Overweight Landing Checklist and reviewed the remaining portion of the QRH from the Emergency Gear Extension to the End; so that we had both seen it before needing to accomplish it.With everything prepared for the return; we notified ATC we were ready for the approach.  I allowed ample time to get configured before the final approach fix.  I instructed my FO to note the touchdown rate of decent and we noted the landing weight as well.  The touchdown rate was less than 50 fpm and I let the aircraft roll most of the length of runway XXL.  Brake temps initially were around 85 degrees; warming to roughly 160 degrees by the time the tug arrived.  Once stopped on the runway; I made a Remain Seated" PA and then spoke to cabin crew as well as made an announcement to the customers.  CFR and airport operations met the aircraft.  In roughly 10-15 minutes our tug arrived and we were escorted back to gate XX.One last component to mention was that we had an Air Carrier X pilot on the Jumpseat.  Once the issue started; he got on the Jumpseat headset and was a good help in monitoring radio calls while we got busy with checklists and briefing the course of action."

column121: On an ETOPS flex power takeoff prior to 80kts ECAM: T/L NOT SET.  Rejected takeoff.  Cleared the runway; ran the QRH Takeoff After Rejected Takeoff Below 80 Knots."  Discussed the possible causes of the ECAM with the FO.  Verified that the Flex temperature had been properly entered and the requirement that the Thrust Levers (T/L) were in the Flex detent.  Taxied out for a second Flex power takeoff attempt.  Prior to taking the runway; verified Flex temperature was on the Perf page.  FO was pilot flying (PF) again.  Flex power was set; and immediately noticed MAN FLEX was not displayed in Flight Mode Annunciator (FMA) column 1 followed by ECAM: T/L NOT SET.  Rejected takeoff.  Cleared runway; called Maintenance Control and was instructed to return to the gate.  Aircraft removed from service.  Resulting maintenance action: replaced engine #1 & #2 T12 sensors and engine throttle control units.Cause: The Airbus AOM discusses this ECAM.  The AOM direction to select TOGA would only apply in the event that the FLEX temperature is not entered (or was inadvertently deleted due to runway change) on the Perf page and a FLEX takeoff is attempted or when the T/Ls are not in the FLEX detent.  This being an ETOPS departure; the decision was made to investigate further by rejecting the takeoff. This decision was validated after getting the same ECAM on the next takeoff anttempt and the subsequent maintenance actions that were taken to return this aircraft to service.  Recommend the AOM expound on the ECAM recommended TOGA selection to include the possible reasons this ECAM may be present.  Our experience and system knowledge prevented us from blindly selecting TOGA and flying an aircraft with a throttle control issue to destination."

column121: This report documents a loss of system A hydraulics on short final followed by a landing and QRH accomplishment.  Landing Gear was pinned and aircraft towed to the gate.  During the approach to ZZZ ILS XX at 800 ft AGL; a Master Caution light illuminated with an associated Hydraulic Elec 2 low pressure light (system A). Pilot Flying (PF) was the FO and Pilot Monitoring (PM) was the Captain. Both pilots acknowledged the light. The PM announced the condition and the PF maintained aircraft control.  Based on the facts that we were fully configured; below 1000'; had sufficient brake pressure; and were landing on a long runway well below required landing distance; we confirmed with each other and agreed to continue the approach to landing and delay the QRH until after landing. The PM subsequently extinguished the master caution light. At 500 ft AGL the Master Caution light illuminated again with associated ENG1 and ELEC2 Hydraulic pump low pressure lights. The simultaneous illumination of both System A hydraulic pump low pressure lights indicated a probable loss of System A hydraulic fluid.  At this point; since we were below 500 ft AGL and conditions were still favorable for a safe landing; we once again confirmed with each other that to continue to a landing was the safest option. At this point in the approach; the PF noted that a small amount of increased right aileron input was required to maintain control. While abnormal; it was easily controllable. From this point on; both pilots focused on landing the aircraft safely. During touchdown and rollout the aircraft performed normally. Automatic spoiler deployment occurred upon touchdown and the aircraft decelerated normally on autobrakes 3. Manual braking was applied shortly after touchdown by the PF. The transfer of aircraft control to the Captain occurred at approximately 70 knots. Initially; nose wheel steering was operational and we cleared the runway on taxiway Charlie cautiously and at a slow taxi speed. Upon the completion of the turn on to taxiway Charlie; the nosewheel steering failed. Once clear of the runway the parking brake was set. At this point we determined that we had a complete loss of system A hydraulics. We informed Tower that we needed to hold position to address a hydraulic leak.  We did not declare an Emergency; as the aircraft was on the ground and under control with the parking brake set.  The Captain then directed the Loss of system A" QRH and the FO read the checklist and we accomplished the applicable items. Communication was established with the Flight Attendants by the Captain and they confirmed that the situation was normal in the cabin.  Since the checklist calls for the gear pins to be installed prior to taxi; we determined the safest course of action would be to shut down the aircraft on the taxiway; have a ramp crew come out to the aircraft; install the gear pins; and tow us to the gate.  The Captain made a PA announcement explaining the situation to the passengers and informing them that we would be towed to the gate and all was under control.  When the tow crew showed up; they plugged in to the intercom and we devised a plan to pin the gear and tow the aircraft to the gate; escorted by airport operations.  We were advised us that they did not have gear pins available.  We then briefed a plan to shut down the aircraft engines; and remain on APU power.  Once safe to approach the aircraft; we would drop the gear pins out of the flight deck window; then clear him to pin the gear.  Once the gear was pinned; we were towed to the gate by the ground crew.  Upon post-flight inspection it was noted that hydraulic fluid was leaking from the number one ground spoiler actuator on the left wing. Also; Airport Operations said that there was hydraulic fluid on the runway.Recommendations to mitigate the riskAfter debriefing as a crew we discussed some other options.  Option 1:  We could have gone around to run the checklist and to devise a plan. However; with the gear stuck down; we had a higher fuel burn rate and no alternate fuel (there is a warning in the checklist about this).  We would have had to maneuver without the use of half the flight spoilers.  We both believed that this option would have prolonged a dangerous airborne situation.  We had the proper configuration for landing; adequate brake pressure; excess runway available (8700' avail).  This option is worth discussing; but we both believed in this particular situation it was better to land.  The difference between a normal landing and a non-normal with loss of A hydraulics is only 400'.Option 2: Stop straight ahead on the runway; pin the gear; get towed to the gate.  We both agree that this may have been a better option.  However; we would have been on an active runway at night;  closing down the runway to other traffic.  That being said; it would have been the most conservative action. Option 3:  Coordinate with ATC to have ARFF available on site and follow us to the gate; since we had a hydraulic leak.  At the time; we did not consider this.  In retrospect; we believe it would have been a more conservative option. If we had accomplished the Non-Routine Landing Considerations QRH; it would have reminded us to do so."

column121: On approach to Chicago; we were cleared for the ILS 9 center. Slowing the aircraft down commanded by ATC from 170 kn to 160 kn; diligently painted a mental model of the traffic around us. We were paired up with Air Carrier X on nine left; nine right; and behind a regional in front of us which I verbalized im actively looking for traffic. At approximately 2000 feet AGL; I verbalize how there's traffic underneath us depicted on the Navigation Display (ND). As my attention went outside the aeroplane I physically saw Aircraft Y climb turn and descend underneath us for which I stated I had the aeroplane in sight within seconds if not tenth of seconds; my first officer was already manually flying the aeroplane preemptively in the best efforts to see and avoid. As as I proactively scan for traffic the only indication of an issue that I had was a second later when the TCAS system alerted us of a traffic advisory. I had not checked in with Tower as my attention was on guiding and managing the safety situation and near miss. Laterally we flew above Aircraft Y vertically last indication I saw on the ND was a vertical separation of about 500 feet if not less. In the best efforts of avoiding further traffic separation my first officer went slightly above wide path if not shallow or decent. I checked in with Tower; our checklist was complete and was clearanced to land and hold short of 9 center. We had another traffic advisory and on the end it was from the aeroplane that had already landed. We landed with no further incident.We had no advisory from air traffic control in protected airspace. Factors that contributed to our success was a good qualified trained crew; pilot judgement; and crew resource management and coordination. I stated my pilot duties to properly and mentally picture our movement through the airspace and how conflicting traffic can be seen and avoided. my first officer assumed the flying duties as expected. I was 10th of a second from taking controls when I needed to however I relied on the good pilot judgement for my first officer to help manage the situation. I can't stress this enough that I could not have done what was required of us unless we properly coordinated as a crew like we did. The professionalism and experience of both of us in the cockpit is inimitable and irreplaceable to safety and security for an efficient and safe operation. My question still stands as far as where and why ATC had no idea of the situation. Furthermore; where was the protected airspace and why was it intruded? The environment that we operated is dynamic so should the availability of protected airspace laterally and vertical. The dimensions should be and meet the operation to the fullest extent to extend bravo airspace if required and other air spaces for special use not just control airspace but specificly more restrictive requirements like bravo airspace. Even if we had an orb of class bravo airspace around the aeroplane; nothing could have contributed more to a successful outcome then two pilots doing the job that was expected of us at all costs.

column121: On Flight ABCD from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on Day 0; we encountered multiple areas of turbulence along our route of flight associated with convective and ride activity depicted on our weather and Sky Path information systems. Prior to departure and throughout the flight; the First Officer and I actively monitored ride reports; weather depictions; and turbulence forecasts in order to mitigate exposure to passengers; flight attendants; and the aircraft.After departure from ZZZ on the ZZZZZX Departure; we initially experienced intermittent light to moderate turbulence during climb and cruise. Based on turbulence depictions along our route; particularly over portions of States X and Y near the ZZZ VOR area; I briefed the flight attendants in advance that we would likely require them to remain seated for an extended period in accordance with turbulence mitigation procedures.As we approached the area near ZZZ; we requested ride reports and altitude advisories from ATC in an effort to identify smoother ride conditions; however; ATC advised that aircraft in the area were reporting similar ride conditions at multiple altitudes. During this phase of flight; we encountered periods of light to moderate and occasional moderate turbulence; intermixed with smoother ride segments. Due to the continuing ride conditions and forecasted turbulence ahead; I directed the flight attendants to take their jump seats and repeatedly advised passengers to remain seated with seat belts fastened.While operating east of the river and north of the ZZZ area; both the First Officer and I began observing abnormal lateral/directional aircraft response characteristics during otherwise routine light to moderate turbulence encounters. Specifically; the aircraft began exhibiting a Dutch roll-type oscillation following even minor turbulence inputs. We noted that the oscillations appeared to amplify with time after turbulence encounters rather than dampen normally.The First Officer; who was Pilot Flying; remained prepared to assume manual control if necessary while I continued monitoring aircraft systems; ATC communications; and cabin coordination. During this time; I made additional passenger announcements emphasizing the need for all passengers to remain seated due to ongoing turbulence. Flight attendants also reported continued passenger movement in the cabin despite repeated announcements.Shortly north of ZZZ2; we again encountered light to moderate turbulence during which the aircraft's lateral oscillation increased further. The autopilot disconnected; and the First Officer smoothly assumed manual control of the aircraft while intentionally avoiding abrupt control inputs in order to minimize unnecessary aircraft motion and provide the best ride possible for the cabin. During this event; the aircraft experienced an altitude deviation of approximately 600-700 feet while in turbulence. I immediately requested and received a block altitude clearance from ATC between FL350 and FL360 to safely manage aircraft control and ride conditions. Other aircraft on frequency were simultaneously reporting similar turbulence-related issues and requesting altitude blocks in the same area.The First Officer stabilized the aircraft promptly; and we returned to our assigned altitude shortly thereafter. While monitoring aircraft systems; I observed the Yaw Damper switch in the OFF position with the associated Yaw Damper light illuminated. I checked the annunciator panel and noted no associated FLT CONT annunciation. Based on system knowledge and QRH guidance; I reengaged the Yaw Damper switch; at which time the Yaw Damper light extinguished and the aircraft's flight characteristics returned to normal. The First Officer concurrently referenced and completed the applicable QRH non-normal procedures while I monitored aircraft performance and flight path.After the aircraft returned to normal handling characteristics; I contacted the flight attendants to assess cabin conditions. The flight attendants advised that there were no injuries among passengers or crew; although several passengers in the aft cabin and one flight attendant experienced nausea associated with the lateral oscillation and ride conditions. At no point did the aircraft experience severe vertical acceleration or abrupt up-and-down movement; the primary ride issue involved lateral oscillation and rolling motion that was particularly noticeable in the aft cabin.Following coordination with ATC; stabilization of aircraft systems; and confirmation from the flight attendants that there were no injuries; we elected to continue the flight to ZZZ1. An ELB (Electronic Logbook) message was sent in flight to advise Maintenance Control of the event and to facilitate maintenance evaluation upon arrival. For passenger comfort; we subsequently reduced cruise speed to Mach .75; and ride conditions improved significantly as we progressed north of State Z. Once conditions permitted; the flight attendants resumed cabin duties; and I made a passenger announcement apologizing for the turbulence and advising passengers that multiple aircraft in the area had experienced similar ride conditions.Upon arrival in ZZZ1; we coordinated with maintenance personnel to debrief Maintenance Control regarding the event and aircraft behavior observed during the turbulence encounter.
column123: While cruising at flight level 360; the aircraft began to respond with rhythmic yoke movement after encountering continuous chop and turbulence events. All appropriate actions to sit the FAs and customers were completed prior to encountering this area of turbulence. Both pilots discussed concerns with the airplanes rhythmic movements. We checked for any anomalies on the annunciator panel as well as the overhead panel. As the pilot flying I chose to request a heading to disengage the LNAV function in an effort to see if this was causing the rhythmic response. As we encountered more turbulence; the movements became more abrupt at which point in time the autopilot disengaged as the aircraft entered into a progressively building dutch roll. I immediately confirmed the auto pilot was disengaged and asked the pilot monitoring to request a lower altitude as I began to turn into the tail role slightly and then maintaining a steady profile with the wings while engaging in a slight descent to counter the roll force. I then asked the pilot monitoring to slow my bugged speed to .75 from .77 which correlated initially with N1 speed recommendations for the environmental conditions. After approx 30 to 45 seconds of dampening the aircraft's movement utilizing flight controls; thrust and speed reduction the aircraft settled into a level profile. During this time we were approved off of heading and into a block between 350 and 360 feet. Once reestablished we climbed back to 36;000 feet and engaged initially the heading function followed by the LNAV function; direct to our next checkpoint and on course; then finally the autopilot flight control systems. At that time we noticed that the Yaw dampener light on the overhead was illuminated; and the magnetic switch was in the off position. Checking again the recall there was no associated flight control light or the master caution annunciator. In accordance with the QRH; we performed the action procedures listed to reengage the yaw damper. There are no further actions or anomalies for the remainder of the flight. The captain completed the appropriate write-ups while we debriefed the scenario. Of note the encounter with turbulence as well as the rhythmic rolling motion; which led to the auto pilot disengaging; and what appears to be the disconnection of the yaw damper; resulted in numerous sick passengers as well as flight attendants in the back half of the airplane. These items were also addressed in accordance with the reporting profiles outlined in the FOM by the CA.

column121: For our flight we had an observer in the back right seat. As the student was initiating takeoff we started to veer to the left of center line so I appropriately added right rudder to get us back on course but when we lifted off; we heard the stall horn and my student added right aileron to get back on centerline. column121: Received the aircraft at ZZZ and determined it was airworthy after reviewing the documents and completing the preflight inspection. The flight departed ZZZ with no delays or issues. Approximately 45 minutes into the flight; we received a HYD 2 LO QTY" crew awareness message; but it disappeared quickly. By the time I opened the HYD synoptic page; it reappeared. When we first looked at it; the quantity in System 2 was at 20%; and we decided to monitor it for a couple of minutes. After 3-4 minutes; it dropped to 18%; and we realized it was actually leaking.We decided not to continue to ZZZ1 due to having roughly 450 miles remaining. The captain relayed this information to dispatch; and dispatch relayed it to maintenance. After a couple of minutes; we received a message directing us to divert to ZZZ2. The captain and I discussed the situation and came up with a game plan: I would fly the airplane and handle the radios while he informed the flight attendants and passengers of the situation; handled the new release; calculated fuel; and programmed the box.I quickly got on the radio and advised ATC; "We have a minor HYD issue and would like to divert to ZZZ2. We are not declaring an emergency at this time." ATC then gave me a heading and altitude toward ZZZ2.By the time we were at 9;000 feet; 250 knots; and approximately 50 miles from ZZZ2; the airplane was fully set up. We decided to review the QRH item "LOSS OF HYDRAULIC SYSTEM 2" to familiarize ourselves with it in case we lost all the fluid prior to landing. We came up with a plan to lower the landing gear early since we were close enough to the field and still had plenty of fuel remaining. One of the items we would lose according to the QRH was normal landing gear operation due to the HYD 2 loss; requiring use of the alternate gear extension lever. We also agreed that if we lost the system completely at any time prior to landing; we would discontinue the approach; run the QRH procedures; and return to land with the required items and equipment secured.I slowed to 230 knots; and we lowered the gear. Approach vectored us for the ILS XXR approach and asked about the nature of the problem. We advised them that we were not declaring an emergency at that time; but Approach provided priority handling. From there; I joined the final approach course and flew the ILS XXR approach into ZZZ2.Shortly after touchdown; we received several red and yellow EICAS messages; and both the master warning and caution lights/buttons illuminated. I did not pay close attention to them because we were in a very critical phase of flight; but I only deployed the number 1 reverser; knowing the lights and messages were related to HYD System 2. We rolled to the end of the runway to avoid overheating the brakes; exited at taxiway 1; and stopped on taxiway 2 facing east.Tower instructed us to switch frequencies to Fire/Rescue for communication. Shortly after speaking with them; we noticed the right outboard brake temperature rising quickly; and we asked them to monitor it in case it caught fire. We waited there for approximately 25-30 minutes; and the brake temperature eventually cooled off. We then taxied to gate XX; and the remainder of the taxi to the gate was uneventful."

I made my first radio call about 8 miles out; stating our distance in cardinal direction from the field and stated we were on a straight in traffic permitting doing a practice approach. We did not hear any traffic calls nor observe anything visually or on ADSB data. I called a 3 mile final; and about a minute later when we were on short final an airplane says they are taking the opposite runway (16) and will turn out early to the west to avoid us. Since we were basically on short final I cued up and said okay we will break off and turn out east to avoid the conflict. It appeared the aircraft was still barely rolling past the hold short line on the 16 side when I said this; so it seemed very obvious to me that he never made a hold short call and just decided to try to cut out in front of us. I would have happily broken off the approach early to accommodate him had I known he was holding but his first call did not come until he announced he was rolling opposite direction. He then berated me for turning east where the jump zone is. I am very familiar with this airport and know the hazards of the jump zone on the east side of the field but there were a few things going through my mind; #1 my first and immediate concern was avoiding the head on conflict created by the other pilot; #2 turning east was of course not my ideal choice but if my understanding was that he planned to turn west then I of course would not turn west myself and #3 I was very confident the jump zone was not active as I fly at this field regularly and am very vigilant regarding the warning calls the skydive pilots give prior to commencing a jump; so given all of these factors I made the decision to make an immediate turn to the east and continued the turn southbound out of the area. I think there should be some advisory circular or other relevant publication surrounding operations at the YOLO County airport in the event an airplane needs to take evasive action and side step towards the east side of the field.

column121: The incident began when the inbound aircraft was entering the alleyway. Because the ramp crew lacked the required number of wing walkers to safely guide the aircraft to the gate; the Marshaller correctly held up an emergency 'STOP' (X) signal to halt the aircraft's progress. The Marshaller consulted with me; asking if we should proceed with only one wing walker or hold for a full crew. I directed the team to wait for a second wing walker to ensure total compliance with safety minimums.I immediately radioed operations to report the staffing shortage and request assistance. While waiting; I noticed extra personnel at the adjacent gate and asked if they could assist with wing-walking duties. They agreed; and as we were actively moving into our proper positions to safely bring the aircraft in; I observed one supervisor walking and another driving in our direction.Once the team was fully in position and the aircraft was cleared to proceed; the ramp crew began actively marshalling the inbound aircraft into the gate. I was positioned as a wing walker; facing southbound toward the runway south of the airport; executing the standard 'proceed to next marshaller' signal. Because of this positioning; my back was turned to the southbound oncoming traffic in the alleyway. The arrival proceeded normally until the opposite wing walker detected an immediate hazard and threw up an emergency 'STOP' (X) signal with his wands. Recognizing the urgency; I instantly mirrored the emergency 'X' signal to ensure the flight crew received a unified; immediate directive to halt. The flight crew reacted quickly and brought the aircraft to a stop.Simultaneously; a truck traveling southbound in the alleyway failed to yield the absolute right-of-way to the arriving aircraft. The driver; seemingly unaware of the active arrival; breached the safety zone and braked heavily at the last possible second. The truck came to a sudden stop right next to my position; nearly driving past me and narrowly avoiding a catastrophic collision with both the aircraft and ground personnel. The immediate situational awareness and rapid communication of the wing-walking team successfully averted a major incident caused entirely by the vendor vehicle's failure to follow airport SOPs.Afterwards; we directed the truck to back up and clear the area. Once the hazard was removed; we attempted to resume the arrival; however; the pilot was unable or unwilling to apply enough engine power to get the aircraft moving again after the sudden stop. Because the aircraft could not complete its forward momentum into the gate under its own power; the crew followed procedures to safely secure the flight.

column121: Push back at XA:21; after engine start successfully; cleared off mechanic; gave marshaller a light flash and pulled up to hold short; I waved and cleared the marshaller off. The marshaller walked with the aircraft to the perimeter road and stayed… I attempted to wave off again but the marshaller stayed in position; this is common in ZZZ. The marshaller was indicating Affirmative/clear the entire time.Ground was very busy; we also had to complete our Takeoff Brief and Before T/O checklist due to the short distance between ramp and runway. I had pulled up to a safe position at the Hold Short. At approximately XA:30 we finally got a word with ground and were cleared to taxi.At this point; to my knowledge; we were not under marshaller control as I had cleared him off; I turned my taxi light on and began to clear left to right; the marshaller was still showing affirmative/clear and did not react to my taxi light; i didnt find this odd since to my knowledge I was no longer under marshaller control. As I cleared to my right and began to move forward a truck broke through the stop bar on the perimeter road at a high rate of speed (they had been previously stopped). I got on the brakes; confirmed idle and put as many lights on as I possibly could to notify of my movement. The vehicle immediately stopped.When I looked back to the left; the marshaller was still showing affirmative/clear; however another ramp individual standing behind the marshaller was actively waving on both directions of traffic. Once the marshaller figured out what was happening he gave me a Normal Stop signal.The truck that had jumped out began to reverse; but the traffic behind him also jumped and was occupying his previous space at the perimeter road stop bar. At this point both the marshaller and ramp individual were telling me to taxi on Clear to Move/Taxi Straight Ahead; however; we could not as the truck was not clear. After much pointing and waving to the direction of the truck; ground crew allowed all vehicles to go in front of us.This entire situation was rather unsafe; had the crew not properly cleared an incursion and collision was imminent; especially when you consider the Marshallese was indicating safe and clear (despite the fact we were not under marshaller controller). There seems to be significant confusion on the clearing off.We finally began taxiing at XA:33; 3 full minutes post taxi clearance. Ground did not query; however; I shouldve reported the incident to Ground Control and did not; this didnt occur to me until cruise and was likely due to how busy the ground frequency was.Re-Training should be accomplished on what clearing off is. A safety notice should be posted in the airport company pages warning crews of this exact situation and to remain vigilant.

column121: While on takeoff roll; as pilot monitoring; the airspeed readings on the FO's and Captain's PFD (Primary Flight Display) were grossly off. I saw the FO's PFD read an airspeed in the 40s while the Captain's PFD read in the 60s. I also noticed the FO's PFD did not read any airspeed until in the 40s. It seemed to be a delay not usual to any aircraft in the fleet. About the same time; the SPS (Stall Protection System) advanced message dinged on the EICAS. The Captain called 'Reject'; slowed the aircraft down without any harsh braking; I called ZZZ tower and told them we were rejecting the takeoff. Tower instructed us to make a right turnoff of the runway and to then stop on an adjacent taxiway to determine our next steps. The Captain called the Flight Attendant and made a PA to the passengers. The Captain also called maintenance and told them what happened; I overheard in the conversation that the Captain was deciding to return to the gate to have the plane looked at by maintenance. I called operations and informed them we would need to return to the gate. I then called ZZZ Tower and was given taxi instructions to return to the ramp and ultimately the gate. We parked at the same gate that we initially pushed off from. The passengers deplaned and we boarded a new aircraft which was taxing in to park next door to gate. I thought the Captain handled the reject superbly especially with low ceilings and IMC conditions. According to the Captain the previous crew informed him that the airspeeds were reading unreliably. The Captain included in his initial pre-takeoff brief a reference to what his intended action would be should he receive any abnormalities regarding any unreliable airspeed indications. The Captain also stated he would see brief 'check EICAS' indications on his PFD. I don't recall ever seeing this message appear on the FO's PFD.Cause: Unknown mechanical fault causing the airspeed indicators onboard to be grossly off in cross reference to one another; making any reading unreliable.suggestion: Repair the mechanical malfunction to the aircraft before placing it back into service.

column121: I had a near miss while landing a glider on runway XX at ZZZ Airport. There was a strong x-wind out of 280* that favored Rwy XX for glider traffic. I had announced entry to left-hand traffic for runway XX and after my announcement; I heard a faint radio call from a powered aircraft announcing that they were on base leg to runway XY. I continued my downwind leg to the south believing that the other Aircraft would be able to land on XY and clear the runway; especially since I was landing short and stopping at the 1000 foot marker;well before the turn off to taxiway 1. My base and final legs were normal; my passenger (a licensed glider piot) and I continued trying to locate the postion of the other aircraft; but we were unsuccessful. There were no further radio calls that we heard. It wasn't until we got closer to the threshold of XX when we realized the other plane was stopped on the west edge of the runway; right in the middle of the piano keys of the threshold. Because of the small profile of the Aircraft; (a Rutan Long-EZ) he was virtually invisible as he blended into the piano keys. I took the necessary evasive actions to avoid a collision; landed; and rolled out to clear the runway with no damage to either aircraft. The other Aircraft continued taxing on taxiway 2 back to his hanger where he put the airplane away. The Pilot admitted that he had heard our radio calls but offered no explanation of why he had continued to the south end of the runway and rolled out to the end of the runway instead of vacating rwy XY at taxiway 1. The aircraft was pointing towards us as we overflew it by ~20 ft. By the time I was able to get back to the hangar the pilot had departed the airport so I was unable to discuss the incident with him. The other aircraft was a Rutan Long-EZ.

column121: I was doing pattern work with a commercial student on a VFR day at FCM with a full pattern of about 4 planes. While about 6 or so laps in and making normal traffic acknowledgments when we had them in sight; we had the incident. On a touch and go we went upwind and got a traffic call to look for and follow Aircraft Y in the downwind. I called traffic was insight off our wing and waited a second for them to pass before turning crosswind. When halfway through crosswind and about to go downwind my garmin 750 showed a traffic alert and the controller asked to verify we still saw the previously called Aircraft Y. I then put the two together to look up about 300 feet and Aircraft Z was basically right above us so I dove down and did a 180 out of the pattern and alert the controller of my action and the issue. The controller said the fly out for a bit then rejoin the pattern with 180. I was very worried about the miss and getting in trouble. I keep thinking back and feel I wasn't wrong with my call based on the controller mentioning traffic in the downwind. One aircraft that I saw was downwind but the other the was missed and almost hit was in the crosswind and I don't called out. This miscommunication was unintentional but also risky and I plan to visit the tower to understand where I could improve next time and see where the mistake happened. If it was my error I believe a sense of being under their eye may have lulled me and also a confirmation bias from when I saw Aircraft Y he called. My garmin and ADS B didn't show tail numbers so I was not able to visually confirm who was who as I normally can too.
column123: To the best of my memory; there were three aircraft in the traffic patter. Aircraft Y was approximately midfield downwind; Aircraft Z was on an extended crosswind to downwind; and Aircraft X was in the upwind. I told Aircraft X his traffic to follow was an aircraft at his 10 o'clock; and he reported the aircraft in sight. I told him crosswind was his discretion to follow that aircraft; which he read back. He turned crosswind early and caused a conflict with Aircraft Y he was intended to be following. I asked him to verify he had the aircraft in sight and when he confirmed again that he had traffic in sight; I instructed him to maintain visual separation. After reading that back; he realized he had the wrong aircraft and informed me; and I told him to fly eastbound to avoid the conflict; and once traffic was no longer a factor; gave him a left 180 to rejoin the downwind. Recommendation:  It would be easier for tower to see these conflicts more clearly if we weren't set so far back from the traffic pattern; especially the north traffic patter which is busiest.

column121: I was inbound for landing at ZZZ after flying a 2 hour cross country flight with landings at ZZZ1 and ZZZ2.  I obtained the METAR at approximately 10 miles south of ZZZ around XA:50.  I did not realize the METAR was nearly an hour old.  The wind was reported as light and variable at 4 knots.  I requested vectors to visually fly the RNAV approach for runway XX from the approach controller as well as clearance for touch a touch and go.  I was advised to fly heading 040.  Later I was advised to intercept and hold at ZZZZZ; the initial approach fix for the approach.  During this interval I began experiencing heavy up and downdrafts which required more workload to maintain aircraft altitude.  I was circling in the hold at ZZZZZ from approximately XC:05 until XC:20.  During this time; I failed to obtain updated weather from the METAR due to my increased workload maintaining altitude.  I was cleared for the approach for runway XX.  While on short final; the tower controller notified me the wind was at 060 at 4 knots.  I realized I was going to have a crossing tailwind and briefly considered requesting to change runways.  Since the wind velocity was low I elected to proceed with the landing.  I safely landed the aircraft on center line without issue.  At this point I succumbed to plan continuation bias and applied full power; and raised the flaps to perform the touch and go.  I did not take into account the full effects of the tail wind and slight crosswind component.  As the aircraft accelerated; it began to excessively drift left of the runway center line.  My airspeed slow to build and was not adequate to rotate.  I aborted the takeoff; and simultaneously applied full brakes while setting the throttle to idle.  I attempted to correct for the lateral drift however was nervous to make excessive rudder inputs considering my speed which was approximately 40-45 knots (airspeed) and higher (unknown) ground speed.  Once I realized the aircraft was going to depart the runway I cut the mixture; placed the fuel selector valve to off.  I departed the left side of runway XX shortly after crossing taxiway 1 and entered the grass running parallel to the runway.  The aircraft continued through the grass. The aircraft entered the displaced threshold for run XY where if finally came to a full stop.  There factors associated with the incident started when I failed to get an updated METAR.  I did not realize how much time had elapsed or that my initial METAR report was old.  Had I received updated weather before I was on short final I would have changed runways.  I had committed to a plan and did not realized the changing conditions.  Additionally when the controlled advised me of the wind on final; I could have aborted the landing and requested to land on runway 090.  Finally after having the smooth and relatively easy landing; I had a confirmation bias that the take off would be the same.  I did not consider the additional take off roll that would be required or the effect of the cross wind which pushed me left.

column121: I was completing the competition landings flight for short field landing competition.Everything seemed as normal throughout the flight. I completed my first attempt at landings as the 3rd aircraft in a heat of 4 airplanes. I had noted on my second climb out that my location with the second position aircraft had become less spaced out than on the initial lap in the pattern. To remedy this; I spaced on my upwind leg significantly so there would be no traffic conflicts on approach. I had waited until position one of the heat had made their mandatory base call to turn crosswind. From this point; I continued downwind as normal; remaining vigilant of the two aircraft ahead of me. As I was on the first quarter of the downwind leg; I heard position 2 call their base. I observed an aircraft head of me turning base to final at this time. I reduced power as normal; added flaps and turned base once I was 45 degrees off of the approach end. I cleared left and right final before commencing my turn. Upon turning final; I had the Runway XX numbers in sight and pitch for 70mph and added flaps 40. Once I had been established on final for about 20 seconds; tower called and said 'Position 2 and 3 you guys appear to be pretty close.' At this time; I looked ahead on runway XX to the aircraft taxi off the runway at 1 and beleived the controller was referring to this.Seconds after the initial call; I heard 'Position 3 go around.' I immedietly commenced the go around procedure. Tower had asked if I had the aircraft in sight to which I responded 'I have them in sight now; apologies for not seeing them sooner.' I beleived he had been referring the aircraft I had seen taxiing off the runway. I then responded 'Will this next lap count as my second attempt?' beleiving since tower called my go around I would be alloted another compeition landing attempt.After taxing back to the shutdown box; I was met by the Cheif Judge of competion who greeted me with 'Hey.' I then said; 'Hey; tower called my go around' to inform the To inform the judges to count my second attempt of landings after the go around. He then responded; 'Tower did not call your go around; the judges did. Do you have any idea why?' Confused; and with the prior aircraft taxi off the runway in mind; I responded; 'Spacing?' He then responded sharply and said; 'You came within 100 feet of another airplane.'Shocked and confused; I stood next to the aircraft and was escorted over to speak with a pilot of another aircraft with the chief judge. The pilot had informed myself and the judge that I was so close; the pilot could see me through their sky light. I spent the rest of the evening confused and shocked until I heard more perspective from eye-witnesses. From what I understand now; the pilot in position 2 had extended their downwind base and final legs significantly. In fact; so far out that they had exceeded the competition pattern limitations by nearly 2.5 times. By the time I had turned based to final; they had extended so far out and were so low that they had become completely obscured to spectators on the ground; and invisible to myself in the aircraft. Based on eyewitnesses; on final approach leg; I had become positioned over top of the position 2 aircraft within 50 feet. I assume they became completely obscured at this portion of the pattern as the aircraft cowling was blocking them. I believe at this point; I had mistaken the position one aircraft's location which aligned perfectly with when position 2 had called their base. Competition landings operations are limited. For landings operations as a heat; only the lead aircraft is squawking and repeating clearances. This puts following aircraft at a disadvantage to identify the building of a near mid-air collision especially when aircraft competing leaves the published pattern limits which all competitors are thoroughly briefed on. This also limits tower's ability to identify this risk as well since only squawking aircraft appear on their scope. In a meeting with competition representatives; I brought up the possibility of having judges equipped with devices to allow a secondary location reference of aircraft other than visually. This would allow them to communicate with trailing aircraft when a aircraft ahead of them departs from the stringent pattern limits which would degrade not only an approach to landing; but safety in general. It is reiterated to pilots to space on the upwind leg; however this does not accommodate for aircraft who complete final leg segments twice the size of their upwind leg.
