column121: It was my take off out of ZZZ. Right as we were about to hit 100 knots or the high speed regime we got a master caution for and right side IRS (Inertial Reference System) fault. Captain said continue so I did. We rotated as normal. However as I started transitioning from flying visually to inside I looked down and realized I had the VERT HDG AND ATT flags as well as no flight director guidance. I glanced over and saw the captains instruments and flight director were there and working. Being a more critical phase of flight I didn't say anything to the captain yet due to not wanting to startle him more than necessary and I knew I could fly based of his instruments and visually. Once we got through 1000 ft and I knew we were safely away from the ground I stated that I didn't have any of that guidance. The captain said well let me take the plane and radios so you can run checklists to try to fix the issues. Once we transferred the controls I started looking through the non normals. I started by trying to look for any checklist relating to my instrumentation failure. I looked and read through display failure but we both stated this didn't make sense cuz the display was fine. After talking we said the first indication was the IRS FAULT light so let's start there. I started reading through that checklist and performing the actions it stated. It was around that time I realized we had performed a bleeds off TO and we hadn't switched the bleeds to the engines yet. So I performed that action before we got into any type of unsafe situation. Continuing that IRS FAULT checklist it had me turn the IRS selectors switch to both on left. As soon as I did that my side had all instrumentation and guidance once again. At this point we had leveled off at 270 because neither autopilot was working and they wouldn't let us into rvsm airspace without a working autopilot. I had sent a message to Maintenance Control stating our failures so that we could try to get the best guidance possible in trouble shooting. We transferred the controls back to me so he could talk to dispatch and manage the situation. Due to being 10000 ft lower than planned we weren't sure we would make it to ZZZ1. So we made a plan to go to ZZZ2 if needed based on how our fuel burn was going. We also made a plan to change controls back and forth so neither of us get too tired due to having to hand fly. We realized after a while we hadn't updated the cruise winds. Once we did that we realized we were right above bingo fuel. Then after flying a little while long we got below bingo so the decision was immediately made to go to ZZZ2. This entire time we were conferring with dispatch and they agreed. On the descent into ZZZ2 every time we started descending my vertical guidance went out on the flight director. So I again just used other instruments to back up my descent and every time we leveled off the vertical guidance came back on my flight director. Once we got on the approach both my vertical and lateral guidance went out. I was comfortable with flying it raw data and visually so continued flying to landing. Due to the added stress of everything that had gone on the entire flight and having to hand fly for over 4 hours by the time we got to the gate both of us felt somewhat fatigued and weren't sure if we really felt safe to continue. I talked to maintenance to add the failures on decent and approach to our list of failures we had already reported. While I did that captain called the chief pilot about everything and why we needed to do now. The manager asked how we felt and he said we are both on the fence. He went through the fatigue questions and he said based on those answers you guys aren't fit to fly and you are fatigued and will not continue. I don't think we did anything wrong on the flight in any way and I think we worked together well to divide or manage the workload. All of that added stress to flying and having to do so much more work than normal I know drained me which lead to me being fatigued.
column123: During the van ride to the airport; the FO and I reviewed the flight plan. The dispatcher notes included 'WILL NEED RWY XXL FOR TAKEOFF IF CALM WINDS OR WINDS FAVOR RWY XXL' and 'PLANNED BLEEDS OFF FOR T.O.' It was also noted in the release that the First Class Cabin outlets were inoperative. We mentioned the noise abatement as a possible reason for the opposite direction takeoff; or better weight/climb performance. Upon reaching the airport; we walked straight from security to the aircraft. Rather than stopping for coffee on the way to the aircraft; the FO decided to return to the terminal for coffee after stowing his bags on the aircraft. After briefing the flight attendants; to include the potential wait of an opposite direction departure and the First Class outlets; the FO had not yet returned to the aircraft. In the interest of time; I completed the entire initialization of the FMC; with the exception of requesting takeoff data. One of our ACARS messages had revealed a weight restriction; so despite the close proximity between the reserve and REMF (Remaining Fuel); I opted not to add additional fuel; and decided to wait until fueling was finished to request more accurate takeoff data. The FO returned with his coffee and then performed the walk-around. While on the walk-around; the gate agent brought down the reconciliation; and I briefed the passengers about today's flight. Upon returning; the FO began his preflight flow; and I went to the bathroom. When I got back; he then went to the bathroom. The flight attendants had completed their checks and were ready to close the cockpit door; but needed to wait until the FO was finished to do so. Once he returned to the flight deck; the door was closed. At this point; I realized that the autothrottle was not engaged; and so I checked the TAKEOFF page in the FMC and realized that neither of us had sent for the appropriate data yet. When asked; the FO stated that he had requested it; but our current weight was sending back an error for RWY XYR. As a result of his lack of initiative; I suggested that he send for numbers on XXL; as dispatch had requested. He did so; and it also returned an error for being overweight. The suggested value; was roughly 300lbs below our current weight; and due to the line of aircraft that had formed for a XYR departure; I was willing to accept this weight since our wait for an opposite direction departure would likely; burn enough fuel. He believed the weight for XYR was close; and so I permitted him to send it again. The required weight for a XYR departure was roughly 1000 pounds below that for a XXL departure. I told him to send for numbers at the maximum weights specified in the error; and if we got below the number for XYR before our opposite direction departure is permitted; we can do that. I also acknowledged that this weight would be extremely close to our required reserve fuel. Once he sent for a successful solution; I reviewed it and realized that the auto function for the bleed air was recommending a bleeds on solution. I then had him send for takeoff data forcing a bleeds off takeoff; at which point our current weight returned a valid solution for RWYXXR. We were past our scheduled departure time at this point; so we quickly briefed the departure; noting the threats of complacency from day-4; the bleeds off takeoff; and the line of aircraft we would be waiting in. Despite acknowledging these threats; I permitted the first error to be introduced by not requesting a more thorough brief of the clearance and SID; or verifying that the selected altitude was correct. It was not. 3000 feet was still selected from the arrival crew; despite our being cleared to climb via the SID; and the top altitude of the ZZZZZX being 13;000 feet.After completing the before push checklist; we notified the ground crew and pushed off the gate approximately 5 minutes late; and a line of approximately 8-10 aircraft had already formed. The ground crew advised us toturn on our lights; at which point the FO turned on two light switches. I did not verify which switches. During our taxi; the ground controller asked us to re-cycle our transponder. The FO had not turned on the transponder during push; and turned it on now. All checklists and callouts were accomplished satisfactorily through our clearance for takeoff on RWY XYR. During the takeoff roll; approaching 100 KIA; a Master Caution illuminated corresponding to an IRS (Inertial Reference System) annunciator. I extinguished it and verbalized continue; followed by the 100 knots; V1; and VR callouts. Once airborne; the FO directed me to retract the flaps and perform the after takeoff checklist. During final flap retraction; the FO verbalized that he had lost some of his displayed instrumentation. I assumed he meant his Flight Director; and opted to take the aircraft as my displays were operating normally. I continued to fly the departure and climb. Approaching 3000 feet; the Flight Director commanded a level off; as this was the altitude selected in the MCP (Mode Control Panel). I began decreasing power and leveling off as I recognized the VNAV ALT in the FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) and cross checked the MCP to deduce that this was not due to the departure. I grabbed the printed PDC and quickly located the clearance to climb via SID. I then resumed the climb noting the next 5000B restriction at ZZZZZ1. Due to the timing of this mistake; it resulted in neither pilot accomplishing the After Takeoff or No Engine Bleed Checklists. This small error that was not repaired during the briefing permitted additional errors to occur; contributing to a lower fuel state.As we continued the climb; the FO continued to troubleshoot his displays and I eventually became aware that in addition to losing the Flight Director (FD); the FO's ADI and HSI were black; with yellow ATT; HDG; and VERT annunciations; but accurate speed and altitude was still displayed. He began searching for a non-normal checklist associated with the malfunctioning display. At this point; I opted to take the radios in addition to flying the aircraft. Passing 10;000 feet I switched the sterile light; 'double dinged' the flight attendants; checked and verbalized that the cabin was pressurizing; and attempted to turn on the autopilot. However; the sterile light was apparently in the wrong position; so instead of turning it off; I inadvertently turned it on. I typically engage the autopilot at this time; but it failed to engage on either the A or B channel. I cycled the FO's FD switch; to make my source the master; and attempted to engage the autopilot again. It did not engage; so I continued to hand fly the aircraft. To prevent myself from overwhelming the FO; who was still searching for an appropriate checklist; I decided not to inform him that the autopilot was not functioning until it became pertinent. The FO reviewed several non-normal checklists and we deduced that they were not the correct checklists. At one point; the Flight Attendants called the flight deck. The FO took the call; as I had my hands full. They were asking why the sterile light had been turned on; and he notified them of our predicament; and I turned the light back off. This was the consequence of yet another error that was not repaired on the ground; adding additional complication to this situation. The flight attendants also informed us that in addition to the outlets being inoperative in the First Class Cabin; they were inoperative in the entire aircraft; all of the screens at the seats were inoperative; and there was no internet connectivity. During this time we passed FL180; and set 29.92 inHg at which point I chimed in that it is possible to use one of the reversionary switches to simply force my display onto his. In reviewing the overhead panel; the FO discovered that the bleed air was not appropriately set. He quickly performed the procedure to set the bleed panel without referencing the No Engine Bleed Checklist. He then set the gear; auto-brakes; and igniters to complete the After Takeoff Checklist. Thankfully the APU was still pressurizing the cabin despite being above 17;000 feet; and maintaining an approximately 5;000 foot cabin altitude. Although we repaired this error before it became an undesired aircraft state; we simultaneously introduced another error as the appropriate checklist was the No Engine Bleed Checklist. Therefore; the APU continued running.Returning his attention to the overhead panel; I attempted to help guide him to the appropriate switch while keeping my eyes on the gauges because I was hand-flying. I then mentioned that there are also reversionary switches on the dash; and perhaps it was one of those. He did move several of these switches but only the upper and lower DU'S (Display Units) changed; so he returned to the overhead. He eventually actuated several of those switches; and again got no positive resolution. As a result; I guided him back to the original indication - the IRS Master Caution. On the overhead panel; the R IRS FAULT and ALIGN lights were illuminated. He located the IRS FAULT checklist. During the climb; ATC eventually cleared us to an RVSM altitude. Knowing that autopilot is a required piece of equipment; I declined that altitude and was cleared to FL270. At this point; I filled in the FO that the autopilot was not functioning. After performing the checklist steps; the FO's instrumentation was restored; but the autopilot still would not engage; and the #2 transponder displayed a fault; so the #1 was selected. We interfaced with Maintenance Control via ACARS for any additional assistance. With the FO's display functioning correctly; I asked if he felt good enough to fly. He confirmed that he was; and I handed aircraft control over to him. We agreed to trading off who would fly every 30-60 minutes to avoid fatigue. At this point; I started my timer and began interfacing with dispatch about our options. This included requesting to transit RVSM airspace as a non-RVSM capable aircraft; which was denied multiple times. While at cruise in ZZZ Center's airspace; we discussed divert options with dispatch and opted to continue as the FMC computed FOB at ZZZ1 was 5.7; which was above the required 5.5. I also sent multiple ELB (Electronic Logbook) reports for the various issues we encountered. We also discussed the possibility that this was a larger electrical malfunction; as opposed to simply an IRS FAULT. I then realized that I had not requested new winds for our lower altitude. After doing so; our calculated FOB decreased. However; dispatch revised the alternate which decreased the required fuel to 5.1; which we were above. As a result of some storms in the area; we needed to use the Engine Anti-Ice; again decreasing our FOB calculation; now below the required 5.1. Shortly thereafter; the center tanks were emptied; the center fuel pumps were turned off; and dispatch notified us that an alternate was no longer required. The required fuel was now 4.4; and the FMC calculated to have 4.7 FOB at ZZZ1; so we continued. As a result of the inadvertent APU usage; the use of ENG ANTI-ICE at cruise; the variations associated with hand flying; and common fuel system anomaly associated with a decreasing FOB after turning off the center fuel pumps; our fuel total slowly decreased below the 4.4 FOB requirement. At this point; the decision was made to divert to ZZZ2. During our descent; the FO's instrumentation began further degrading. During descents in VNAV; LVL CHG; and V/S; the FO would lose his vertical Flight Director; but it would reappear at the level off altitude. I offered to fly as my display was functioning correctly; and he declined. I made sure to keep an eye on our flight path; and the FO was doing a great job without my interference. We were cleared to fly the visual approach to RWYXZR at ZZZ; and backed it up with the ILS. We discussed the possibility of his Flight Director malf

column123: While on vectors for the RNAV RWY 34 approach at HPN; leveled at 3;000 ft MSL; I observed traffic at our 12 o'clock position; approximately 400 ft below us. Shortly after; New York Approach advised us of helicopter traffic to our right; 400 ft below; which was the same traffic we had been monitoring. We advised ATC that we had received an RA due to that traffic. No further incidents occurred. We continued the RNAV RWY 34 approach and landed without further incident.Cause: TCAS RA triggered by helicopter traffic during radar vectors on approach. column121: We were flying into SDL. Winds were mostly calm but favoring runway 3 (I believe it was 320 at 3kt) and visibility was clear and unlimited. We do not have any approved approaches to this runway; so we were planning a visual approach using the Garmin visual". My partner and I both noted that the PAPIs for runway 3 are 4°. We also referenced the RNP Y & Z approach angles. We noted that the approach angles for those are both 3°. We are not approved for these approaches so we were simply referencing them for situational awareness and noting how they avoid the terrain to the southwest of the airport. Sometime during our approach brief we decided that a 3° glide path for the Garmin visual approach would suffice for terrain avoidance. We were proceeding to the airport from the west when we were cleared for the visual about 9 mi west. We cancelled IFR and proceeded to turn onto a left base for runway 3. We did this by proceeding direct to the "STRAIGHT" waypoint on the visual. My partner set a lower altitude; I forget the exact amount but I believe it was the Garmin calculated altitude that coincided with the "FINAL" waypoint. My partner engaged VNAV and APR mode. We began our descent on the VNAV profile. As we began the turn from base to final; the glide path was captured which I believe created a pitch down moment. It was in the turn and simultaneous glide path capture that we received at GPWS "terrain" and "pull up" alert. It took a moment of recognition but my partner disconnected the autopilot and we leveled off our altitude of approximately 3000' MSL. Immediately after level off; we stopped receiving the GPWS warning. Our pre briefed pattern altitude was 3000' MSL so already being there and having the GPWS alert stop; we did not perform a full escape maneuver. We also knew that the terrain was behind us during our level off. At this point we were still in a position to commence a stable approach; so we continued and landed without further event. Looking back there are a few things that I would have done differently. I do believe that we should have programmed the VNAV profile to match the PAPIs approach angle of 4° instead of the standard 3°. That would have given us more altitude over the terrain. I also think that we should have performed an escape maneuver. Even if it meant only climbing another 1000' it would have been the safe and correct thing to do. It also would have given us more time to do a lap in the pattern and re-attempt the approach with a 4° approach angle or a closer in base leg to avoid the terrain. Going forward; I will be much more caution of the terrain to the south west. We train and brief so much for approaches to runway 21 into SDL; but runway 3 should also be treated with equal caution. I do believe that perhaps we need a feasibility note or FOQA alert published for this runway and lack of approved published approach and the terrain. We simply don't have any guidance currently and perhaps a guided visual approach would be helpful in the future as well.Suggestion: I do believe that perhaps we need a feasibility note or FOQA alert published for this runway and lack of approved published approach and the terrain. We simply don't have any guidance currently and perhaps a guided visual approach would be helpful in the future as well."
column123: Going into SDL between XA:00-XB:00 local; the wind was slightly favoring runway 3. In SDL I have never landed runway 3. Looking at the available approaches there were only two RNP approaches that we were not authorized for. So we decided to use the visual approach the Garmin builds. We weren't worried about terrain coming in for runway 3 like we usually are for runway 21. We also did not see anything in the feasibility notes regarding suggestions for runway 3. After getting cleared for the visual approach we joined the visual approach set at a 3 degree glide slope. On a roughly 5-6nm final we got a pull up" message. Surprised; I deactivated the autopilot and pulled up. The message immediately cleared and we continued the approach; flying about a dot high or so the rest of the way. In hindsight there were things we could have done better. The PAPI's were set to a 4 degree glideslope and we should have matched the visual approach glideslope to that as well. The reasoning for keeping it at a 3 degree glideslope was the RNP approaches (although not authorized) used a 3 degree glideslope. So I am assuming the Aircraft's terrain sensitivity is part of the reason they're not authorized for the RNP approach's. Secondly; we should have flown a full go around and rejoined the pattern. This was agreed upon after landing.Suggestion: I would suggest adding a feasibility note recommending a 4 degree glideslope on the visual runway 3. Or I would suggest to join final inside maybe a 4nm final for runway 3."

column121: On takeoff from runway XXR (ZZZ long runway) with passengers; we aborted takeoff due to a Master Caution prior to 80 kts. This airplane had a current MEL for L FULL AUTHORITY DIGITAL ENGINE CONTROL (FADEC) FAULT (73-XX-XX-X) and was reportedly occurring during takeoff roll for another crew. Because it was already written up; we made a point to discuss the possibility that it may pop up again on our takeoff roll; but we would go unless there was a different Master Warning (red) or Master Caution (amber) prior to 80 kts. The brief goes something like this with the added discussion of that MEL:We will abort for anything prior to 80 kt.  • Between 80 kt & V1; we will abort for…  1.Engine failure… 2.Fire… 3.Red Master Warning… 4.Loss of directional control… 5.or Aircraft is perceived to not fly. • After V1; we will take it airborne. You'll fly; I fix; we can request headings; run our checklists; & come back & land on runway we are taking off from. If we need a longer runway; we can go to ZZZ1 airport.  • Questions/Comments/Concerns? After adding power and about 60-70 knots (it was prior to our 80 kt callout) I recall a chime and a yellow master caution redirecting my eyes to the EICAS; expecting to see an amber "L FADEC FAULT"; but it was an amber "L TR FAIL". I called out "Abort; abort; abort". My copilot's hand was still on the thrust so we aborted. There might have been a 2-3 second reaction time from when we saw the message to the actual aborting of the takeoff.The airplane had reported to the company we were close to or at V1 when the throttles were pulled back. It's possible that this was the case in terms of processing; communication and reaction time; but was not our intent if this was the case."

column121: I was operating from ZZZ as the First Officer and pilot flying. The aircraft was an Airbus A319.  It was the first flight of the day. Upon arriving to the aircraft; the plane had been powered up (assuming by maintenance); however APU was off; Pre-Conditioned Air (PCA) hose unplugged and tangled up by aircraft nose. The three temperature sensors in the plane read; CKPT 90; FWD 94; AFT 98". This became a top priority to try a cool the airplane prior to boarding. With the APU Bleed on; we were able to cool the aircraft and no issues noted. All things considered normal up until after engine start. We noticed Pack 1 was still showing a fault; but both myself and the Captain agreed it was probably a "sticky valve" and once we added a little bit of engine power; that issue would go away. Prior to calling for taxi clearance; the fault went away and everything was normal. However; when taxing out to the runway; the fault came back; but would go away when engine thrust was added and would come back again when thrust was brought to idle. This process repeated itself for about 3 cycles until we decided to tell Ground Control we'd like to pull over and troubleshoot the fault. The CA worked with dispatch and maintenance to eventually MEL Pack 1. Maintenance gave us the MEL 21-XXX "Packs Pressurized Flight (A319) X. Option 2 - (Limited Effectivity) (Speed Brakes Operative)". The main takeaway for this MEL is that the aircraft altitude is limited to Flight Level 370. The day prior; the same CA and I flew another very similar A319 with an inop APU and a MEL'ed Pack 1. The MEL associated with that flight was 21-XXY ""Packs Pressurized Flight (A319) Y. Option 1 - (Limited Effectivity) (Speed Brakes Inoperative)"; with the main takeaway from that; was it had a max altitude of Flight Level 310. Our filed flight plan for our flight was Flight Level 350. We had some discussions on what the differences were and why on one flight we had Y and this one we had X. We discussed the two different altitudes and noted our flight level was right in between them and would monitor the cabin altitude. But according to the MEL that maintenance gave us; FL350 was still legal and we pressed on. On the climb out the aft cabin was "ok" with temperature; but the front was high 70s/low 80s and the cockpit was 90°+; with the aircraft not cooling down on one Pack. While still in the climb to FL350; I started having the discussion on different possibilities to resolve this issue. We were in the process of reaching out to Dispatch via ACARS to send us a fuel plan with a much lower altitude so we could potentially use the APU Bleed to cool the plane off. During that time; we were passing FL330 in which the CA mentioned the cabin altitude passing ~8;000'; which then prompted him to immediately request a level off; then a lower altitude. Our descent started somewhere in the mid FL340s heading back down initially to FL330; never reaching our filed FL350. That's when we received the Master Warning and the "CAB PR EXCESS CAB ALT" ECAM. We donned the oxygen masks; established crew communication and continued the ECAM steps. I took the aircraft and the radios and requested a descent down to 10;000' and a westbound heading to get us heading back over land (our flight path was in a Northeast heading out over the water). The CA was busy with checklist; dispatch; flight attendants and passengers; so I initially elected direct ZZZ1 to have something to aim for. I'm not sure the exact altitude the cabin got to; but it was less than 14;000' because there were no issues or indications of a pressurization issue in the back since the passenger oxygen masks did not deploy and the Flight Attendants had no idea any issues were going on up in the flight deck. Once at 10;000'; the cabin altitude was back to normal (300' or so) and we were able to take our masks off; regroup and come to a logical solution for what would be next. Dispatch requested us to head back to ZZZ; which we deemed was safeand appropriate. We landed back in ZZZ with no further issues and taxied to the gate. Our debrief questions that we wanted answers for; 1. Was there any correlation at the start of the morning trying to cool off an extremely hot airplane; and essentially overworking the packs? 2. We still never received an explanation for the 2 different MELs and why they would have 2 different max altitudes?Cause: The temperature of the aircraft was unacceptable; especially with the plane already being powered up; a working APU (that was off) and working PCA which the hose was disconnected. It set the tone of the morning with; "here's something else we have to deal with." -Recommendation: With summer pretty much here; and with locations that are known for hot summers; planes need to be cooled prior to crews getting there.Having a fault while on taxi out is distracting; especially when running checklist and dealing with Ground ATC. To then have a fault that affects the cooling of the aircraft; which again was already an aggravation for the entire crew (flight attendants included). The cockpit temperature was extremely distracting; and it took away some of our situational awareness away with the Pack 1 MEL and the cabin altitude.Having essentially the same aircraft the day prior with the same issue(s); yet a different max altitude per a different MEL has huge expectation basis. Having a better understanding of what and why maintenance is giving us that MEL as well as addressing our concerns about the max altitude would be very beneficial. It's practically impossible for our specific situation where the CA is dealing with all of that while I'm monitoring ATC frequencies. No blame or fault to the CA; again for the reasons listed; but all of my questions came after he was done talking to maintenance and answers were left to interpretation of how we were reading the MELs."

column123: During climb; the forward flight attendant called and reported that she smelled smoke/fumes in the galley area and that she was not feeling well. I requested priority handling to ATC and told them we wanted to return to ZZZ. I had the FO send dispatch an ACARS message about the event and where we were going. I made a passenger announcement about the event while the message was being sent.We had no indications of a malfunction on EICAS. Our only indication of something abnormal was the smell/odor. We got an expected runway of ZZZ XXR from ATC. We got our performance data; briefing for RNAV Y XXR complete. Descent and approach checklists were completed a little late because we were low when it all started. The approach to XXR was completed normally as well as the landing. They reported that they found nothing and we taxied to the gate. Once the door was opened EMS was waiting. No one was in need of medical attention. Then fire department did a thermal scan of the galley area and found nothing. We deplaned the passengers normally and notified dispatch of the end of the situation.Cause: I am unsure of what cause the smell/odor/fumes.Suggestions: I don't have any suggestions at this time.

column121: Flight number: ABCD / ZZZ-ZZZZAt XA:07; ZZZ parking position was 1. Taxi clearance was received from Tower to taxi via 1 across Runway XX and continue via 2-3 to Runway XX. (Clearance from the tower was obtained to taxi via 1 across Runway XX and continue along 2-3.) The aircraft taxied out via 1-2-3 to Runway XX.At XA:14; the tower cleared the preceding aircraft for takeoff.At XA:16; the tower instructed: 'Aircraft X; cleared Runway XX line up and wait after arrival.'At approximately XA:15 at ZZZ; Aircraft Y was on short final for Runway XX.As CM2; I read back: 'Line up and wait Runway XX; Aircraft X.' Approximately one second later; I added: 'Line up behind; Aircraft X.' No correction or clarification was provided by ATC following either readback at the time.In a dynamic runway environment at ZZZ Runway XX; the crew's actions; including runway entry during the rollout phase; were based on real-time interpretation of the received transmission and a visual scan of the runway environment.After establishing position on the Runway XX centerline; the preceding aircraft had not yet cleared the runway. Tower then instructed the subsequent arriving aircraft to go around and advised that our runway entry was not authorized. We were subsequently instructed to vacate Runway XX via Taxiway 4 at ZZZ. The event was subsequently classified as a runway incursion.Contributing Factors (Human Factors)Contributing factors included ambiguity in the timing structure of the clearance phraseology ('line up and wait after arrival') in the context of operations on Runway XX at ZZZ; requiring real-time interpretation in a dynamic runway environment.VHF communication characteristics and associated audio conditions may have resulted in perceived audio degradation and reduced intelligibility of the transmission. Post-event review of recorded ATC communications was conducted using a high-fidelity audio playback system with slowed playback to enhance intelligibility. This review suggested that portions of the transmission may have been subject to audio degradation during high cockpit workload conditions; resulting in reduced transmission intelligibility.The flight crew independently perceived the transmission in real time as a Line Up and Wait-related clearance.The absence of ATC correction to two separate readbacks may have reinforced the crew's understanding of the transmission.At the ZZZ Runway XX 3 intersection; runway guard lights were available as the primary visual cue; and no runway stop bar system was present. The available lighting configuration provided limited additional visual confirmation or redundancy for runway entry verification between ATC and flight crews. This may have reduced an additional layer of defence that could otherwise assist in resolving ambiguity or reinforcing runway entry status during high-tempo operations.Safety Actions TakenContinuous traffic monitoring was maintained prior to runway entry at ZZZ Runway XX. No evasive maneuver was required during the event; and no collision or loss of separation occurred.Corrective Action / PreventionIn future operations at ZZZ; greater emphasis will be placed on positive confirmation of runway status prior to entering a runway under LUAW clearances; particularly when sequencing is referenced in conjunction with arriving traffic.Enhanced cross-checking of ATC instructions between crew members will be reinforced to mitigate potential interpretation divergence. Additional awareness will be maintained regarding VHF communication degradation and the importance of seeking explicit clarification when any ambiguity exists in runway-related clearances.

We were at an assigned altitude of 9000. Around that time the conditions started getting a little turbulent and I was trying to assist my student with loading the approach while he flew the plane (it was his first time in IMC and I just wanted him to work on flying). I normally keep very close track of his altitude so I can prompt corrections but got momentarily distracted loading the approach and getting the weather and when I looked back he was over 200 ft below altitude. This is absolutely my fault as I should have kept a closer eye knowing he struggles with holding attitude at times. As soon as I checked it; he noticed it and started correcting but by that time we were probably almost 300 ft low. Right then springs approach contacted us and advised to climb; check our altitude and low altitude alert. We immediately went full power and got back up quickly. This was not safe and I have learned a lot about when to step in as the instructor and how I need to be even more vigilant; especially when on an IFR flight plan as I don't want to cause traffic issues or terrain dangers. This was a r3ally big learning experience for me as an instructor and something I will absolutely learn and change because of.

column121: I was cleared for a straight in landing on runway 22 due to approaching the airport from the east. The active runway at the time for other arrivals was runway 12. I have flown to TUS a lot in the past. Normally after touchdown tower will instruct me to do a 180 on the runway and back taxi to alpha and contact ground / proceed to the FBO. Or sometimes I will be instructed to make a left on delta 3 and contact ground. In this case the controller was busy transmitting to another aircraft by the time I had slowed down so I made the first available exit which happened to be taxiway alpha 2. After vacating onto alpha 2 I realized I was now directly in the approach path / area of runway 12 with Aircraft Y on a few mile final for this very runway. I decided to hang another left and get clear of the area on taxiway delta to prevent a problem before contacting tower who then handed me off to ground. The ground controller did not mention anything about an incursion and instructed me to taxi along delta to the ramp as usual.The situation still felt weird to me after the fact however because while I taxied on delta to the ramp I crossed over a red marking on the pavement that said 30-12" that would imply I was just on an active runway without a clearance even though the taxiway turnoff that brought me here didn't say anything. After looking through other safety reports I am not the first person to get confused by the taxiway layout at this specific intersection despite having lots of experience operating here. When you are rolling out on runway 22 taxiway alpha 2 looks like a completely normal turn off. No special markings on the runway and no red signs for an intersecting runway approaching. Alpha 2 is also depicted like any other taxiway on the airport diagram on initial glance. Once you are on alpha 2 however you are on runway 12 and that becomes apparent when you vacate runway 22 and now see runway 12 right in front of you. When you then make either a left or right onto delta you cross over a pair of hold bars that read in red letters on the concrete "30-12" again implying you are / were on a runway even though the taxi diagram depicts it as a taxiway and there are yellow stripe markings on the ground. Upon review after the situation it appears this is known as a "aligned taxiway" which the FAA has since prohibited being used for new construction or reconstruction of taxiways presumably because it confuses pilots. There is currently a hot spot on the airport diagram for one side of the intersection however it does not mention the above scenario but instead only acknowledges that pilots tend to cross the hold markings when taxiing to runway 12 via delta presumably due to the uncommon layout of the intersection.I believe that something design wise visually needs to change at this intersection to prevent future issues and needless pilot deviations as in the case of some other safety reports. Pilots are misinterpreting the existing markings and signage and the airport diagram doesn't add much clarity to the situation especially when the hot spot marking is only on one side of the 3 possible incursion points. In the meantime the best remedy is a reminder to be very vigilant when taxiing near runway intersections and always making sure to have the airport diagram pulled up on an EFB or printed out on paper however in this case that did not help me since my immediate focus was on safely vacating the runway I had just landed on."

We flashed the flight plan on climbing to 110; but ZZZ didn't take the handoff in time.  We did not get permission to issue the IFR flight plan.  ZZZ called and gave us control as Aircraft X entered their airspace.  The climb to IFR avoided a potential collision with the VFR traffic.   Recommendation: D side training at the same time the R was training with busy and complex traffic had us all behind.  I should of stepped in the get control with ZZZ as soon as I realized Aircraft X was up on our frequency and we were taking action to avoid the traffic in ZZZ's airspace.

column121: Working combined positions as normal this early in the morning. Slightly more complex because of lower weather in ZZZ1 area but nothing too bad. Aircraft X was 1 of three aircraft being sequenced with the third being a flight school who had already requested an unusual pop up IFR and had been difficult to deal with. There was icing for the departures from ZZZ as well which the Aircraft X had experienced earlier adding  a bit of complexity. Again; nothing too unusual. The previous days had been bad thunderstorm days and I was working multiple extreme complexity sessions with metering to ZZZ and already was feeling pretty beat down and tired  by the week but was powering through. Aircraft X was set up on approach; read back correct. It was a 'T' shaped RNAV approach. I noticed almost immediately that he blew through the turn to final; but just barely and looked to be correcting which he said he was when questioned. At this point he's a few hundred feet below the Minimum IFR Altitude (MIA) but has been established and cleared on a segment of the approach and had been following the routing and altitudes fine.Shortly thereafter I realized his correction was wrong; he was well below my MIA as he was following altitude guidance on approach but obviously had 'slopped'/missed the turn to final and I issued the first low altitude alert. Aircraft X seemed confused and he asked 'was that for me?' to which I replied 'yes; low altitude alert; Aircraft X climb and maintain 080 immediately; approach clearance cancelled' he then began his climb. I showed him about a mile and a half south of approach course that he thought he was on. I then had to re-sequence the aircraft to make Aircraft X last. I was working multiple departures out of ZZZ while this was happening. Once getting him level at 080; I asked him about being off course. He said something about the GPS being weird at the turn to final; asked for the approach straight in. I told him he had to be resequenced which I started to work on. Feeling completely unlucky and beat down I told the Supervisor 'i need to get off position now' which could have been accomplished by breaking training that was on the adjacent scope D side that had no traffic. But they opted to let me sit there and wait for someone who was coming back from break in the next 5 minutes. So; I continued to work planes under stress and duress.Overall; I had already thought that there had been a lot of unprepared and unprofessional pilots this morning with the unexpected lower weather condition in ZZZ1 area. Was asked for visuals when ceiling was overcast 026. people filed to satellite airports with no approaches. Aircraft asking for inactive runways; approaches that are out of service etc. Pop up IFR's immediately after take off. Pilots are not preparing properly. Furthermore; taking action to get a controller off position imminently when they ask needs to be a priority of any means possible following an incident. Sure this wasn't the worst/most imminent incident but if a controller is saying they need off to clear their head; it is a safety issue for management to not take immediate action to address that.

I applied the brakes and set the parking brake to see the light illuminate. We moved back about 2 feet and I called the ramp agent to make sure everyone was ok and verified chalks. I'm not sure what happened; if I just  forgot all together to set the brake; if I didn't pull quite hard enough to set it; or if it just released on accident. I would like to say that usually the marshaller will give you the signal that the chalks are in. But the person marshalling us stepped away to put the chalks in. column123: After parking at Gate XX with wing walkers; we believed that the parking brake had been set. CA called for the Shutdown Checklist after we had both run our flows. Upon reading the first line item from the Shutdown Checklist (Parking Brake"); we noticed the aircraft rolling backwards and that the parking brake was not set. Toe brakes were applied and the Parking Brake was set. CA made contact with ramp personnel to ensure that everyone on the ramp was safe. The ramp personnel confirmed the red "brake" light was illuminated when he approached the aircraft to apply wheel chalks. Ramp personnel said when he knelt down to place the chalks; the aircraft began to roll backwards. The aircraft rolled approximately 2 feet backwards. We are still not entirely sure how it happened. Maybe the parking brake lever just was not applied fully or it was somehow bumped and released soon after being set. Either way; it was off when it should have been set; and closer attention should have been applied to ensure this. Luckily there were no damages or injuries.Cause: The overall cause of the incident was the flight crew not verifying that the parking brake was fully set before releasing the toe brakes and beginning the Shutdown Checklist. Complacency played a major role in this event.Suggestions: Be more thorough and attentive in all phases of flight. The flight is not over just because you made it to the gate. Don't rush to the Shutdown Checklist. Ensure that all flow items are fully completed and that the aircraft and its surroundings are in a safe environment before running any and all checklists."

column121: Flight from ZZZ on a A321T model. After number 1 engine start after our initial pushback from gate XX at ZZZ; we received Elec Gen 1 fault ecam message.  We followed the ecam actions to reset the Generator but was unsuccessful.  We asked ramp if we can hold our current position and the Captain called Maintenance Control to ask if there is another procedure to follow and how to proceed. We were advised to return to the gate for maintenance to board the aircraft.  After further inspection maintenance advised us that they were going to apply MEL (24-XXX)  They asked us to start the #1Engine so that they could disconnect the Integrated Drive Generator (IDG) as to their procedures. APU was checked and as per the MEL; should remain on for the entire flight. Additional fuel was loaded on the aircraft and we pushed back for departure.During our initial climb through approximately FL240 the APU did an auto shutdown. We accomplished our procedures and transfer of aircraft control from the Captain(PF) to the FO(PM). The captain proceeded with checklists and communications between dispatch and the cabin to come up with a solution. With concurrence from dispatch the decision was made to divert to ZZZ1; the closest suitable airport since we were operating on just one generator. We notified ATC  and started towards ZZZ1 airport while the Captain continued with the necessary checklists.  One of the checklists was for an overweight landing. Captain accomplished that checklist and we decided to request priority handling so that ZZZ1 would have the fire trucks ready to meet us upon arrival to inspect the aircraft.Approach and landing was without issues; landing at 180.0 lbs. speed at touchdown 145 kts and rate of decent 200fpm. Brake temps never exceeded 200 degrees after touchdown with brake fans on. We cleared runway XXL and after an inspection we were cleared to the gate.Cause: During the event I feel like our CRM was very good; reverting to our training. We worked together and had a positive outcome in the end. My one suggestion would be; even if some item is deferrable by MEL/Configuration Deviation List (CDL) doesn't always suggest that it is the correct action for that particular mission. In this case; we had a multiple hour flight ahead of us while needing to run the APU continuously. That in turn required us to have a bigger fuel load for APU operations and the fact that we restricted below FL330. It was a nice VFR day in Area X but it could have been the opposite. Operating on one generator could have been a whole different animal had the weather not been as good as it was where she had the failure. Also; the extra fuel caused us to be heavier than we needed to be; and luckily we were in a T-model A321; with less passenger seats. In short; deferrable doesn't always indicate a wise plan of action depending on the situation.

column121: Final approach into ZZZ on the RNAV XX. I received a low altitude alert from ATC after intercepting the final approach course on the RNAV XX into ZZZ.  I was cleared to maintain 2400 until intercepting; with a final approach fix intercept of 2500.  As I was intercepting; the aircraft continued descending; down to approximately 1500 MSL.  After receiving the low altitude alert from ATC; I immediately climbed back up to 2400.  I was handed off to tower; and did not have any further discussions with ATC over the matter. I was not given a phone number or asked to call ATC once on the ground.I believe I inadvertently put the autopilot into pitch mode.  I think it had to do with when I adjusted the altitude alerter.  I was descending to a clearance of 2400 while being vectored to final; but during my final vector I was told to maintain 2500 and cleared RNAV XX; which I asked ATC to confirm (because I was already below 2500) and they responded back with 2400.  I think moving my altitude alerter from 2400 to 2500 put me into pitch mode; which I did not catch.  I was fixated on the CDI as I was watching for my course to come alive and capture while I was turning to my cleared vector heading of 210.  Because of my fixation on the CDI; I missed that I had not leveled out at 2400.I believe the reason I went into Pitch mode is because I moved the altitude alerter from 2400 to 2500; then back to 2400.  However; because the autopilot in Aircraft X levels out (on the descent) 100' low; I believe I was actually slightly below 2400; as the plane was capturing; and then I moved the alerter to 2500; then back to 2400.Human Performance Considerations: I was alert; well rested; and otherwise in excellent condition for being PIC.  I was not distracted; but I did fixate on the Horizontal Situation Indicator (HSI) for my course capture as the plane descended well below the authorized altitude. I noticed the error a moment before and was just beginning to react when ATC issued the low level alert.To avoid recurrence: I need to not fixate and continue my instrument scan; especially during a critical phase of flight; and confirm Autopilot mode more diligently.

column121: The primary objective of the training flight was to improve and master landing techniques in the Pipistrel Alpha Trainer aircraft. At the time of the flight; I had accumulated approximately seven (7) hours of flight experience in this aircraft make and model.During one of the landing attempts; while on final approach at approximately 200 feet above ground level (AGL); I encountered gusty wind conditions that adversely affected aircraft control and approach stability. As the aircraft transitioned through the landing phase; I failed to apply sufficient aileron correction to compensate for the crosswind and gusting conditions. Additionally; I did not maintain adequate power to preserve the desired approach airspeed and positive control of the aircraft.As the approach became increasingly unstable; I delayed initiating a go-around procedure. Although I ultimately requested that my instructor assume flight controls; that request was made later than it should have been. During the landing rollout and recovery sequence; the aircraft momentarily departed the runway environment before control was regained and the situation was safely resolved. No injuries occurred; and the aircraft was secured without further incident.Upon reflection; several contributing factors were identified:Limited experience in the Pipistrel Alpha Trainer (approximately seven hours total time in type).Inadequate crosswind and gust correction inputs during the landing phase.Failure to maintain proper airspeed through appropriate power management.Delayed recognition of an unstable approach.Delayed decision to execute a go-around.Delayed transfer of flight controls to the instructor.Lessons learned from this event include the importance of maintaining positive aircraft control throughout all phases of flight; recognizing and responding promptly to unstable approach conditions; and executing an immediate go-around whenever approach parameters cannot be maintained. Additionally; effective crew coordination and timely communication with the instructor are critical to safe flight operations.Moving forward; I will place greater emphasis on stabilized approach criteria; crosswind correction techniques; power management; and early decision-making regarding go-arounds. I will also seek additional landing practice in varying wind conditions and will not hesitate to request instructor assistance at the earliest indication that safety margins are decreasing.This event serves as a valuable learning experience and will be used as a tool to strengthen my overall airmanship; aeronautical decision-making; and aircraft handling skills.

column121: I was conducting a long cross-country flight. Flew for a total of 8.2 Hobbs. Preflight was normal; no issues with aircraft; and set out. No issues for the entirety of flight; until nearly 30 minutes out from arrival back at ZZZ around 35 or so miles north. Minutes away from entry into the Mode C veil of ZZZ1 the transponder began turning on and off again; resetting itself. I tried turning it on and off to reset it; but it then refused to turn back on. I began skirting around the veil to troubleshoot; when shortly after the Garmin radio/nav setup failed. Thankfully; the aircraft is a analog six-pack so flight remained nominal. I immediately suspected alternator failure; and checked the ammeter; to still see it curiously showing charge. So at the moment; I simply suspected a Garmin system failure. I still had an alternate radio/nav system through Bendix/King setup; and I began getting the ATIS for ZZZ and planning the entry. Midway through that ATIS; that system died too and reinforced that suspicion of an alternator failure. Now with no comms; transponder; and navigation system; I thankfully had my foreflight pulled up and loaded with the flight plan and navigated off of that. During these events; I realized that with no radios; there was no way to enable the pilot operated lights at ZZZ. I began formulating a worst case scenario of calling ZZZ1 or ZZZ2 to communicate the issue through bluetooth and my Bose A20's; but I saw through Foreflight ADS-B In; thankfully; there was someone doing touch and goes at ZZZ and knew the lighting would be on. So I continued heading towards ZZZ; skirting the Mode C veil and staying low; and saw the lights were indeed on. From there; I decided it best to land at an airport with lights currently on that I was familiar with; rather than risk it at a local airport outside of the Mode C veil with no lighting; or to enter busy airspace with no lighting and transponder and disturb the heavy traffic flow unless absolutely necessary were ZZZ lights to go out and the manager not accessible via bluetooth. Also of note; I had around two hours of fuel remaining and was not in a critical emergency state yet. It was around the approach about 15 miles out I began testing the exterior lighting and noticed I had no strobes; no beacon; navigation lights were still oeprational; and I suspected my landing light was either out or would be out upon arrival. I entered the Mode C veil with no transponder knowing ZZZ lighting was still on and remaining hypervigilant to aircraft. The approach lights for XX remained on; and the prior aircraft had fully landed and taxied clear of all runways; when I turned a longer final. With no landing light and no operational flaps; we put it down successfully.After landing; and shutting down; I checked the alternator and belt and found no obvious abnormalities. I squawked the aircraft and reported it to maintenance for further investigation. Ammeter at the time was still showing a positive +1or2 amps of charge. Prior to shutdown.

column121: Day 0I am a recreational flyer; but I became a Part 107 certificate pilot last year to be knowledgeable about drone regulations.Around XA:00 today; I launched my DJI Air 3s drone by the field at Location X. My flight was for recreation; and my flight plan was to fly a short distance over the river to take a photograph of a landmark on the east bank through the 3x zoom lens on my drone.About a minute after taking off; I lost connection with my drone. As I waited prayerfully for my drone to reconnect and return; a law enforcement officer saw me and came up to me and informed me about a TFR that was in effect in the area. The officer was courteous and professional and explained to me that they had identified the drone and were able to use a radio signal to disable my connection as a safety precaution. After notifying me about the TFR; the officer asked his coworker to release the drone; which quickly returned to my launch point. They inspected it and gave it back to me.I had in my possession my driver's license; Part 107 Card; and UAS registration certificate as is required per part 107/the weight of the drone. I provided all this information to the officer; showed him the sticker on my drone that had the drone's registration number; my phone number typed on it; and an indication that my drone was remote ID compliant as per 14 CFR Part 89. I also showed him my DJI phone app to show him that I had not yet taken a picture that day.I take pride in being a responsible drone pilot; and I am reporting this incident because I think there was an error with my AutoPylot app (version 1.21.1) and possibly an FAA database that did not allow me to see the TFR on my iPhone.Prior to launching my drone; I used the AutoPylot app to confirm I was in Class G Airspace; was not in an area that required LAANC approval; and that I was not close to a no-fly zone.After packing up my gear; I started looking at my app to see if I had missed something. I am very familiar with what a TFR looks like in this app (red circle) because there is one regularly in place around the local stadium near where I currently live. I checked that my settings allowed me to see all map layers and they were active. I later closed and reopened the app and the TFR appeared. This is concerning because the law enforcement officer told me that the TFR was already in place when I launched my drone.I then searched the TFR.FAA.gov website for more information; and to my surprise; no TFR was visible on the map on this page (note: at the time I am writing you; it is visible for other areas which suggests to me that the website is functional). Additionally; no information related to a TFR is listed for today's date on the NOTAMs list for the area. In addition to this information; I want to assure the FAA that I am well-informed of the responsibilities of flying a drone. I purposefully chose my launch location due to my ability to maintain VLOS; fly during a time with appropriate lighting and weather conditions; and fly far away from people and boating routes. I am familiar with the area having previously lived nearby for several years; and I researched the latest regulations prior to my flight.Please let me know how if I can provide additional information about this incident.

We called clearance to verify no EDCT. ZZZ Clearance Delivery notified us we had a wheels up time in about 20 minutes. I called Dispatch to confirm and asked the Flight Attendants how soon they could board. I notified the gate agents to start boarding in 5 minutes. We started boarding all passengers with 2 flight deck jumpseaters. We pushed around XG36. After going through the normal pushback procedures; we were cleared to taxi on 1 to holding pad 1 where we would incur an ATC delay to ZZZ1. We decided to shutdown Engine #2 while we waited out our 30 minute delay. While taxiing on 1 and around the time of shutting down Engine #2 we received an ECAM for 'ENG 1 STALL'. While starting Engine #1 we noticed it hang up slightly and accelerate slowly from N1 45% through N1 52%. Once parked in the holding pad I called Dispatch/Maintenance Control for guidance and to see if they received any data from the aircraft. Maintenance Control advised us that they did in fact received an alert on the #1 engine and advised us to return to the gate for maintenance. In addition; I notified the passengers of the unfortunate news that we had to return to the gate now for Maintenance.Once ZZZ operations decided on returning us back to gate we notified ground and started the slow process of taxiing back to gate. I got out of the aircraft to speak with gate agent that we would need to deplane all passengers and that there would most likely be a gate/plane change. The mechanics came on board and debriefed myself and the FO. While passengers were deplaning I called Dispatch to inform them that Maintenance personnel recommended an aircraft swap (#3). The dispatcher informed us of our new aircraft #. I informed the Dispatcher that I would be notifying scheduling of a fatigue call. Prior to notifying scheduling; I notified the crew of my intentions.I subsequently called scheduling and was released from duty. column121: After a number of operational distractions on our first leg to ZZZ earlier that day we taxied out late on a single engine (#1) headed for ZZZ1. While on Taxiway 1; we attempted to start ENGINE #2 using APU bleed air and received an ECAM message indicating insufficient bleed air pressure. The start attempt was terminated. The ECAM message cleared without secondary indications. We attempted to start ENGINE#2 a second time with the same results. About the time the second start was terminated; an aircraft behind us reported visible sparks coming from the underside of the right (#2) engine.We stopped short of Spot XX on Taxiway 1 and requested a Crash Fire and Rescue (CFR) inspection through Ramp Control. CFR response time appeared longer than expected; approximately five minutes. There were a number of comm challenges with CFR but we eventually received an all clear. With a CFR escort; we taxied back to the same gate on a single engine; completed our inbound checks and deplaned the aircraft.After debriefing two mechanics we completed the Electronic Log Book (ELB) write-up. I instructed the First Officer to contact Dispatch while I contacted the Chief Pilot. Considering the cumulative distractions and threats of the day; I determined that the most prudent course of action was for my First Officer and me not to continue the next leg to ZZZ1.I communicated this assessment to the Chief Pilot; who encouraged me to characterize the situation as either fatigued" or "not fit for duty." I believe this situation is more appropriately categorized as a Human Factors issue and that replacing the crew was in the best interest of safety and operational decision-making. The Chief Pilot was resisting that assessment..Risk factors included:Late-night operationsHunger and cumulative fatigueMultiple maintenance and operational delaysEmergency response involvementReturn-to-gate following engine abnormalitiesLack of immediate replacement aircraft optionsElevated operational stress over an extended period.The Chief Pilot understandably may not have been fully aware of the cumulative operational context. In situations like this; management should rely heavily on the personnel with the greatest situational awareness: the operating flight crew.The Chief Pilot appeared uncertain and repeatedly referenced checking with Crew Scheduling and other management pilots. He later stated that he was relatively new to the position. Pilot pushing is rarely overt. It is not the Chief Pilot "putting a gun to your head." It is more subtle than that. It occurs when pilots experiencing and managing evolving operational risks; request support for a reasonable; fact-based safety decision; only to encounter resistance or hesitation from management instead of support for Captain's authority and the safety values.Pilots are highly susceptible to mission completion bias. For an experienced pilot to objectively assess the totality of circumstances and conclude that continuing the operation is not prudent is not a trivial decision. When that occurs; management should support that judgment."

column121: I was just made aware of the runway excursion on Day 6. In the morning of Day 0; two student pilots and one instructor pilot were practicing a soft field take off on runway XXR at ZZZ. The student pilot lined the aircraft up on the centerline for takeoff and; when cleared by ATC; started the roll down the runway. There was a right crosswind during the takeoff. We started the takeoff with proper wind correction; but as we continued through the takeoff; both Flight Instructor (IP) and Student Pilot's (SP) attention was on the pitch attitude for the soft field takeoff. The student pilot had entered an excessive amount of positive pitch; and the instructor pilot stepped in to help correct the excessive pitch and to maintain flying in ground effect; as our speed was getting pretty low. While making these corrections for the soft field takeoff; the IP did not input the proper crosswind correction; causing the aircraft to be blown off to the left of the runway. After getting the aircraft to a stable airspeed and pitch attitude; the instructor pilot then realized we were left of the centerline and maneuvered back to be lined up with the runway. During this occurrence; neither the instructor pilot nor either of the student pilots saw; felt; or heard any collision between the aircraft and any runway signs or lights. The instructor pilot stated to the students how unsafe the takeoff was; but due to being unaware of any collision; the instructor pilot did not file a safety report. The crew failed to do a detailed enough post-flight inspection and missed the signs of damage from the runway sidebar light on the bottom right side of the horizontal stabilizer. Although neither the instructor nor any of the students was aware of the collision with the runway light; it was made clear that there was impact and damage done to the aircraft's airframe. The Instructor is completing a recurrent training to take action and learn from his mistakes.

column121: The recent reduction in Merrill Field tower operating hours has created a significant safety concern due to conflicting information being provided regarding after-hours operations.Pilots are relying on published procedures contained in the Alaska Supplement and Merrill-specific Part 93 references; while others are reportedly receiving verbal guidance from FAA personnel that different procedures apply when the tower is closed. As a result; pilots operating at the same airport are following different expectations for traffic pattern direction; arrivals; departures; and traffic flow.This is not merely a regulatory interpretation issue; it has become a flight safety issue. Reports from local operators indicate that aircraft are conducting opposite-direction pattern entries and conflicting maneuvers based on differing understandings of the applicable procedures. In some cases; this has resulted in head-on encounters and other situations requiring pilots to take immediate action to avoid conflicts.Merrill Field is a high-volume airport operating within complex Anchorage-area airspace. During the Alaska summer season; traffic levels remain significant after tower closure; increasing the risk associated with inconsistent pilot expectations and non-standardized operations.Immediate clarification and dissemination of the expected procedures for Merrill Field when the tower is closed is needed. Whatever the FAA determines to be the correct procedure; it is essential that all operators receive the same information through official channels such as NOTAMs; FAA Safety Team publications; Alaska aviation outreach; airport safety bulletins; and updates to published guidance. Standardized understanding among pilots is critical to preventing further conflicts and reducing the risk of a serious accident.

column121: Experienced engine roughness and surging at cruise near ZZZZZ intersection; approx. 13 miles ZZZ. Symptoms included a rough running rough; and surged between 1000 and 2300 rpm constantly; the a/c was unable to maintain 6500' altitude consistently. Immediately I executed a turn to head towards ZZZ1 as I had it in sight and there was still some daylight left. To triage; I increased throttle to full; increased my mixture; turned on carburetor heat; cycled through the magnetos to check spark plug issues. I elected not to switch fuel tanks as the fuel selector was already on 'Both'. I also noted lower CHTs on cylinders 1; 3; and 5 per the engine monitor.I drifted down to 5000' and was able to maintain partial power approximately 5-10 knots above glide speed with engine surging. I contacted ZZZ Center and let them know I was having engine trouble and asked for vectors to the closest field (I did not elect for emergency services). Because I was able to maintain altitude; I determined it was feasible to head to the closest field which was ZZZ. I was able to make the field and performed a power off steep spiral into a straight in approach. Throughout the approach and descent I was never able to reestablish full power to the engine. I performed a ground runup with the engine continuing to sputter slightly. I believed it was either severe carb icing; or some form of vapor lock. I also inspected the engine post-flight and did not see any immediate damage to the engine or cylinders.I left the aircraft tied down and the operator's mechanic inspected the engine more closely. They discovered a wasp's nest in the fuel vent and a leak in the fuel line between primer. This likely caused excessive leaning of the mixture and a partial vapor lock. I did not experience any indication or symptoms of the oncoming failure during runup nor during the cruise portion. Oil temperature and pressure continued to be stable through the entire sequence of events. And no indication of fuel contamination or vent blockage during preflight inspection.

column121: On Day 0 and Day 1; I made 5 UAS flights totaling approximately 35 minutes from Location X. During this time; I was not aware of a TFR that was in place. I was attempting to fly directly up and hover my UAS over Location X for recreational pictures and videos. I checked the map in the DJI Fly app used to control the UAS and it appeared to show only a restricted flight zone for ZZZ Airport; which I was just outside of. The status indicator in the top left corner of the DJI control app showed green indicating good satellite connection and showed the message 'Takeoff Permitted'; which I believed confirmed that no flight restrictions were in place. I maintained line of sight; kept the UAS over private property; remained below 400 feet and believed I was following all FAA UAS operational rules. I was not aware of the TFR until the final flight when I was approached by law enforcement personnel.Reviewing my DJI app flight log shows the following:On Day 0; I made one flight for approximately 2 minutes and landed without incident. On Day 0; I made another flight for approximately 7 minutes and landed without incident.On Day 1; I made one flight for approximately 23 minutes and landed without incident.On Day 1; I made another flight for approximately 2 minutes; lost connection and the UAS returned to the take off point.On Day 1; I made another flight for 3 minutes. As the UAS was hovering I was approached by several law enforcement personnel. They informed me I was inside a TFR and directed me to land the UAS. I immediately landed the UAS and complied with all instructions. They informed me I should use an FAA approved mobile app to monitor for current TFRs and that the manufacturer's proprietary drone application was not sufficient. This issue was caused by inexperience; insufficient understanding of how TFRs work and the incorrect assumption that the UAS manufacturer's control application showed both temporary and permanent flight restrictions; which I now do not believe it does. I have no experience operating this UAS or other types of flight experience and should have waited but I was excited and wanted to try it out.In order to prevent this from occurring again I have downloaded the FAA approved AutoPylot app to remain aware of all NOTAMS and TFR's and I have completed the FAA WINGS safety course ALC-42: Airspace; Special Use Airspace and TFRs (Know Before You Go: Navigating Today's Airspace).To prevent this in the future; I believe training certification should be required to purchase and operate all drones. The extremely small size; low cost and ease to purchase my DJI drone gave me entirely the wrong idea about how serious the regulations are for its operation and I had no idea I could get into such trouble for its use.  In conclusion; I regret flying my drone before I fully understood its possible implications. I should have had a better understanding of the FAA rules and restrictions. Thank you for taking the time to read this and I hope it contributes toward something useful for the future.

column121: My student began to set up for eights on pylons; a commercial single-engine ground reference maneuver. The objective was to have her practice explaining and demonstrating the objective; tolerances; and execution of the maneuver. Her pylon selection was satisfactory. However; she was going to begin the maneuver noticeably low at about 1100' MSL where pivotal altitude today was closer to 1400' MSL. She was reminded of this and she climbed to 1400' MSL using the pivotal altitude table. She began the first turn a few minutes later which was performed well. She recovered to 1400' MSL and began setting up for the second turn in the maneuver. But in doing so; a combination of turbulence and overbanking caused my student to get too low. Overbanking in this maneuver causes pylons to seem to move forward; resulting in an illusion that the aircraft is higher than actual altitude. This prompts the pilot to push forward on the controls when otherwise unnecessary. My student was inadvertently overbanking the airplane (not keeping the bank fixed); resulting in a large descent to which I did not intervene in time. She was reminded to keep the bank angle fixed. In the process of instructing her to do so; we descended to 681 indicated altitude which I believe is below 500' AGL; prompting this report. Besides greater vigilance on behalf of instructors like myself who may find themselves too low; it is important to draw the line higher such that students do not get anywhere near the 500' AGL limit. Fixation on pylons and bank angle may be beneficial to the maneuver itself but can cause a loss of altitude awareness which has resulted in controlled flight into terrain in past general aviation accidents. I plan on drawing the line higher for students performing this maneuver; especially for students who are new to the maneuver from the right seat or students who have not flown the maneuver for some time.
